en: The *Vibhaṅga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), Scroll One.
Translator unknown; appended to the Later Han Records.
The verse spoken during the Jianchu era states: "Kāśyapa contemplates the root of the True Dharma" means that he contemplates...
The teachings and discourses of the sutras are extremely numerous. How is this known?
Kāśyapa immediately compared them to clarify their relative quantity.

The comparison of strength begins with ten donkeys: the strength of ten donkeys is not equal to the strength of one ordinary camel; the strength of ten ordinary camels is not equal to the strength of one ordinary elephant; ten ordinary elephants are not equal to the strength of one *sūkṣmapāda* (fine-footed) elephant; ten *sūkṣmapāda* elephants are not equal to the strength of one *caura-bhakṣa* (thief-eating) elephant; ten *caura-bhakṣa* elephants are not equal to the strength of one *padma* (lotus) elephant; ten *padma* elephants are not equal to the strength of one *nīlapadma* (blue lotus) elephant; ten *nīlapadma* elephants are not equal to the strength of one *raktapadma* (red lotus) elephant; ten *raktapadma* elephants are not equal to the strength of one *śvetapadma* (white lotus) elephant; ten *śvetapadma* elephants are not equal to the strength of one *himavat* (Himalayan) elephant; and ten *himavat* elephants are not equal to the strength of one *gandhahastin* (fragrant elephant).

From donkeys up to fragrant elephants constitutes one portion; in this manner, there are eighty-four thousand such fragrant elephants. Comparing the inner and outer surfaces of their hides, scriptures written to fill [spaces as large as] these numbers of elephants could be carried upon them.
Regarding the matters Ānanda has heard and known, their general outline and approximate total can be roughly discerned;
yet were one to attempt to expound each of their words and characters, one could not finish them even in a lifetime.

I reflect that the sūtras and the Dharma are exceedingly vast; how may they be caused to circulate throughout the world so that sentient beings for a thousand generations may receive the grace of the Dharma?
Contemplating this ultimate principle deeply, who is capable of compiling these teachings?
Only Ānanda was capable of compiling it.
Kāśyapa immediately struck the *gandī* to assemble the community.
At that moment, eighty-four thousand arhats arrived in response to the summons; these were all stainless ones who had attained liberation through both parts (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).
The reason these worthy sages and saints are summoned is that they are all fully capable of entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Those who enter this absorption can cause sentient beings to obtain merit in the present life and rescue them from their suffering and distress.
In the great trichiliocosm, the number of those who are free from attachment and the like is incalculable; excluding those in the three lower realms, each category is doubled.

Here, we record only those of sharp faculties who are liberated-in-both-ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) and who are able to deliver sentient beings through the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); for this reason, they are called fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
How is this clarified?

Formerly, when Śakra, Lord of Devas, reached the end of his life as his merit was exhausted, five auspicious omens appeared; his heart was immediately filled with fear, and he sought protection and deliverance.

Just as he was about to go to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek salvation, he reflected that while the Buddha’s grace is vast and patient, he feared his life would not be spared due to the urgency of the situation.
He then thought of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others, yet he feared they too might be unable to save his life.
Only Mahākāśyapa, through the power of the meditative concentration of total extinction (*nirodhasamāpatti*), was able to immediately rescue him from this peril; he went at once to where Kāśyapa was.
At that time, Kāśyapa was just about to go to a poor household to bestow blessings upon them.
Reflecting deeply, he wished to manifest his celestial body, yet feared that Kāśyapa would not accept his offering.
Thereupon, midway along the road, he manifested a grass hut and appeared as a weak and sickly man within it.
When Kāśyapa came to beg for alms, the sick man immediately reached out his hand and gave him food.
Kāśyapa received it in his bowl, and it transformed into nectar.
Then [the deity] returned to manifest a celestial body in the midst of the sky. Kāśyapa said:
"Why do you deceive me with a lie?
The deva replied, "I am not speaking falsely; I have given with utmost sincerity."
"I am Śakra, Lord of the Devas. Five omens have appeared and my life is about to end; therefore, I have come to seek a boon.
I pray that you will save my life.
Kāśyapa then silently consented.
When Śakra went to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma, he fell asleep for a brief moment; upon waking,
the Buddha said to the Lord of Devas,
“You have already died just now.”
"Now he has been restored to life and shall no longer die.
He returned to his original form;
this was precisely the manifestation of Kāśyapa’s power of meditative concentration in the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The reason why Kāśyapa’s power of the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*) is supreme is that Kāśyapa was originally a pratyekabuddha.

Now, the dharma of a pratyekabuddha does not involve teaching or transforming others through speech; it specializes in moving others through supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and manifesting transformations through samādhi.
Although Mahākāśyapa was an Arhat who had attained realization, his fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) still remained.
As for the eighty-four thousand followers previously recorded, their virtue and capacity for spiritual resonance were equal to those of Kāśyapa.
An objection is raised:
Because Kāśyapa was originally a pratyekabuddha, his superiority is extolled.
Are these arhats also pratyekabuddhas?
The answer is:
Although he is not a pratyekabuddha, he has extensively practiced the samādhi of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and his power is identical [to theirs].
For this reason, it is said that Kāśyapa and the Saṃgha are fields of merit for sentient beings.
The verse states, "All have attained arhatship with liberation of mind," which refers to those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

The verse states, "Having been freed from the place of bondage, they are fields of merit," meaning that the eighty-four thousand followers gathered by Kāśyapa all attained liberation both ways. Because the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) enables sentient beings to escape suffering in the present life and subsequently attain nirvāṇa, they are called "fields of merit."
The verse "assembling the four classes" is an abbreviation.
In principle, there should be four classes, indicating that there are further eight classes.
Humans and devas:
Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, and śramaṇas;
the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, Māra the King, and Brahmā—these constitute the eight classes.
There are twelve divisions in total; as for the mention of four divisions, this is merely a rough enumeration of their essentials.
That all phenomena are profoundly deep refers to the twelve links of dependent origination.
The Buddha explained to Ānanda that the twelve links of dependent origination are profoundly deep and subtle. Ānanda asked,
"In what way are these links of dependent origination so profound and subtle?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Do not say it is not profound and subtle.
In a previous life, you also said it was not profound.”
In the past, there was an Asura King whose body was eight thousand yojanas tall, with the upper and lower lips separated by one thousand yojanas.
The king had a young son whom he cherished dearly, often holding him in his lap.
The ocean is three million three hundred and sixty thousand li deep; the Asura stands in its center with his belly and navel level with the surface.
When the son sees his father, he considers the ocean shallow and desires to enter the water.
The father said:
"No. The sea is deep; it will swallow you."
Thus, wishing to enter, the father immediately released him; he plunged into the bottom of the sea, filled with terror and lamentation.
The father then reached out his hand and seized him as he emerged from the water, saying:
"I told you it was not possible, yet you did not believe me."
"How is he now? At that time, the king was my own self; the son was you.
In the past you did not believe in the profound; for that very reason, you do not believe now.
You should simply reflect that you cannot even comprehend that ignorance conditions volitional formations, let alone understand the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
“The Tathāgata has spoken of four inconceivable things. What are these four?
Sentient beings are inconceivable; worlds are inconceivable; nāgas are inconceivable; and Buddhas are inconceivable.”
Therefore, the world is inconceivable. Formerly, when Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was debating with a brahmin, the brahmin said of himself:
"Once, while I was reflecting by a pond, I saw four kinds of military forces entering through the hollows of lotuses."
He was immediately struck with wonder and astonishment, not knowing whether his eyes were playing tricks upon him or if this was actually real.
When he spoke of it to others, no one believed him.
He then went to where the Buddha was and said, "What I have seen is like this."
The Buddha said:
"This is a factual matter, not a falsehood.
When the asuras raised their fourfold army to battle with the devas, the asuras were defeated; they retreated and entered these hollows of the lotuses to hide themselves."
"This is beyond the reach of thought and deliberation; therefore, it is said that the world is inconceivable.
Regarding the world, some say it was created by Brahmā, while others say it was created by the six heavens."
The brahmins further say:
"Who created Brahmā? Some say that Brahmā has a father; others say he created himself.
Regarding the statement that there is a father, the father is the lotus.
If it is asked from where the lotus emerges, the answer is:
it emerges from the center of the *Uttara-kuru* continent.
"From where did Udayana emerge?
He replied, "He emerged from King Sañjaya.
Again he asked, "From what clan did King Sañjaya emerge?"
It was said that he belonged to the Kṣatriya caste.
Furthermore, it was said that Brahmā belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste; how then can you now say he emerged from the Kṣatriyas?
What kind of statement is this?
It is further said that at the time of the kalpa-conflagration, the coarse [elements] can be distinguished. Why is this so? It is said:
at the time of the kalpa-conflagration, from the surface of the earth upward to the fifteenth heaven, everything is utterly consumed and reduced to ashes.
It might seem as though it can be known;
however, there are the Thirty-three Heavens (Trāyastriṃśa) situated sixteen [yojanas] above, which, although burned here, remain in other worlds.
Judging by this, it cannot be known.
This is the inconceivability of the world.
What is meant by the inconceivability of sentient beings?

It is said that after the kalpa-fire has burned everything, water fills the place where the fire was; then, driven by the *vāyu* winds, palaces are constructed, beneath which there is "earth-fertility" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*).

The various devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven came down to the earth to sport; they gradually tasted the "earth-fat" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), whereupon their bodies became heavy and they were unable to return.
Those who consumed it in excess were transformed into women.
Gradually diminishing further to mere pancakes and grains of rice, they lose their supernormal powers and radiance, returning once more to the human state.
Good conduct leads to rebirth in the heavens; evil conduct leads to the three miserable realms. Thus beings transmigrate through the five paths of existence without any fixed standard.

Even if one wished to exhaustively investigate the fundamental origins of a single individual, one would still be unable to know them; how much less could they be conceived or measured in the case of all sentient beings?
This is what is meant by the inconceivability of sentient beings.
What is meant by the inconceivability of the nāgas?
All those who raise clouds and bring forth rain do so through the agency of the nāgas; does the rain issue from their eyes, ears, nose, and mouth, or does it issue from their bodies?
Does it issue from the mind?
There are also five kinds of devas who dwell upon Mount Sumeru and are likewise able to send down rain.
Why, then, distinguish between the rain of the nāgas and the rain of the devas?
Regarding "heavenly rain," that which falls as fine mist is so called;
that which falls coarsely is the rain of the nāgas.
What are the five kinds of heavens?
First, the Ekāṃśacara gods; second, the Mūrdhata gods; third, the Pramardaka gods; fourth, the Bali gods; fifth, the Cāturmahārājika gods.
When the Asuras raise their armies and ascend to heaven to fight, they first battle with the Kūṭadanta devas.
Having gained victory there, they proceed next to the summit, then to the Pramada and the Four Great Kings, and finally to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When the gods of the lower four heavens wish to fight, they repel the enemy with rain; they possess no other weapons.
There are two kinds of rain:
the rain of joy and the rain of anger.
Gently falling rain is joy; thunder, hail, and lightning are anger.
The asuras also cause rain to fall, the devas also send down rain, and the nāgas also cause rain to fall.
Each brings forth its own rain, and thus the principle cannot be fixed.
Therefore it is said that the rain of the dragons is inconceivable.

As for the inconceivability of the Buddha: once, when the Buddha was in a quiet chamber, various Brahmā deities, as numerous as the sands along the banks of the Ganges, came to where the Buddha was, desiring to know which samādhi he was in; yet they were unable to know in which meditative concentration or samādhi he resided.
Such secret matters manifested through supernormal powers are inconceivable even to those of the Two Vehicles, let alone ordinary people.
Ānanda deferred to the Elder Kāśyapa, saying:
"The Elder is capable of expounding the Dharma for the assembly."

The reason for this is that these elders and long-standing disciples are highly learned and well-versed in what the World-Honored One has entrusted; for the sake of future sentient beings, he wishes to ensure that the True Dharma remains long in the world, and it is for this reason that the Tathāgata offers him half of his seat.
"Since the Venerable One is the Elder of the Sangha and possesses vast and profound wisdom, we pray that you will compassionately bestow the Jewel of the Dharma upon us at this time.
The foreign master said:
"The reason Kāśyapa did not preach the Dharma was that among the four types of eloquence, he lacked the eloquence of speech."
It is further said:
He was originally a pratyekabuddha who manifested transformations through his supernormal powers (ṛddhi), yet from the beginning he did not expound the Dharma.
Kāśyapa declined the honor, saying that he was aged and decrepit, his mind clouded and prone to forgetfulness.
The answer is:
How could the true Dharma of the Four Noble Truths ever decline or perish?
It is like a diamond that cannot be diminished; rather, it is the four great elements of birth and death that undergo increase and decrease.
The Sarvāstivādins further state:
Among the nine types of arhats, those who are subject to regression do so due to how many factors?
There are four factors:
My years have advanced into decline, I am oppressed by the suffering of illness, I have a fondness for traveling afar, and my taking of medicine has been irregular.
It is due to these four matters that I have committed errors and lapses of memory.
"How could you forget the true dharma and sublime wisdom?
Kāśyapa exhorted Ānanda, saying:
"You are currently in the prime of your years, and furthermore, you possess the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of equality, and the power of dhāraṇī and strong memory."
"The Buddha has repeatedly instructed and entrusted you in his discourses.
For this reason, you must proclaim the Dharma of the sutras.
How do we know that Ānanda possesses equal wisdom?
Formerly, to the east of Śrāvastī, there was a great nyagrodha tree whose shade covered five hundred chariots.
In the city there was a brahmin who was proficient in the art of calculation, being the foremost among the ninety-five kinds of practitioners.
Meeting Ānanda beneath this tree, he said to him:
"People say that among the disciples of Gautama, you are foremost in wisdom."
"Is there not such a thing?
He replied, "What I know is but little."
He said: "I wish to ask about one matter.
How many are there in total of this tree's trunk, nodes, branches, and leaves?"
Ānanda raised his head to look at the tree and replied to him, saying,
"This tree has such-and-such a number of stems, nodes, branches,
and leaves," and then he immediately departed.
The brahmin thought to himself from behind:
"This śramaṇa surely does not know how to count, yet his answer upon seeing me was such as this.
Now I shall test him."
He immediately gathered sixty leaves from various places and buried them in the earth.
When Ānanda returned from his almsround, he asked again:
"I forgot to count them earlier; please tell me the number once more."
Ānanda raised his head and looked at it a second time, then replied,
"Why are the leaves on this tree so few?
He spoke again:
“How many are missing?
He replied, “Sixty are missing.”
The brahmin immediately joined his palms in reverence and apologized,
saying, “This is unprecedented.
He then asked again:
"Are you an Arhat? He replied, "No."
“Is he an Anāgāmin or a Sakṛdāgāmin? He replied, “No.”
“Is this a stream-enterer? He replied, “Why do you ask?”
He asked again,
"Do you have a teacher? He replied:
“There is. The prince of the True Pure Land who has left the household life and attained Buddhahood is my teacher.
He thought thus to himself:
"This is merely the teacher's wisdom; it is not what I myself know.
He then followed [the Buddha] to the place where the Buddha was, requested to become a śramaṇa, and immediately attained arhatship.
From this, one knows that Ānanda possessed equalized wisdom (*samatājñāna*).
The reason Ānanda deferred to Kāśyapa was that he was both the senior elder (*sthavira*) and his object of veneration.

In five hundred previous lifetimes, Kāśyapa had always been his father; thus, due to their long-standing recognition of one another and their deep-seated reliance on mutual respect, Ānanda held him in profound esteem.

The reason Kāśyapa was so earnest toward Ānanda was that he had accumulated profound karmic conditions in the past and left behind a legacy of grace for his successor; furthermore, Ānanda’s equal wisdom and powerful memory were preeminent among the assembly.
Among the eighty thousand scriptures collected as the legacy, none could precede these two.
The two were mutually indispensable, like the blind and the lame relying upon one another;
they benefited each other.
If two people suddenly encounter a single piece of gold weighing a thousand catties, and they wish to share it together, their strength is insufficient to lift it;
yet if they wish to divide it, they cannot apply enough effort to do so.
Thereupon, they deliberated together and joined their efforts to bring it back, whereby it was finally put to great use.
This may be called "mutual wisdom"; the analogy for Kāśyapa and Ānanda is just like this.
The two men were in perfect accord, and thus the Jewel of the Dharma endures forever.
At that time, Ānanda had preached immeasurable sūtras; who could possibly compile them all into a single collection?

These "immeasurable sūtras" refer to the twelve divisions of the canon, which are vast and exceedingly numerous. They were preached according to the occasion without regard for sequential order; thus, what was spoken as a single matter might be referred to as ten matters.

Sometimes ten matters are discussed while only two are analyzed; sometimes three matters are discussed while eleven are explained. When the sequence is disordered from top to bottom, it cannot be considered a single collection.
Furthermore, there are those who say that when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he may speak of exhortations, or speak of severing the fetters, or speak of being born among gods and humans.
Speaking from this perspective, they cannot again be considered a single aggregate.
Ānanda reflected: "One follows one, two follows two, three, four, five, six, and so on up to ten, causing each category of things to adhere to its own kind."
Some might say that such reasoning is untenable, for according to the Buddha’s own words, they cannot be compared sequentially.
Ānanda then reflected further:
"The teachings of the Sūtras are vast and extensive; they should be divided into three collections."
As Ānanda alone gave rise to this thought, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven secretly informed him, saying:
"It should indeed be divided into three parts.
He then followed what the deva had instructed and divided it into three portions:
One part consists of the Sūtras;
two parts consist of the Vinaya;
and three parts consist of the Abhidharma.
The *sūtras* are the teachings spoken by the Buddha;

whether for the sake of celestial kings and emperors or for non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners, they provide distinct explanations according to specific circumstances so that each may attain understanding and liberation.
*Kṣepa* (契) is like a thread; it connects and binds principles so that they become enacted laws, hence it is called *kṣepa*.
*Vinaya* (毘尼) refers to prohibitions and regulations.

For the sake of the two divisions of the Saṃgha, it expounds the examination of evil and the restraint of what is improper—whether consisting of two hundred and fifty or five hundred matters—citing the Dharma to prevent misconduct.
Just as a king’s secret treasury is not under the jurisdiction of external officials and is therefore called the "inner treasury," so too is this Vinaya-piṭaka;
it is not something that śrāmaṇeras or lay followers (upāsakas and upāsikās) may hear or see, and for this reason it is called the "Vinaya-piṭaka."
Abhidharma is the Great Dharma.

It is called "Great" because it is the great wisdom regarding the Four Truths and the vanguard banner of all dharmas; it severs all false views and the vast delusion of ignorance. Therefore, it is called the Great Dharma.
It is also called the "Peerless Dharma" (Anupama-dharma).
Because the eight knowledges, the ten wisdoms, and the untainted right view transcend the obstacles of the three realms and have no equal, it is called the Peerless Dharma.

Kātyāyanīputra compiled various sūtras, excerpting and condensing their essential wisdom and presenting it for the Buddha’s approval; therefore, it is called the Great Dharma Treasury (Mahādharmapiṭaka).
Ānanda further reflected:
"The meaning of these three piṭakas corresponds to the three liberations."

Why is this? The sublime wisdom of the Sūtras accords with the principle of emptiness; the Vinaya’s restraint of evil is darkly aligned with signlessness; and the right view of the Great Dharma traces its path to wishlessness.
Therefore it is said that the Three Piṭakas and the Three Liberations are the dark traces where the profound meets.
Ānanda further reflected:
"The great root of the Sūtras is divided into four sections according to their meaning."
Why is this? Because the texts and their meanings are intermingled, they should be arranged such that matters follow principles and the Great and Small vehicles follow one another in sequence.
First is the *Ekottarika-āgama*; second is named the *Madhyama-āgama*; third is named the *Dīrgha-āgama*; and fourth is named the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.
Taking "one" as the foundation, it proceeds to ten; as the numbers one, two, and three increase according to the circumstances, it is called *Ekottara* (Increasing by One).
As for "Middle," it is neither large nor small, neither long nor short; because the matters therein are appropriately moderate, it is called *Majjhima* (Middle).

"Elder" (Chángzhě): It refers to the narration of events from long ago, spanning kalpas without interruption, tracing the origins and details of their causes and conditions; as these matters have passed through the eras of seven Buddhas and the seven treasures of the sage-kings, it is called "long."

"As for the *Saṃyukta* (Miscellaneous), the various sūtras therein deal with the severing of fetters; they are difficult to recite and difficult to memorize. Because their subject matter is so varied and fragmentary that it easily causes people to forget them, it is called 'Miscellaneous.
After Ānanda had completed the compilation of the Tripiṭaka, he recorded ten sūtras as a single verse.

The reason for doing so is that, fearing those who recite and study in the future might forget or err, he has combined ten sūtras into a single verse so that by seeing the title they may recall the original text and awaken through their own contemplation.

That which is called the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) was not spoken by a single person; it includes what was spoken by the Buddha, what was spoken by his disciples, or what was chanted in praise by various devas. It also recounts past causes and conditions, such as the births of Bodhisattvas throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Because its texts and meanings are diverse and exceed those of the [other] three *piṭakas*, it is called the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
When the Buddha was in the world, King Ajātaśatru questioned the Buddha regarding the conduct of a bodhisattva.
The Tathāgata fully expounded the Dharma for him.
Suppose the king were to ask the Buddha:
"What is meant by 'Dharma'?
He replied: "Dharma is the Bodhisattvapiṭaka."
"All the various Vaipulya and orthodox sūtras are matters contained within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
During the time of the former Buddhas, these were already designated as the Mahāsattva Piṭaka.
That which was compiled by Ānanda is precisely what constitutes the present Four Piṭakas.
Taken together, these constitute the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

There is also one dharma-principle that is profound, difficult to maintain, and difficult to recite, such that one cannot even remember it: this is the dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It has no form and no image, and thus cannot be guarded or maintained; it is silent and soundless, without mind or thought, and tranquil, free from ideation. It is the foremost emptiness, for its meaning is non-dual.
It cannot be fathomed, hence it is called "difficult to uphold";
there are no words with which to respond to it, hence it is called "difficult to recite";
there is no intention with which to contemplate it, hence it is said to be "unthinkable."
What is called the profound meaning is as follows.
Furthermore, the "one dharma" is the root of all numbers.
One is the beginning of numbers, and ten is the end of numbers.
Finally reaching ten, it again begins from one.
Even when reaching ten million, it always begins with one.
In this way, these various ones are inexhaustible.

Within the various sūtras, sometimes a single meaning, a single dharma, a single practice, or a single event follows each other in succession without losing their continuity; therefore, it is said that "each follows the other in succession without losing its thread."
Regarding the two dharmas in relation to the two: some call them good and evil, some call them cessation and contemplation, and some call them name and form.
Cessation is the void; contemplation is the real.

"Stopping" (śamatha) refers to samādhi and meditative concentration; it is a state of profound stillness where conceptualization is extinguished and all mental attachments vanish in darkness, hence it is called "emptiness.

"Contemplation" (vipaśyanā) is said to be "reality" because, through its analytical discernment of practice, it clearly distinguishes right from wrong and good from evil, such that the mind remains unconfused; hence it is called "reality."
Regarding the three dharmas, there are three: giving (*dāna*), merit (*puṇya*), and reflection (*cintā*).
These three practices are the worldly dharmas for rebirth in heaven; the practice of the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*) is the dharma for reaching nirvāṇa.

Regarding all things that exist as triads—the three types of conduct, the three kinds of merit, and the three divisions of the Dharma-body—these three aspects follow one another like a string of pearls.
This applies likewise to the four dharmas in relation to the four, and similarly for the five.
The five dharmas follow the six; the six follow the seven. The eight dharmas have extensive meanings; the nine follow the ten.
From the ten to the eleven dharmas, these various numbers all correspond in the same way, with categories of two or three things following one another.
Ānanda immediately ascended the seat;
the seat was a lion throne (*siṃhāsana*).

The reason the sutra uses the lion as a metaphor for the throne is that the lion is the king among beasts, who always dwells on high ground and does not occupy low places; therefore, it is used as a metaphor for a high seat.

Furthermore, he took up his fearlessness: Ānanda possessed immeasurable and vast learning, being peerless and fearless among the śrāvakas; therefore, it is called the "Seat of Fearlessness. It was in this manner that Ānanda ascended the high seat.
Maitreya praised him, saying, "Excellent! How well spoken!

Maitreya did so because he feared that Ānanda might combine the Bodhisattva-dharma with the Tripiṭaka, thereby failing to distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles, and treating brass and gold as if they were strung through the same ring.
For this reason, I earnestly entreat you to divide [the teachings].
In the past, the Great Heavenly Holy King possessed the four Brahma-palaces; through successive succession, as many as eighty-four thousand kings all came to possess these Brahma-palaces.
Only Mahādeva alone is a mahāsattva; all others are merely men of minor character.
From this it may be said that the Mahāyāna is difficult to discern, as many follow the path of the śrāvaka.

Maitreya also knew that Ānanda had categorized the Tripiṭaka; nevertheless, fearing that future students would exclusively practice the teachings on emptiness to sever the fetters and attain realization, he therefore expounded the Mahāyāna and established it as a separate collection.
Therefore, it is said that the six perfections and various practices are the essential core of the Great Being’s vision.
Regarding giving, there are two kinds:
giving out of faith and giving out of fear.
When one establishes the faculties and attains patience, it is called "giving out of faith.
When one is coerced by external power and not by one's own mind, it is termed "giving out of fear.
That faith leads to liberation while fear seeks only merit—the distinction between the monastic and the lay follows naturally without needing further explanation.
That person said:
"Those who give away their heads and eyes are at the seventh stage or above;
those who give material wealth are at the sixth stage or below."
Those who regress from this do not fall back into the cycle of birth and death, but will surely reach nirvana.
How is this made clear?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) does not explicitly state it, but the *Madhyamāgama* says that sixty bodhisattvas attained the path of arhatship; this is the evidence for it.
Precepts like a vajra refer to Mahāyāna precepts;
precepts like an unbaked earthen jar refer to Hīnayāna precepts. Why is this so?
The "Vajra" is that which cannot be destroyed or broken.
In the past, there was a Bodhisattva bhikṣu of incomparable beauty who, while going out on his almsround, encountered a beautiful woman on the road.
When the woman saw the Bodhisattva, desire arose within her, and she wished to become his wife.
She then reflected to herself:
"This is impossible to achieve."
"Only when I sit together with you shall I resolve upon the unsurpassed aspiration.
Knowing the woman's mind, the Bodhisattva stepped forward and sat with her.
After a short while, he reached out and pulled her toward him, but the bhikṣu remained silent and did not respond.
He approached her again, but she remained as silent as before.
The bhikṣu then preached the Dharma of emptiness to her, saying:
"From where did the eye originally come?"
Where did it go? If you wish to say it came from your parents,
this eye did not exist even before they had met.
When it later perishes, where does it go?
From this it may be said that the eye has no inherent existence.
The same applies to the five sense faculties.
Suddenly and brilliantly he realized emptiness and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

One should have taught him existence, yet instead one taught him emptiness; the Dharma of a Bodhisattva requires entering into existence while teaching emptiness, and therefore this did not fully accord with his original intent.
At that time, Ānanda saw this bhikṣu sitting with a woman, which violated the decorum of a bhikṣu.
He immediately returned and informed the Buddha:
"I have just seen a bhikṣu sitting together with a woman."
The Buddha, knowing this beforehand, remained silent.
The bhikṣus, understanding that Ānanda had addressed the World-Honored One, said:
"We thought that if we did not go ourselves, those who slander us might fall into sin."
Just as he was about to manifest his supernatural power, the Buddha did not permit it; he simply flew directly to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"The bhikṣu who violated the Vinaya that you saw earlier is this very bhikṣu who has now flown here."
"Do you see anyone who violates their vow of celibacy who is able to fly?
Previously, when this bhikṣu was sitting together with a woman, she thought to herself:
'If this bhikṣu sits with me, I shall resolve upon the unsurpassed mind.'"
This bhikṣu, knowing the woman’s intention, sat down with her.
He immediately taught her the Dharma of emptiness, analyzing that the eye is empty, and that the five sense faculties are likewise so.
The woman was immediately struck with fear and attained the fruit of the Path.
Because fear had arisen in her mind and she was terrified of birth and death, she attained the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Had this bhikṣu previously taught her the practice of existence (saṃskāra), she would have returned to her original intention.

"By this matter, it is known that this bodhisattva has not yet attained non-retrogression and has not yet perfected the skillful observation of others' minds; this is what is called the adamantine precept."
What is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) means that when one is reviled or disparaged, one accepts it silently without retaliation.
When a bodhisattva practices patience, they always regard self and other as equal through universal loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Since self and other are thus made equal, there is no distinction between enemy and friend.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The compassion of the Hīnayāna is like skin and flesh; the compassion of the Mahāsattva penetrates to the very marrow.
How is this made clear?
If a person were to cut off a bodhisattva’s hands and feet, and they were transformed into milk, this would be a manifestation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The bhikṣu Kṣānti is an instance of this very matter.
It is like a mother who, upon giving birth to a child, immediately has milk flow;
this is what is naturally transformed by the power of such compassionate mindfulness.
Because the Great Being entered the samādhi of loving-kindness in this manner, he was able to cause the milk to flow.
When the practice of loving-kindness reaches its ultimate, even if one holds a bow and arrows, sentient beings will instead come to seek refuge with oneself.
When loving-kindness is not thorough, even if one does not hold a staff, all who see one will flee and abandon them.
Based on this evidence, the distinction between the Great and the Small Vehicles has existed from of old.
Regarding those who perform good and evil deeds: "performing good deeds" refers to diligently cultivating various meritorious virtues.
As for "evil deeds," it is as when the youth Agnika in a former life slandered Kāśyapa Buddha, saying:
"A bald-headed śramaṇa—how can he have the Way?
The Way is difficult to attain; how could he possibly have attained it?
Because of this, he subsequently underwent six years of diligent austerity before finally attaining the Way.
Within the Dharma left behind, the bhikṣus constantly engage in disputes; this is a retribution for speaking what ought not to be spoken.
As for the ascetic practices of six years, they were practices that ought not to have been performed; this too is a retribution.
These constitute the evil conduct of a bodhisattva’s body and speech.
Entering into meditative concentration and stillness, they remain serene and unmoving.

With wisdom, they know the number of motes of dust and the number of grains of sand in the Ganges River—countless even over billions of years; what is understood through their luminous insight is inexhaustible.
These matters of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are entirely contained within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka and should not be combined with the Tripiṭaka.
Ānanda wished to distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles through their respective causes and conditions, so that they would not be mutually confused.
The principle is inherently empty and difficult to clarify.
A Great Being who doubts emptiness does not take it as realization; thus, it is called "hesitation" (*hu-xi*).
*Fenbie Gongde Lun*, Scroll One.
*Fenbie Gongde Lun*, Scroll Two.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Later Han Record.
Regarding Maitreya being called "the Good One" (*śubha*): it is because he has compiled these great dharmas of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) as a single part.
This is precisely the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
"Severing the fetters" means severing all views, fetters, and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"Accomplishing the fruit of the Way" refers to the matter of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) in the Mahāyāna.
As for Ānanda’s speaking only of "hearing" and not "seeing," how could it be that he did not see the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma?
The reason he spoke of "seeing" as being incorrect was for the sake of the fourfold assembly of the future; thus, he was not permitted to say that he saw it.
If one were to say that he saw it, then the subsequent four assemblies would consider Ānanda’s statement that he saw it to be false.
For this reason, he merely says he heard it and does not say he saw it.
Initially, he preached the Dharma to deliver the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya; later, in the kingdom of Magadha, he subdued the three Kāśyapas. Śrāvastī is Kapilavastu.

If the location where a sutra was preached cannot be identified, one simply refers to it as being at Śrāvastī; this is because the Buddha resided in Śrāvastī for twenty-five years, which was longer than his stays in any other country.

The reason it has endured for so long is that its land is most exquisite and abounds in rare wonders; its people are flourishing and possess the highest sense of righteousness and principle; and the Jetavana Vihāra possesses extraordinary spiritual efficacy.

While the community of monks was gathered in discourse, several thousand monkeys came and stood to the left and right, listening in silence without a sound; likewise, all manner of flying birds gathered there as well.
When the assembly of monks had just concluded their duties and each had returned to his quarters, the *gandī* drum struck, and they gathered once more.
This was because the country abounded in benevolence and compassion, such that beings of different species would naturally congregate there.

The Buddha may sometimes temporarily accept an invitation, or he may, through his supernormal powers, adapt his manifestations and immediately return to his original location; for this reason, it is sufficient to refer simply to Śrāvastī to understand the essential point.

The reason for specifically mentioning the names of Jeta and the two persons who were solitary orphans is that these two individuals have passed away and now reside in the heavens, where they likewise assemble with the various devas to preach the Dharma and provide instruction.
At that time, they thought to themselves:
"We were originally the donors for this community of monks; why are our names no longer mentioned?
It was precisely because he wished to address their thoughts that he specifically named two individuals.
Regarding the statement that one should practice a single dharma, this is also not explained in sequential order.

If we follow the chronological account of the teaching of the Dharma, it should begin with the preaching of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, followed by the subduing of the three Kāśyapas in Magadha.

Because he addressed the name of the presiding monk of that vihāra, saying, "You should practice a single dharma," it is because the principle and flavor of this one dharma are no different from those of the four dharmas.
One dharma also severs the fetters, and four dharmas also sever the fetters; both lead to Nirvana, for though the paths differ, they reach the same destination.
There are twenty-one fetters in total, which are further expanded into thirty-six.
Although the numbers may expand or contract, they all constitute these fetters.

In every matter, there are one hundred and one relaxations, which further amount to eighty-four thousand; thus, whether it be a single dharma or ten million, they are all simply paths to the Ultimate Way.
It is like a lion killing an elephant or a rabbit; the death is the same in both cases.
Because their underlying principle is no different, one begins with a single dharma.
Heedfulness is the essence of this single dharma.
Someone asked:
"Precepts should come first; one ought to uphold the precepts before recollecting the Three Honored Ones.
Another said:
For a beginner, one first recites the Three Honored Ones, which is the Three Refuges; then, directing the mind toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one receives the precepts in succession.
Based on this, it follows that the precepts should be understood after the fourth stage of mindfulness.

Regarding "the thought of the suffering of the body in quietude," it means that by contemplating the thirty-six impure and loathsome substances of the body, one attains self-awakening and can thereby achieve the Way.
How is this clarified?
Formerly, there was a bhikṣu practicing the *āraṇyaka* life who went on almsround and encountered the daughter of an elder from whom he sought food.

Both the bhikṣu and the woman were handsome; when the woman saw the bhikṣu, she immediately gave rise to thoughts of desire, and when the bhikṣu saw the woman, he likewise conceived lustful intent. His mind being stirred, his hand trembled, and as he offered the rice into his bowl, he spilled it onto the ground by mistake.
The woman laughed at her own strangeness.
Seeing that the woman’s teeth were white, the bhikṣu immediately attained self-awakening and said:
"In a woman's mouth, there is nothing but bone."
As the Buddha said:
"Within the human body there are three hundred and twenty bones, six hundred joints, seven hundred thousand vessels, and nine hundred thousand pores."
"Entering through one aperture and exiting through nine, it leaks impurities; there is not a single thing therein to be craved.

Contemplating the thirty-six components of the female body with such earnestness, his hair stood on end in horror. As he focused his mind on self-examination, he immediately realized the emptiness of the body and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
He further thought to himself:
"It is because of this woman that I have seen the Dharma; she is my true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
I must now repay her kindness."
He then again explained to the woman the method of contemplating the body that he had previously understood.
The woman’s mind was immediately opened, and she also attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
From this it may be said that mindfulness of the body is supreme.

Regarding the mindfulness of death: one reflects that when a person’s merit is exhausted and their life comes to an end, they see omens of hell and are struck with such terror that they lose control of their bowels.
Whether they see the realm of hungry ghosts or the realm of animals, they are terrified by whatever destiny they perceive themselves falling into according to their past conduct.
Though the mind desires to depart, it is instead drawn back by its counterpart.
If one is to be born as a human, it depends upon the union of parents.
If one is to receive a male conception, one feels desire for that woman.
If one is to receive a female womb, one feels desire for that man.
Provided there is no illness or difficulty and these three conditions do not fail, one then enters the womb.
Once received, one identifies it as one's own; through a weekly transformation, the skillful winds carve and shape it until, at thirty-eight weeks, its form is complete.
If one is reborn in the heavens, celestial music will come to welcome them; unable to contain their joy, they immediately lose control of their urine.
These are the omens of the five destinies, each seen according to its specific nature.

For those who are about to die and must depart, even if they have already maintained clear precepts and deeply contemplated impermanence—realizing that life passes as swiftly as lightning or clouds drifting across a courtyard, and that no one escapes the arrival of old age, sickness, death, and loss—[they still face this].
One constantly contemplates these transformations to achieve self-awakening; therefore, it is called "mindfulness of death.
As for the ten preceding recollections, the Buddha himself spoke of them, and since no one had asked about them, they were not explained.
After ten recitations, the bhikṣus questioned the Buddha, who further expounded upon it, analyzing and explaining each point in detail.

As for the "venerable disciples," this refers to the five hundred arhats, each of whom excelled in a particular field: some were foremost in wisdom, some in supernormal powers (ṛddhi), some in eloquence (pratibhāna), some in merit (puṇya), some in observing the precepts, some in contentment, and some in preaching the Dharma—each being the foremost in their respective domain.

Regarding the principle of discussing the elder brother first and the younger brother later: Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the eldest, and Subhadra was the youngest; this is the essential outline of the stages of the Buddha-dharma.
If one were to take those who are wise, sagacious, and erudite as the leaders, this would indeed be the Dharma of the Brahmins.
As for the mention of "one thousand two hundred and fifty," this refers to those who are his constant attendants.

As for the statement that there were five hundred people: when the Buddha accepted the invitation from Lake Anavatapta, he selected five hundred suitable individuals who followed him immediately to the palace of the Dragon King. Why was this?
This Anavatapta Spring is not a place where those with outflows or obstructed forms can circulate.
When Ānanda compiled the sūtras, he assembled eighty-four thousand arhats; by this account, their number is incalculable.
This sutra is now being brought forth by exactly one hundred people; the foremost among them have mastered all four assemblies, each being the very best of two hundred and twenty.
As for the rest, how could they possibly be counted!
The person said:
"This sūtra originally contained one hundred matters, which Ānanda entrusted to Udāyin.
Twelve years after the *Ekottarika Āgama* was produced, Ānanda entered parinirvāṇa."

At that time, the bhikṣus each practiced sitting meditation and no longer engaged in recitation; they said, "The Buddha has three modes of action, and sitting meditation is foremost," and so they eventually abandoned their chanting and recitation.
After twelve years, the bhikṣu Udāyin also entered parinirvāṇa; consequently, ninety matters were lost from this sūtra.
The foreign Dharma masters have transmitted it among themselves through oral recitation alone, refusing to commit it to writing.
At that time, what was transmitted consisted of only eleven matters;
since then, the authentic tradition has been preserved solely in the extant text as it exists today.
Nevertheless, the Sarvāstivāda school lacks both the introduction and the final eleven matters; as the scripture wandered through the ages, much more has been lost.

The reason I specifically entrust this disciple, Aṅgula-mālya (Zengyi), is that he has specialized in the study of the *Ekottarika Āgama* since the time of the seven Buddhas; previous sages have likewise all entrusted him with this scripture, and for this reason, I, Śākyamuni, now further diligently charge this bhikṣu with it.
At that time, Udāra’s disciple named Sujāta had received and recited the *Ekottarika Āgama* from his teacher; he had correctly mastered eleven items when Udāra entered parinirvāṇa.
The Tripitaka masters currently existing in foreign lands are all those transmitted by Śākyamuni; teacher and disciple have handed them down to this day without interruption.
This is why Kāśyapa often referred to Ānanda as a "child," for he had treated him with the paternal affection characteristic of many generations of their lineage.
At that time, Ānanda’s sister was a bhikṣuṇī; hearing Kāśyapa’s words, she felt great resentment, thinking:
"Ānanda is intelligent and widely learned, one whom all people look up to."
"And yet you, Venerable One, call me a child?
Kāśyapa said to the bhikṣuṇī, "Sister!..."
Ānanda has two things that are shameful.
What is the cause for regret?
It is precisely because Ānanda urged the Buddha to ordain his mother that the Dharma was diminished by a thousand years; this is the first.
Ānanda had sixty disciples; recently, thirty bhikṣus returned to the status of laypeople.
The Buddha’s teaching on the method for ordaining disciples is that if there are those at home who possess faith and come seeking the Way, one should test them for seven days.
If those from outside schools come seeking the Way, they should be tested for four months.
Why are they not treated equally?
It is because those from outside schools may harbor malicious intentions, seeking to find fault; therefore, one first tests them to ascertain their utmost sincerity.
Otherwise, Ānanda, had you ordained them as soon as they arrived, this would have been a second cause for shame.

As for why these thirty bhikṣus returned, it was because they heard that among the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist paths, Ānanda was foremost in equal wisdom (*samatājñāna*); having come to seek ordination from Ānanda, they wished to request that equal wisdom.
However, because Ānanda did not explain the knowledge of equality to him, he felt it did not accord with his original intention and thus returned.
Upon returning, he was certain to slander Ānanda, claiming that he lacked the knowledge of equality.

The analogy of saving disciples is like a fish giving birth to ten billion or more offspring: if it thinks of them, they are born; if it does not think of them, they rot away. Disciples are also like this:
if one applies the mind to instructing and admonishing them, they achieve accomplishment; if one does not apply the mind, they regress.
"Is this not truly shameful!
Because this bhikṣuṇī harbored a mind of resentment toward Kāśyapa, she manifested her form and entered hell immediately.
It was because Ānanda possessed such a deficiency that Kāśyapa regarded him as nothing more than a child.
Ānanda himself recounted that in the past he had been a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Āyuṣmat.
Having received the final instructions of his father, the Great King, he ascended the throne and governed the realm.
As he was about to renounce the world, he further entrusted the Crown Prince, Suvīkṣaṇa, with the administration of the state.
This succession was handed down from one to another without ever being interrupted for a moment.
Formerly, it was inherited from father to son; now, it is transmitted from teacher to disciple.
In the past, they did not yet lose the teachings of the outflows (sāsrava-dharma); how much less now should they lose the most true and wondrous Dharma?
Therefore, he cites his own realization to demonstrate that they are certainly capable of receiving these bequeathed scriptures.
Regarding the instruction that one should maintain mindfulness and reverence for the Dharma:
in the preceding verse, the Three Piṭakas and the four Āgamas have already been distinguished.

Furthermore, in the prose commentary, it is stated that even within a single verse, all the dharmas of the Three Piṭakas can be fully contained; how much more so, then, could they not be contained within the *Ekottarika-āgama*?
The reason for this further section of verses being spoken is that a thought arose in the minds of the devaputras:
"Is it that Ānanda is unable to compose verses to preach the Dharma?"
"Why do you again utter such deceptive words?
Ānanda, knowing what was in the minds of the sons of the gods, said to them:
"Even if the sūtras carried by eighty-four thousand elephants were all composed in verse, I would be able to compose them all in verse."
"How much more so, Ānanda, could this brief teaching not accomplish its purpose?
It was because he wished to accord with the inclinations of the various devas.
Furthermore, he expressed all dharmas in verse to exhort and instruct the devas and those beings of sharp faculties who would attain understanding upon hearing verses."
The Dharma is that which was stated in the preceding chapter: "Commit no evil, practice all that is good, and purify your own mind; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
It is said that this Dharma can bring about the three vehicles, sever the three evil destinies, and provide the fullness of all fruits, yielding retribution in both worlds.
Because there are differences in the quality of their talents, they are provided with inducements to advance.
A verse says:
"Those of the highest caliber uphold the Tripiṭaka; those next best uphold the four Āgamas; or those who can receive the Vinaya-piṭaka—these are the jewels of the Tathāgata."

The reason it is called a "treasure" is that it is analogous to a king who possesses a treasury and does not allow outsiders to know of it; he entrusts its management only to his inner ministers who are of one mind with him.

The precepts are likewise: only those who can uphold the two hundred and fifty or five hundred rules are granted them; they must not be made objects of mere admiration for external laymen and laywomen, and are therefore likened to the treasures of a king.

If one’s strength does not equal that of those who master both Piṭakas, yet one merely upholds the Abhidharma, one will be able to subdue the non-Buddhists; among the ninety-six paths, there will be none that do not return to this school.
Why is this? This peerless and wondrous wisdom can resolve the most subtle obstructions, making them suddenly expansive, level, and upright.

Even those who possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and abide through kalpas cannot escape being constrained by the four deviations; therefore, those of external paths dare not even peer within its gates.
Ānanda’s chanting of these ten verses as a sublime exhortation was precisely for the sake of these thirty thousand devas and humans.

Long ago, when the Buddha had first attained enlightenment and was at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, turning the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths for the five men including Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya, the Buddha said: “Kauṇḍinya!...”
"You should know the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

When he spoke these Four Noble Truths directly, Kauṇḍinya had been mired in existence for so long that even upon hearing this teaching of wisdom, his mind was still not enlightened. Thereupon, [the Buddha] spoke of emptiness for him: "Kauṇḍinya!..."
"You should know that all things obstructed by the four types of wisdom are entirely empty and likewise impermanent.
They are like illusions and transformations—neither real nor existent.
Kūṭadanta immediately understood and attained the vision of the path.

The four men did not yet understand; the Tathāgata again observed the root of their minds and saw that two of them were ill with attachment to sensory contact (*sparśa*), dwelling on memories of the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) at home and indulging in them with self-indulgence, clinging to them and unable to let go.
Administering medicine according to the illness, he then spoke of the samādhi of non-conception:
"All that you conceive of returns to extinction; why then do you allow your mind to run wild, placing it wherever you please?"
As soon as they were so conceived, the two attained the fruit of the path (srotāpatti).

As for the other two, their minds constantly desired to be born in the Brahma Heaven and become kings there; because they were obstructed by these thoughts and could not release them, this became a further burden.
The Tathāgata, perceiving the state of their minds, further preached to them the wishlessness [of all phenomena]:
"That which you seek and aspire to—the sovereignty of the Brahmā Heaven—cannot provide ultimate liberation; it all returns to decay and extinction, for nothing therein exists eternally."
"You should abandon what you seek; making renunciation your priority is the foremost path.
Upon these words, they immediately attained liberation and realized the fruit of the Path.
The five men had each been obstructed by different things, and thus their respective understandings were not the same.
Regarding what are called the three turnings of the Four Noble Truths: within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), there are all four truths.
"Truth" (*satya*) refers to insight (*vipaśyanā*), while "concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to calm abiding (*śamatha*).
When calm abiding and insight are practiced in tandem, they together treat the disease of delusion and craving within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*).
The twelfth is the breaking of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, he preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly; sometimes he spoke of the Four Noble Truths and sometimes of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), expounding each according to what the sentient beings before him were to hear, without any fixed measure.
There were kings, householders, brahmins, and lay devotees who either invited him for offerings or came to inquire of him.
Regarding all that was to be said, Ānanda asked: "How is this named?"
"Should it be said that he heard it?
Or should it be said that he saw it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the future, when the Dharma is being preached to the fourfold assembly, one should say 'I have heard,' and must not say 'I have seen.
If one says 'I have seen,' it would be false. Why is this?
That which has been heard belongs to the past; that which is seen belongs to the present.
Just as it can only be said that the seven Buddhas of the past "heard" [the Dharma] and not that they "saw" it, so too shall it be for you in the future.
Therefore, it is said: "Thus have I heard.

The reason I so earnestly entrust this to Ānanda is that although the Buddhas of the past had attendants, none were like Ānanda in understanding the Buddha’s intentions. In the past, he had already made offerings to twenty billion Buddhas and constantly served as their attendant; yet he did not seek the exhaustion of outflows, but always vowed to attain equal wisdom (*samatājñāna*) to understand the Buddha’s intentions.
For this reason, one now receives its retribution: when beholding others' eyes, one must grasp their meaning without failing to accord with propriety and principle.
Among all Buddhas, none is more valiant and diligent than Śākyamuni; yet among brothers, Maitreya ought to be foremost, yet now he is instead at the rear.
Why is this? Thirty kalpas ago, there were three bodhisattvas who were traveling together upon a mountain.
At that time, they saw a starving tigress about to devour her own cubs.
One person thought to himself:
"This tiger is already an animal, yet it devours its own offspring; there is suffering in death, and this mother lacks compassion.
As for my current body, it is a composite of the four great elements and must inevitably return to death; I shall now use my own body to save the life of that cub."
The two refused to comply; they were just about to go to the market to buy meat to save their son's life when one of them reflected:
"If we go back and forth like this, our son's life will not be saved."
"I shall instead cast myself down from the mountain to save my son's life.
He immediately threw himself from the mountain top, rushing toward the tiger's mouth.
His body remained safe and sound, and the tiger did not dare to devour him.
The reason for this is that one who enters the Samādhi of Compassion cannot be harmed by anything.
Therefore, he pierced himself with bamboo so that the tiger might have food to eat.
Through such heroic courage, he immediately transcended nine kalpas and now stands before Maitreya.
Speaking from this perspective, the Way has neither beginning nor end; it is the resolution of the mind that comes first.
Therefore, now that I have attained Buddhahood, I entrust these bequeathed scriptures to Ānanda.
In the future, you shall be renowned for hearing [the teaching] in this way;
why then do you speak of "at one time"?
Is this a reckoning of days and months?
Is this a designation for a person? Answer:
It is both a reckoning of time and a designation for a person.
Some say there are two further names: either Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa.
There are again two further names: either of the Gṛhapati caste or of the Śreṣṭhin caste.
They may be in the heavens or among humans.
Since these various "may be" locations are not a single place, it is called "at one time.
*Bhagavān* is a title for the World-Honored One (*Lokanātha*).
Because his fetters and latent tendencies are entirely exhausted and none can surpass him, he is called the Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
All the devas of the three realms come to revere him as their teacher, and the eight classes of spirits likewise honor and respect him; therefore, he is called the World-Honored One (*Lokanātha*).
He who is able to subdue Māra is likewise the Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
Because such praises as these are immeasurable, he is titled the World-Honored One.
[This was spoken] at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Prince Jeta was the legitimate son of King Prasenajit.
He possessed a park and fields of eighty *qǐng*, where the ground was level and the trees were lush; many birds and beasts came daily to gather there.
Jeta kept his mind fixed on the Buddha and constantly desired to build a vihāra for him.
Before he had even finished his preparations, the elder Sudatta came again to request the purchase of the land.
Jeta was somewhat close with the elder and always enjoyed joking; thus, he gave his consent in jest.
Having received this prediction, Sudatta was filled with great joy. Looking back at his attendants, he said, "Quickly prepare the carriage and elephants; carry gold to spread upon the ground.
They immediately carried out the gold and gathered it to be spread across the land, until in a short while forty *qǐng* were completely covered.
Gṛhapati said: "Stop, stop!
I was merely speaking in jest; you need not spread this further."
Sudatta immediately went with the prince to the king’s presence and reported this matter.
The king said,
"The Dharma admits of no double-tongued speech."
"Once a decision has been reached, there is no reason in principle to regret it.
Jizi said, "I shall take the portion of the tree; you may then take the land."
"The two of you may together establish a vihāra, consisting of seventy-two lecture halls and one thousand two hundred and fifty rooms.

Within it, the ground shall be level and even, fruit trees abundant, flowing springs and bathing pools with water of temperate warmth, clear and bright in every direction, remaining unchanged through both winter and summer."

Having completed the construction of the city, they together invited the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One then dwelt therein with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, and the donors provided them with the four requisites without lack.
Because Ānanda-bhadrika was a high minister of that kingdom, he yielded precedence out of respect; therefore, in various sūtras, Jeta is always mentioned first.
Because their names are linked by virtue of their shared merit, and because they cannot be separated from one another, they are always mentioned together as a single designation.
Regarding the Buddha’s address to the bhikṣus:
why did he not address the laymen and laywomen, but only the bhikṣus? Among the fourfold assembly, the bhikṣus are the foremost;
furthermore, they are the masters in destroying evil, severing all outflows (*āsrava*) through the outflow-free dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*). For this reason, he addressed them first.
A bhikṣu is also called a śramaṇa.
A śramaṇa is one whose mind has attained rest; having ceased from worldly desires, he is tranquil and free from attachment.
He is also called a "remover of hunger" (pohiṇa), for while worldly people are famished by sensual desire, the bhikṣu removes this craving and the thought of such hunger.
The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma, and the bhikṣus are able to receive it; they sever birth and death and reach the gate of Nirvāṇa. For this reason, he addresses the bhikṣus alone.
"One should practice a single dharma" refers to mindfulness of the Buddha.
What matters are to be kept in mind when recollecting the Buddha?
The Buddha’s body is adamantine and free from all outflows; when he walks, his feet remain four inches above the ground, and the marks of thousand-spoked wheels appear upon the earth.
May all the insects and ants beneath your feet remain safe and secure for seven days; should their lives come to an end, they shall all be reborn in the heavens.
Long ago, there was an evil bhikṣu who was originally a non-Buddhist; he wished to don the robes [of a monk] in order to slander [the Dharma].
Following in the footsteps of the Tathāgata, many flying insects died where he left his footprints; people said, "He has trampled and killed the insects.
Yet, although the insects had died, upon encountering the place of the Buddha’s footprint, they immediately returned to life.

When he entered a city or town and stepped upon its threshold, heaven and earth shook greatly; a hundred kinds of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, and all manner of ailments—including deafness, blindness, muteness, lameness, and physical deformities—were naturally cured.
Regarding the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, those who behold them attain liberation according to their conduct.
The merit by which they are saved is beyond measure; how could the illumination of their wisdom-pristine clarity ever be underestimated?
The Buddha is the sovereign of all dharmas; he unites all practices, prioritizing the act of carrying others across.
Such is the meaning of "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānusmṛti). What, then, is the recollection of the Dharma (dharmānusmṛti)?
The Dharma refers to the outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), the desireless dharmas (*vītarāga-dharma*), the path dharmas (*mārga-dharma*), and the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);
it is that which leads from desire to the state of being free from desire.
The Buddha is the master of all dharmas; the Dharma is the master of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Someone asked: "Which came first, the Dharma or the Buddha?
The answer was:
The Dharma comes first.
How is this known?
As the Sūtra says:
The Dharma gives birth to all Buddhas; the Dharma produces the Buddha-way.
Speaking from this perspective, the Dharma comes first.
It is also said:
If this is so, why does one not first bring the Dharma to mind, rather than first bringing the Buddha to mind?
The answer is:
although the Dharma is subtle and wondrous, there is no one capable of knowing it.
It is just as if there were precious treasures hidden within the earth everywhere, yet people remained impoverished and lacked the means for their livelihood;
then a person possessing supernatural powers points out the location, enabling them to obtain these treasures to provide for themselves and relieve their destitution.
Someone asked:
"Which is superior, the treasure or the person?"
He said:
"It is because man prevails.
How do you say he prevails?
Though hidden treasures may be numerous, they cannot be seen without supernormal powers;
since it is through people that these means of livelihood are obtained, how could the precious treasury itself be considered noble within the earth?

The Dharma is likewise: although its principles are profound and subtle, they cannot be discerned without the Tathāgata, nor can they be fully expounded without the World-Honored One. Therefore, mindfulness of the Buddha comes first, and the Dharma follows as second.
What is the recollection of the Sangha?

The Sangha refers to the four pairs and eight classes of noble persons, the twelve virtuous ones. Having abandoned worldly greed and contention, they are the pioneers who open the way to merit. Among gods and humans, there is no path that is not traversed by them; thus, they are the excellent field of merit for the benefit and protection of all sentient beings.
How is it known that the Sangha is a field of supreme merit?
Formerly, there was a bhikṣu of meager merit named Brahmadatta who, being among the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty monks, caused the Sangha to be unable to eat.
Not knowing who was at fault, the Buddha then divided them into two groups.
Within one group, he further caused the other group not to eat.
He then divided this remaining group into two halves, and from within that half, he again caused the other half not to eat.
In this manner, they took turns dividing the food in half until there were only two people remaining, yet even they could not eat.
Eventually, he was left alone; only then did he realize that he lacked merit.
Wherever the food was served, when it reached his bowl, it would spontaneously vanish.
The Buddha, pitying their distress, personally took food from his own hand and placed it into their bowls; through his supernormal power, he caused it not to vanish.

Desiring that they might obtain merit while still in this body, the Buddha had the two bhikṣus who had attained extinction stand at his left and right, and he bestowed the food upon these two bhikṣus who had attained extinction.
In all cases of the samādhi of cessation, one immediately attains merit.

Next, have a bhikṣu enter the samādhi of loving-kindness and stand to the left and right; next, employ the two [samādhis] of compassion; next, the two of sympathetic joy; and next, the two of equanimity, causing each to take turns in succession until the four immeasurables are fully completed.
At that time, King Prasenajit heard that this bhikṣu was of little merit and that the Buddha had compassionately provided him with food.
[The king thought], "I too shall now provide merit for him.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to bring rice.
At that time, a crow flew in and carried off a single grain of rice;
the man rebuked it, saying, "The King is providing merit for Brahmāda; why have you taken it away?"
The crow then carried it back to its original place.
The reason for this was that because this bhikṣu had received the power of the merit from the Saṃgha, he could not be harmed by birds or beasts.
By means of this testimony, one knows that the Saṃgha is a fertile field of merit.
Having already attained liberation for themselves, they are further able to lead others to the path of the Three Vehicles; such is the significance of the Dharma of mindfulness toward the Saṃgha.
Next, as for the contemplation of the precepts, what is its meaning?

From the five precepts, the ten precepts, the two hundred and fifty up to the five hundred precepts, all serve to restrain body and speech and check various errors and deviations. By curbing the six sense faculties and severing all desires and thoughts, one becomes pure both inwardly and outwardly; this is what accords with the nature of the precepts.
In the past, there were two bhikṣus who traveled together to the place where the Buddha was staying. On their way, they passed through a vast marsh and were exhausted from lack of water.
At that time, there was a small pool of stagnant water, but it was filled with many insects.
A certain bhikṣu reflected deeply upon the prohibitions of the Vinaya, prioritizing non-violation above all else:
"If I drink this water, many living beings will be killed.
I would rather perish for the sake of preserving my precepts than die with regret."
Thereupon, his life ended and he was immediately reborn in the heavens.
A certain bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I should drink water to preserve my life so that I may reach the presence of the Buddha."
"How can one know what realm one will be reborn in after death?
He then drank the water containing insects, killing a great many of them.
Although he was able to see the Buddha, he remained far removed from the Teaching; weeping toward the Buddha, he said to himself:
"A companion of mine has passed away.
The Buddha pointed upward toward the heavens and said,
"Do you recognize this deva?"
"These are your companions.
By the power of observing the precepts in their entirety, they were reborn in the heavens and have now come here.
Although you see me, you are still very far from me."
"Though he has lost his life, he remains constantly within me.
That you have come now to see me is merely to behold my physical form; how could you recognize the ultimate, wondrous precepts?"
Speaking from this perspective, by upholding the precepts without transgression, one shall attain whatever is wished for.
Among the ten recollections, the precepts come first; among the six perfections, giving comes first.

The reason why the sequence is not equal is that the "Ten Recitations Precept" belongs to the tradition of the Śrāvakas; since the Dharma for disciples prioritizes the restraint of the body, it is placed first.
For the Dharma of the Mahāsattva, generosity is paramount. Why is this?

A Mahāsattva is one who is born among gods and humans with the intent to provide relief and benefit; as for the essentials of providing relief and benefit, there is no means of salvation other than giving.

Now, for sentient beings who preserve their lives, clothing and food are of primary concern; therefore, through the gift of material wealth, one first rescues their physical form, and subsequently, through the Dharma, one guides and governs their spirit. Thus, the Mahāsattva prioritizes giving.
Now, there are two kinds of precepts:
there are mundane precepts and there are supramundane precepts.
The five precepts and the ten wholesome actions constitute mundane precepts; the three samādhis constitute supramundane precepts.
The two hundred and fifty precepts up to the five hundred precepts are likewise mundane precepts; the sublime wisdom of the Four Noble Truths constitutes the precepts of the Path.

Merely practicing and maintaining these precepts does not lead one out of the three realms; it is by employing wisdom to govern the precepts that they become untainted (anāsrava), thereby conforming to the precepts of the Path.
The precepts of the Śrāvaka school are like flowers upon one's lap; they scatter as soon as one moves.
The precepts of the Mahāsattva are like flowers worn in the hair; they remain unmoved whether walking or standing still.
Why is this? Those of the Lesser Vehicle restrain their physical forms, such that any movement transgresses ritual decorum.
Great Beings govern their minds, and thus are not bound by external rules.

Because their scales and models differ, they are distinguished by their physical forms and minds; yet, despite these internal and external differences, both reach Nirvana—this is why it is called "mindfulness of precepts.
As for why mindfulness of giving leads to the attainment of Nirvana, it is because giving consists of both material giving and the giving of the Dharma.
By means of the gift of material wealth, one attains the gift of the Dharma; because one fulfills the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one reaches nirvāṇa.
As for "recollection of the heavens," this refers to the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are two kinds of devas:
those who enjoy merit and those who possess the Way and virtue.
The *srotāpanna* devas of the desire realm have forever departed from the three evil realms and advance upward into the Hall of the Path.

In the realm of form, within the eight heavens of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), those who further cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* advance to achieve the untainted state (*anāsrava*) and attain *nirvāṇa* right there, never returning to the world of transmigration.

As for the ordinary beings among the gods—those who dwell in the ten wholesome paths of action, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments—they receive blessings therein; yet when their blessings are exhausted, they fall back down, wandering through saṃsāra without end.

What is called "recollection of the devas" (devatānusmṛti) means recollecting those who have attained the Path, concentrating one's mind to emulate them and yearning for their conduct; with the mind neither wandering nor distracted, one likewise reaches Nirvana—therefore it is called "recollection of the devas."
"Mindfulness of cessation" means that the mental activities and perceptions have ceased; because the five desires do not arise and one is tranquil and permanently settled, it is called "cessation.
Generally, there are two kinds of cessation:
the externalist brahmins who restrain their physical forms to seek merit also speak of "cessation."
For the Śramaṇa, the fetters of the four fruits are eternally extinguished;
this is true cessation. How do we know this is so?
Formerly, there was a bhikṣu named Sūrata, who traveled throughout the city of Śrāvastī to teach and transform others.
At that time, to the west of Śrāvastī, at the place where Aṅgulimāla used to kill people, there was a level and spacious area with many trees.
