At that time, there was a brahmin sitting in meditation beneath a tree; he did not eat the five grains but subsisted only on fruits and gourds, and if there were no fruit, he would eat grass and vegetables to sustain his vital energy.
Clad in garments of tree leaves, his body was emaciated and could barely support itself.
At that time, Śūra passed by and saw him; thinking he was a practitioner of the Way, he sat in meditation to test his mind and discern whether he was in a state of concentration.
Seeing that his original intention was to seek the position of this king, he thought:
"Is this man not a great thief?"
Just as he was about to depart, he feared that he might later fall into transgression;
yet if he were to attempt to transform him, the man would certainly not follow his words.
"I must employ skillful means to deliver this person," he thought.
He then sat in meditation beneath a tree; not far away, he remained for seven days without moving or wavering.
After the seven days had passed, he rose and went before the brahmin, snapping his fingers to awaken him, saying: "Companion!"
"How is your health?
After a long while, the brahmin slowly raised his head and replied, "I am poor and have nothing with which to offer you; what can I do?"
The bhikṣu said again,
"I shall now give you one thing.
He then transformed himself into a chicken.
"You may kill this chicken and eat it.
The brahmin was startled and said, "I would not even kill a louse or a flea; how much less would I kill a chicken?"
The bhikṣu said, "Your original intention was to kill countless people; killing this single chicken is hardly worth mentioning.
The brahmin replied again:
"How could I have killed so many people?
The bhikṣu replied,
"When you were formerly sitting here in meditation, you desired to become this king."
When a king governs and transforms the world, how many people can he possibly kill each day? Yet he speaks of "not killing.
This rooster is none other than the consciousness within your own mind.
If this rooster can attain the Great Way of Non-action (wuwei), what need is there for a king?
He then reflected: "This bhikṣu knows the thoughts within my mind;
he must surely be a noble one!"
"You should follow his teaching.
He preached the Dharma for him again, and he immediately attained the fruit of the Path.
Although the body of this brahmin was tranquil, his mind did not rest.
Only after one has personally attained the killing of consciousness can it be called "resting.
Therefore, the subsequent explanation states:
"The mental intentions and perceptions have ceased."
One who contemplates the body observes the thirty-six impure substances and foul impurities of the body; by contemplating them with clarity and without distraction, one also attains nirvana.
How is this known?
In the past, there was a bhikṣu who practiced as an araṇyaka and constantly went for alms. He ate by the side of a river and, having finished his meal, washed his bowl.
At that time, on the bank of the upper reaches of the river among the graves, there was a recently deceased woman; the wind blew her hair, and it suddenly fell into his bowl.
The bhikṣu took this hair in his hand and examined it closely; it was exceedingly fine and beautiful, and he spoke to himself:
"If this were horsehair, it would be far too fine."
"If it were a man's hair, it would be too soft and fine.
If it is tied and cannot be untied, it must certainly be a woman's hair.
He then tied it, and it could not be untied.
He then gave rise to this thought:

"This hair is like this; the person must be exquisite. His face is the color of peach blossoms, his eyes are like bright pearls, his nose is like a cut tube, his mouth is as if containing vermilion, and his eyebrows are like centipedes."
Having made this discrimination, he immediately gave rise to a lustful mind and followed the current in search [of her], imagining he would see her form and features.

Pursuing her without ceasing, he saw a woman whose body had already been half-devoured by a jackal; her flesh was putrid and foul-smelling, yet her hair still remained. Grasping the hair and comparing it, he found its length and appearance to be similar [to his memory]; thus, the lustful thoughts he previously harbored were suddenly and naturally dispelled.
He further observed them again, discerning and examining them:
"When this person was alive, his appearance was handsome and refined; now it has been ruined and brought to decay for all to see.
The conceptualization I previously gave rise to was merely a desire for the body and an attachment to sensual craving; it was for that reason that such a thought arose."
"His body is thus; how am I any different?
To examine my own body with truth, it is a composite of the four great elements; when merit is exhausted and conditions depart, it naturally dissolves.
Witnessing this transformation, his mind attained awakening, and he immediately reached the stage of the Path.
Speaking from this perspective, those who practice mindfulness of the body attain the fruits of the śramaṇa.
As for mindfulness of death, the practitioner reflects:
"Life passes away without ceasing; the faculties disintegrate like rotten wood, and the life-faculty is severed."
"One should contemplate impermanence to awaken oneself.

Formerly, there was a bhikṣu named Vakkali who practiced meditation and cultivated the Path for many years, yet his outflows were not eliminated; he grew weary of his own body, regarding it as a great burden."
He frequently contemplated self-harm, thinking:
"The reason people cannot attain the Way is precisely because of this body, which remains entangled and transmigrates; when will it ever cease?
He then took a knife in his hand and was about to cut his own throat, but then reflected once more:
“The World-Honored One has given this instruction: ‘My disciples must not harm themselves.
Nevertheless, I now wish to seek nirvāṇa.
Within nirvāṇa there is no body; therefore, I shall first eliminate the body to attain the unconditioned.”
Immediately, he raised his sword and cut his own throat; his head fell and his heart was pierced through, and he attained arhatship on the spot.
Knowing that he had already realized the Way, the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to cremate his body.
Therefore, mindfulness of death also leads to nirvana.
The preceding ten recollections of the Buddha were taught as a general exposition for sentient beings of sharp faculties.
The subsequent explanation is provided for sentient beings of dull faculties, in order to analyze and clarify its meaning.
As for fame and reputation, one will later become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
As for attaining great karmic fruition, one will later become Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
As for the universal arrival of all virtues, one will later obtain the retribution of Brahmā.
Those who attain the flavor of the ambrosia will subsequently become *pratyekabuddhas*.
Those who reach the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) will subsequently obtain the fruit of an *arhat*.

Although the ten recollections mentioned above do not contain these five phrases, the reason they are added here as various rewards is to clarify that the principle of *buddhānusmṛti* (recollection of the Buddha) is profound and subtle.
The Buddha said:
"When my disciples enter parinirvāṇa, it is all because they have attained nirvāṇa through the repayment of causes from past conditions.
Maudgalyāyana was beaten and Śāriputra suffered the descent of his intestines; likewise, these five hundred disciples each attained extinction through their respective past conditions."
Only Ānanda was most skillful at entering nirvāṇa.
When Ānanda was about to enter nirvāṇa, he first manifested an auspicious omen of light.
A brahmin who had studied arithmetic under Ānanda saw that Ānanda’s countenance was radiant and informed King Ajātaśatru, saying:
“Ānanda’s countenance is unlike its usual state; is he about to enter parinirvāṇa?
The king immediately dispatched men to pursue Ānanda.
Ānanda had already reached the bank of the Ganges River midway with five hundred disciples, where they were boarding a boat intending to cross.
When they had reached the middle of the river, the King reached the opposite bank.
As Vaiśālī had received word of Ānanda’s arrival, it had also dispatched five hundred youths to welcome him.
Wishing to satisfy the intentions of both kingdoms, he used his supernatural powers to cause the boat to halt in midstream.
At that time, he ordained two disciples:
the first was named Makhādeva and the second was named Moggallāna.
He addressed Makhādeva:
"You shall go to Karṇa to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish.
Since the Buddha-dharma has not yet existed in that land, you must ensure it is widely propagated there.
He then addressed Maheṃdra, saying:
"Go to the kingdom of Siṃhaladvīpa and cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish there.

Having finished these instructions, he performed the eighteen transformations, emitted fire to cremate his body, and divided the śarīra relics into two portions so that each family might receive them for veneration.
This is due to the power of mindfulness of the Buddha; therefore, one attains mastery.
*Fenbie Gongde Lun*, Scroll Two; *Fenbie Gongde Lun*, Scroll Three.
The translator’s name is lost; this is appended to the Later Han Records.
Regarding the Buddha’s address to the bhikṣus: out of great compassion, the Buddha wished to cause his disciples to fully understand the meaning of mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti).

It was like a father’s earnest admonitions to his descendants, desiring that they achieve perfection without ceasing. They were to focus single-mindedly on mindfulness of the Buddha, contemplating the Tathāgata’s form with their eyes never departing from it, just as Ānanda contemplated the Buddha without weariness and with a mind that never ceased its recollection.
At that time, an abscess broke out on Ānanda’s back, and the Buddha commanded Jīvaka to treat Ānanda’s ailment.
Jīvaka addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I do not dare to bring my hands near Ānanda’s back.”
The Buddha told Jīvaka,
"Treat him without hesitation.
I shall personally preach the Dharma to Ānanda, so that he will not feel the pain."
The Tathāgata had Ānanda gaze intently at the marks and signs of his physical excellence, and the Buddha spoke for him, saying:
"The body of the Tathāgata is of the nature of adamant; it is indestructible and is accomplished through the merit of three thousand two hundred blessings."
Ānanda gazed at him with unwearied eyes, listened with tireless ears, and his mind remained undistracted.
Then Jīvaka lanced the abscess on Ānanda’s back and applied medicinal ointment.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Do you feel pain on your back? He replied:
"I was unaware. This lack of awareness of pain was due to mindfulness of the Buddha.
It is that which is accomplished by the Ten Powers and the Four Fearlessnesses.
In the past, there was an elder who, while leading a slave to pay homage at a stūpa, said:
"Namo to the World-Honored One of Ten Powers.
The slave, following behind, paid homage and said:
“Homage to the Tathāgata Ekādaśabala.
The elder said, “The Tathāgata possesses exactly ten powers; how can there be eleven powers?”
The slave said,
"What suffering is there for one with eleven powers?
Just do not speak of nine powers."
"If one says that the eleven powers are further augmented by one additional power, what fault would there be?
The Great Master returned home in silence.
He then asked the various Dharma masters:
"How many powers does the Tathāgata possess?
He replied, "There are some who say there are three powers, some who say there are ten powers, and others who say they are innumerable."
Speaking from this perspective, it is not limited to ten.
The elder immediately left the household life to study the Way, being freed from servitude to become a master of his own house.
To say "four" is not to imply insufficiency; to say "innumerable" is not to imply redundancy. Adapting to the times and responding to beings, there is no fixed measure.
One who contemplates the Dharma proceeds from desire to non-desire, from desire to the Path, from the outflows to the outflow-free, and from the conditioned to the unconditioned.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, the World-Honored One was teaching the Dharma and transforming beings in the kingdom of King Udayana.
At that time, he ascended to the Heaven of the Thirty-three to teach the Dharma to his mother, Māyā, and after ninety days, he returned, descending to the north of the city of Kāśī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā thought to herself that she wished to go forward alone to see the Buddha.
At that moment, the various kings, having not seen the Buddha for ninety days, were all filled with a longing of thirst and reverence, and they came together in a great assembly like clouds.
"I am a bhikṣuṇī; it is not appropriate for me to remain amidst this noisy crowd.
I shall employ a skillful means to ensure that I may go first.
She then transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), accompanied by a retinue in accordance with the manner of a sage king.
When the various minor kings saw the Holy King, they each fled and dispersed.
The bhikṣuṇī then restored herself to her original form, whereupon she saw the Buddha, paid homage, and inquired after his well-being.
The kings each came to see the Buddha and, no longer seeing the Holy King, realized he had been transformed by the bhikṣuṇī; they then addressed the bhikṣuṇī, saying:
“Was what we just saw such a deception?
At that time, the Utpala-lotus thought to himself, “I am the very first to have seen the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the Utpala-lotus:
"You yourself claimed to be the very first to see the Buddha,
yet there was another who saw him before you.
"I do not know who that was."
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti is currently mending his robes in the mountains to the east of the city of Rājagṛha.
A deva spoke to him, saying:"
"The Buddha has descended.
Subhūti said, "As his disciple,
it is my duty to go to pay him homage and inquire after his well-being."
He reflected further to himself:
"Where is the Buddha? Is this golden form the Buddha?"
“How much gold, then, is there?
The Buddha said:
“All dharmas are empty and non-existent.”

If one understands that the twelve links of dependent origination are empty—neither created nor made, neither a person nor a man, without a life-principle and not a possessor of a life-principle—then this constitutes seeing the Dharma.
Seeing that the Dharma is without a life-principle and that there is no possessor of a life-principle is to see the self.
He immediately joined his palms, rose, and called out,
"Vāṇa! At that very moment,
[the other] returned to his seat and continued mending his robe.
"Speaking from this perspective, Subhūti, you have already seen the Buddha before me.
The Buddha is the sovereign of all dharmas; to understand and realize the emptiness of dharmas is itself the recollection of the Dharma.
"Mindfulness of the assembly" refers to the assembly of noble and holy ones.

Generally, there are many kinds of assemblies; even among the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths, each has its own assembly. Some are harmonious, while others are discordant, yet they all likewise restrain themselves by means of precepts and discipline.
Some practice meditative concentration, while others regard the state of non-perception as the ultimate excellence; each believes in their own practice and considers it to be the truth.
However, because they do not attain the true Noble Eightfold Path, they are unable to reach Nirvana.

Although there are those who possess the five supernatural powers and maintain their lifespans, as well as those in the state of non-conception who extend their existence for kalpas, none are exempt from birth and death.
Only the noble assembly of the Tathāgata—the four pairs and eight ranks of practitioners—is no longer adrift upon the four currents nor sought out by the nine cessations.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Among the ninety-six kinds of monastic communities, the Buddha’s Sangha is the most authentic.

The fourfold assembly of the Tathāgata all share the same Śākya lineage; this is likened to the four Ganges Rivers, each having five hundred tributaries, all of which merge into the great ocean to become a single flavor.

The assembly is also like this: whether they are of the Kṣatriya caste, the Brāhmaṇa caste, the Gṛhapati (householder) caste, or the Vaiśya caste—among these four castes, those who have gone forth as practitioners all share the single clan name of Śākya, without any other distinct names.
Because that which is encompassed by this is so vast and its meaning so profound, the "Assembly of Monks" (Saṃgha) includes those of the Three Vehicles:
the Arhat Saṃgha emerges from within it, Pratyekabuddhas are also among them, and the Mahāyāna Saṃgha is likewise therein; for this reason, it is called the "Field of Blessings" (Puṇyakṣetra).
Within the three realms, there is no place more beneficial for aiding and benefiting sentient beings than this most excellent ground.
Although the Tathāgata has already attained perfect enlightenment, he constantly returns to the Saṃgha to perform repentance, because the ground of the Saṃgha is profound and substantial.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time and their disciples who are pratyekabuddhas have all attained nirvana through the Sangha; it is just as the bhikṣu Brahmadatta relied upon the noble assembly to achieve his complete deliverance.
Regarding the mindfulness of precepts (*śīlānusmṛti*): it means practicing pure morality and being endowed with all forms of restraint (*saṃvara*).
It is like a potter who prepares and refines clay, awaiting those who seek vessels, so that they may be made large or small, square or round, each according to their desire.
The precepts are likewise: if one aspires to be reborn in heaven, one will receive blessings within the three realms;
if one seeks to sever the fetters and pursue the Way, one’s aspirations will be fulfilled according to one's intent.
They are like an auspicious vase (maṅgalakalaśa), from which whatever a person desires can be obtained upon taking it.

Taking the precepts as the foundation, one concurrently practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and various samādhis; by severing the seven latent tendencies and the nine fetters, one advances toward the realization of nirvāṇa.
This is likened to a vessel formed from clay, which can no longer be destroyed.
Regarding the mindfulness of giving, it is said that there are two aspects to giving:
either giving with an owner or giving without an owner.
Furthermore, there are two further types of giving:
The first is called giving with attachment, and the second is called giving with detachment.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of giving:
first, the gift of material wealth, and second, the gift of the Dharma.
"Giving" refers to a gift with an owner; "relinquishing" refers to a gift without an owner.
Relinquishing means abandoning the fetters; giving means that the recipient before one receives wealth or the Dharma.

As for why giving leads to Nirvana: when one gives wealth or the Dharma to others, if the mind does not hope for recompense and does not discriminate between self and other, then through these three factors being unimpeded, it is identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If one can abandon the fetters, that too is nirvana.

Regarding the abandonment and the attainment of nirvana together, it is like an elephant pursuing a skilled rider: whether advancing or retreating, as long as there is meat to be gained, advancing will break the enemy army while retreating leads to one's own destruction; in either case, the eating of the meat is certain.
Regarding the recollection of devas, there are three kinds of devas:
the devas of elevation, the devas of birth, and the pure devas.
What are the devas of elevation?
This refers to the Wheel-Turning Sage King, who is elevated by the multitude.
He is called a "deva" because the Sage King teaches the world through the ten wholesome paths of action, causing all people to be born in the heavens.
Because he stands above all men, he is called "Heaven.
Some have even said:
"The Sage-King surpasses the Buddha."
Why is this so? When a sage-king governs the world, no one falls into the three evil realms;
yet when a Buddha appears in the world, the three evil realms are not severed.
For this reason, he is superior.
Or it may further be said:
the Buddha is superior to the noble wheel-turning monarch.
Therefore it is said that [the Buddha] is superior: while the Sage Kings taught the world through the ten wholesome paths of action, which do not exceed the realms of humans and devas;
the Buddha appeared and taught the world so that one may attain Nirvana.
It is for this reason that he is superior.
What is meant by "being born in heaven"?
From the Four Heavenly Kings up to the twenty-eighth heaven, all those who receive blessings are beings born in heaven.
It is called "being born in heaven" because their transmigration continues without ceasing, and they do not escape birth and death; therefore, it is termed "being born in heaven."
What are the Pure Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa-deva*)?

They refer to the three types of persons—the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Śrāvaka—who have all exhausted their fetters and outflows, transcended the triple world, and are pure and free from desire; therefore, they are called the Pure Heavens.
The eight Śuddhāvāsa heavens transcend birth and exertion, yet do not reach the ultimate purity; they occupy the intermediate state between them.
They are what those who contemplate the heavens long for.
Through mindfulness of arising thoughts, even the act of lifting [the body] can lead to the principle of Nirvana.
Why is this? In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a couple of lay devotees who had no children or grandchildren.
The two of them were diligent in their practice, keeping the Three Jewels in their hearts.
At that time, the wife died early and was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as a celestial maiden, peerless in her beauty and rarely equaled among the gods.
The woman thought to herself, "Who is worthy to be my husband?

She surveyed the world with her divine eye and saw that her former husband had left home to study the Way; though advanced in years, he was dull-witted and lacked wisdom, possessing only single-minded faith, and his constant practice was the sweeping and cleaning of stupas and temples.
Seeing that she was diligent in her practice and ought to have been reborn in heaven, he thought, "She will surely return to be my wife.

At that time, while sitting in meditation at night in a quiet chamber, he suddenly beheld a brilliant light. Wondering at this extraordinary phenomenon, he raised his head and looked up, whereupon he saw a celestial maiden. He asked her the reason for her presence and from where she had come.
The goddess replied, “I have come from the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Originally I was your wife; now I am a goddess.”
"In the heavens, there is no one who can rival my husband. Observing your diligence, you ought to return as my husband; for this reason, I have come to declare my intention.
Having finished speaking, she suddenly vanished and returned to the heavens.
From that time forward, the elderly bhikṣu redoubled his diligent practice and further repaired the old temple.
Without slackening morning or night, he accumulated great merit until his blessings and virtue became preeminent, whereby he was reborn in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita.
The heavenly maiden again observed him with her divine eye and saw that he was destined to be reborn in the fourth heaven;
she came back and said to him, "Having accumulated such diligence, you have already transcended my realm; I shall no longer be able to be your wife."
Having finished speaking, he departed.

The bhikṣu redoubled his diligence, surpassing his former state; by day he practiced walking meditation, and by night he engaged in dhyāna contemplation. His mind became increasingly clear as he contemplated the Four Noble Truths, and before long, he attained arhatship.
Regarding what is called attaining Nirvana through mindfulness of the devas:
"mindfulness of rest" refers to the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
There are two kinds of rest:
There is mundane rest and there is supramundane rest.
As for mundane rest: it is like being exhausted from laboring and work, pausing briefly to relax; therefore, it is called mundane rest.
One who rests in the Way refers to a person established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
How do we know this is so?
Formerly, there was a bhikṣu named Saṃgha who sat in meditation near the side of a great road, his mind fixed in concentration.
At that time, five hundred chariots passed by with a most tumultuous roar, yet he heard nothing;
then again, there was a clap of heavenly thunder, and shortly thereafter the earth shook violently, yet he heard nothing at all.
Many have passed by, and dust has settled upon his robes over a period of time.
Suppose a person were to come along and see this bhikṣu sitting upright and motionless; would he not perceive that dust has settled upon his robes?
The bhikṣu, awakened from his concentration, shook off the dust.
He asked again,
"Were you sleeping just now?"
He replied, "No. He asked again:
"If you were not asleep, there was a carriage passing by just now, as well as thunder from heaven and an earthquake.
You remained silent and unperturbed;
how could this be? He replied:
"At that time, I had entered the Samādhi of Rest; therefore, I simply heard nothing at all.
By this it is said that one who attains the Samādhi of Rest does not alter their resolve even if heaven and earth were to collapse; hence it is called the Samādhi of Rest.
To practice mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breath) means to bring to rest all mental wandering and distraction.
There is not only one path leading toward the Way; the methods for awakening each have their own specific locus.
How do we know this to be so?
In the past, Śāriputra once made offerings to fourteen hundred million Buddhas and heard the Dharma from them, yet he never practiced or mastered *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
In the era of Śākyamuni, he began to penetrate the Dharma of emptiness under the guidance of the bhikṣu Aśvajit and immediately attained the path of vision.
The Buddha fully expounded wisdom to him; his outflows were exhausted and his fetters were severed, so that he is now foremost in wisdom.
One does not attain nirvana by means of *ānāpāna* (breath-counting).

In the past, during thirty kalpas, Maudgalyāyana made offerings to various Buddhas and practiced the Mahāyāna path, yet he was unable to bring it to completion; only upon encountering the World-Honored One did he retreat from that and achieve the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
From antiquity until now, he has never practiced *ānāpāna*.

Although the bhikṣu Kāśyapa also once made offerings to thirty thousand Tathāgatas, he likewise never practiced *ānāpāna*; though he should have attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he has now regressed to become an Arhat.
In the past, the bhikṣu Aśvajit also made offerings to the seven Buddhas and did not practice *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), yet now he has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
In the past, Ānanda also made offerings to twenty thousand Tathāgatas; from those Buddhas he received and inquired about the teachings of the Dharma, yet he too did not practice *ānāpānasmṛti*.
Only Rāhula and Mahākapphiṇa, having practiced *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) since ancient times, have now likewise attained the Way.
From this it may be seen that the path leading to the Way is not of a single form.

Ānāpāna consists in knowing whether the breath is long or short, cold or warm, slow or rapid; from the coarse to the subtle, one gradually restrains distracted thoughts until they reach the state of subtlety.

Some attain awakening through the regulation of breath; some through analytical understanding; some through the ascetic discipline of *dhūta*; some through extensive learning and a powerful memory; some through supernormal powers and the discernment of subtleties; and some through exemplary conduct and instruction. As it is said, these are different paths that lead to the same destination.
"Mindfulness of the body" refers to the analytical discernment of the four great elements.
It means to understand that the five aggregates are equally like an illusion or a dream.
How is it known that mindfulness of the body leads to the attainment of nirvana?
Formerly, one hundred years after the Buddha had passed into nirvana, there was King Aśoka who ruled over Jambudvīpa; he possessed eighty-four thousand ministers, ladies, elephants, and horses.
At that time, as the king was touring the borders of his kingdom, he saw that King Yama had eighteen hells, where there were also ministers and officials interrogating the prisoners.
The king asked those around him,
"Who are these people?"
He replied, "This is the King of the Dead, who presides over the discernment of good and evil.
The king said:
"The King of the Dead is still able to inflict punishments upon offenders in hell;
I am a living king—am I not able to do so as well?
He then questioned his various ministers:
"Who is capable of creating hell?
The ministers replied,
"Only those who commit the most heinous evils are able to create hell."
The king commanded his ministers to search for such a wicked man.

The ministers immediately went out to seek him and saw a man sitting on the ground weaving woolen cloth; beside him were a bow and arrows as well as fishing hooks, and he was furthermore feeding sparrows with poisoned rice while simultaneously weaving cloth, fishing, shooting birds, and catching sparrows.
The minister returned and reported the matter to the king, saying, "The man is so wicked.
The king said, "This man is extremely evil; he will surely be able to manage the affairs of hell."
The king sent a messenger to summon him, saying,
"The king wishes to see you.
The wicked man replied:
"I am a small man, lacking in knowledge and wisdom.
Why does Your Majesty employ me? He said:
"The King specifically wishes to have you manage the affairs of the hells.
The man immediately returned home and said to his elderly mother:
"The King has summoned me.
The mother said to her son,
"Why has the King summoned you?"
The son said,
"The King wishes to have me attend to the affairs of hell.
His mother said:
"Go away! How shall I live without you?
The mother then embraced her son's feet and would not let him go.
As the son intended to depart, he drew his sword and struck his mother, killing her before proceeding to the king's presence.
The king asked, "Your mother will not let you go; by what means have you been able to come? He replied:
"He has come after killing his mother.
The king said,
"He is truly an evil man."
"He will certainly be able to manage the affairs of hell.
He then entrusted this man with the task of constructing the city of hell, establishing the boiling cauldrons and the sword-trees.
He immediately invested this man as the King of Hell, appointing ministers and subordinates for him, each with their own assigned duties, just like those of King Yama.
The king issued a decree, saying:
"If anyone enters this city, regardless of their status as noble or lowly, they shall be punished immediately.
The king said:
"Even if I enter within, do not allow me to leave.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu named Sujāta who regularly went for alms.
Arriving outside this city gate, he saw fine flowers and fragrances; thinking there were people inside, he immediately entered the city.
Seeing only those being punished for their crimes, he was struck with terror and wished to flee.
At that time, the hell-wardens would not allow him to leave, intending to lead him to the boiling cauldrons.
The practitioner entreated them, saying:
"Be patient with me until noon," he said.

While they were still speaking, a man and a woman were caught committing adultery; intending to punish them, they placed them inside a mortar and pounded them, whereupon in an instant they were transformed into foam.
When the practitioner saw this, he first recalled the Buddha’s words:
"The human body is like a mass of foam.
"Truly so," he thought.
Furthermore, it soon changes again to white; then one contemplates the human body as being like a heap of white ashes, subject to constant transformation and never remaining the same.
It is like an illusion or a magical conjuration; when examined with discernment, it is not real.
Immediately, he attained awakening; his outflows were exhausted and his fetters were untied.
As the wardens again urged him to enter the boiling cauldron, the bhikṣu smiled.
The wardens, filled with rage, had four men seize him by both armpits and cast him headfirst into the cauldron.
Immediately the water grew cold, and the bhikṣu instantly transformed himself into a thousand-petaled lotus flower, sitting cross-legged within it.
The wardens of hell were struck with wonder and said to King Aśoka:
"There is a strange occurrence now within the hells."
"I pray that Your Majesty will deign to come and look upon it.
The king said, "I have a prior agreement: even if I were to enter within, I would not be permitted to leave."
"How can I possibly enter now?
The official said to the king, "Simply enter; there will be no harm."
The king followed him inside.
Seeing the ascetic seated upon a lotus flower, he asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am a man of the Way.
The man of the Way spoke to the king:
“You are a fool,” [the other said]. The king asked, “Why do you call me a fool?”
The practitioner said:
"When you were originally a young boy, you offered a handful of earth to the Buddha. The Buddha accepted it and made this prayer of blessing:
'In the future, you shall become a king over Jambudvīpa as an Iron-Wheel-Turning King named Aśoka, and within a single day, you shall erect eighty-four thousand Buddhist stūpas.'"
"Is this prison a Buddhist temple?
The king’s mind was immediately awakened; he then came forward to repent his transgressions and took Shanjue as his teacher.
Thereupon, he disbanded the prison and promoted merit, erecting eighty-four thousand temples and shrines.
Speaking from this perspective, the meaning is that by contemplating the body, one attains nirvana.
How is it that by contemplating death, one reaches nirvana?

Formerly, King Aśoka served the Dharma with such diligence that he constantly provided five hundred members of the Sangha within his palace with the four requisites without deficiency; furthermore, he provided for five hundred forest-dwelling mendicants outside the palace and sent five hundred others to bring offerings to support them.
Furthermore, he provided for the poor and destitute at the four city gates.
As his offerings continued for a long time, his wealth and treasures gradually diminished.
At that time, there was a younger brother named Sugatodana, who did not believe in the Triple Gem.
The minister Yaśas and his wife Śubhāṅgī were likewise unbelievers.
The three shared a common purpose in resenting the king, and they repeatedly admonished him, saying:
"Your support of these ascetics has exhausted the nation's wealth."
"What use is this? The king said,
"You must guard your mouth well."
"Indeed, when a gentleman lives in this world, that which leads to his own ruin is his evil speech.
Śuklodana said to the King: "These various practitioners are all young men;
their appetites for delicacies run wild and their passions are intense. Since they dwell amidst women in the inner palace, how can they be trusted?"
The King replied, “The Daoist practitioner employs legal restraints to protect himself and maintains discipline by observing prohibitions; he is not to be overcome by sensual desire.
Later, when Śuddhodana went out hunting, he saw a herd of deer with a man among them. He surrounded them to capture them and succeeded in catching the man.
He asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I lost my parents when I was eight years old; I fled into the mountains where I was suckled by a deer, and thus have come down to this day.
He asked again, "When the deer had no milk, what did you eat?"
He replied,
"I follow the deer to eat grass and leaves to sustain my life.
He asked again:
"Is there any desire in your mind?
He replied, "There is."
He then took him back and reported the situation to the King, saying:
"This grass-eater has such a gaunt and emaciated body, yet he still possesses lustful desires.
How much more so for those practitioners who eat and drink to their heart's content until their bodies are plump and robust—how could they possibly be free from lustful desires?"
The king thought to himself, "By what skillful means can I convert this younger brother?
He immediately devised a stratagem, feigning a desire to go on an excursion; he gathered a great multitude of men and soldiers and prepared his administration to depart.
The king, having stolen back inside, remained hidden and did not show himself.
Previously, the king had consulted with his ministers, saying:
"If I depart, he shall be installed as king."
The ministers immediately urged him to try on the royal robes, but he feigned reluctance.
The ministers said, "Just put them on; we shall wear them."

He immediately donned the celestial crown and royal robes, and everyone cried out, "Ten thousand years! His attendants stood in attendance on his left and right according to the custom of a holy king.
Seeing that he was now firmly established, King Aśoka came from outside and said, "How do you fare, Great King?"
Upon seeing the king, the younger brother was ashamed and did not know where to go.
King Aśoka said, "I have merely gone out for a brief excursion; why have you all committed such an act?"
"Is my iron wheel not there?
Why do you act so recklessly? I shall kill you in an instant."
He immediately ordered his ministers to remove the shackles and secretly dispatched a messenger to inform the practitioner:
"Keep this intention well in mind; you shall come to rescue and entreat me.
[The king replied: "I am about to kill you."

"I consider that since you have been king for but a short time, you have not yet been able to exercise your will at full length; therefore, I shall now grant you seven days as king, according to my royal law, with all ministers and attendants, palace women and courtesans, and the serving of food and drink."
"Enjoy yourself for seven days, and then you shall undergo the ultimate rite.
He immediately acted according to these instructions; although the seven days were completed, his heart felt no joy.
When the practitioner came to invite him, he took up his bowl and staff and proceeded to the gate of the royal palace.
The king asked,
"What do you desire, O practitioner? He replied:
"I beg for the dead man.
The king said, "This criminal deserves death; he cannot be given to you."
"Alms-seeker, mendicant.
The mendicant spoke again:
"I am merely a mendicant; I shall cause you to study the Way."
The king asked,
"Can this man study the Way? The practitioner then questioned him:
"I now request that you become a śrāmaṇera.
Are you able? He replied:
"Even if he were made a slave, he still should not be rejected, let alone as a śrāmaṇera.
The king said, "It is difficult to be a man of the Way; have you truly considered whether he is capable?"
"The way of a practitioner of the Path requires coarse clothing and meager food, merely sustaining the physical life to practice the Way.
You are accustomed to comfort and luxury; how can you endure such asceticism?"
He replied, "I am still destined to die; how could I not endure ascetic practice?
The king said:
"If he is capable, permit him to beg for food for seven days.
The king then ordered within the palace:
"When Sugataḷu comes to beg, give him the most wretched food—leftovers that are filthy, foul-smelling, and repulsive."
"Even though he wears tattered robes and constructs various dwellings, and though he begs for alms and receives only poor food everywhere,
because his resolve to avoid death is so profound, he accepts these meager meals with a willing heart."
When the seven days had passed, the king saw that she was free from regret and immediately granted her permission to enter the religious life, saying:
"You have often said:
'The life of a practitioner is one of leisure and joy; it is difficult to believe for those with many worldly attachments.'"
"The alms-food you have received was still refined and exquisite even within my palace;
yet the food begged by this practitioner is even more so than this.
Since his sustenance is such as this, how could he possibly possess sensual desire?"
He then ordained Shan-nian as a śramaṇa.
The king dispatched a messenger to Śilāvatī City, where [Shan-nian] practiced various meditative contemplations within that city, sometimes among burial mounds and sometimes beneath trees.
At that time, while he was among the burial mounds contemplating corpses, he saw at night a hungry ghost striking one of them.
He asked, "Why are you striking this corpse?"
He replied,
"This corpse has troubled me so much while I sat here that I struck it.
The practitioner said:
"Why do you not strike your own heart? What benefit would there be in striking this corpse?
After a short while, another deva scattered mandārava flowers over the corpse.
The practitioner asked again,
"Why scatter this stinking corpse? He replied:
“Because of this corpse, I have attained birth in the heavens.
This corpse was my virtuous friend; therefore, I have come to scatter flowers as a repayment for its past kindness.
The practitioner said:
"Why do you not scatter flowers within your own hearts, but instead scatter these foul-smelling flowers upon this corpse?
For the roots of both good and evil are all produced by the mind; have you now abandoned the root to grasp at the branches?"
At that time, Sugāṭu thought to himself:
"I have obtained life from death; by this cause and condition, I shall surely attain liberation.

Thereupon, he contemplated the body with mindfulness of death, reflecting and discerning until he fully understood impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and immediately attained arhatship.
Speaking from this perspective, even those who contemplate death shall attain Nirvana.
*Fenbie Gongde Lun*, Scroll Three; *Fenbie Gongde Lun*, Scroll Four.
The translator's name is lost; this is appended to the Later Han Record.

The reason the Tathāgata extensively taught each of the four assemblies as being foremost was so that, within the Dharma left behind for future末代 (final ages), there might be those of the four castes, non-Buddhist students, Brahmins, and the four assemblies' disciples who would engage in mutual disputes, claiming themselves to be honored while deeming others inferior.
Such individuals as these are beyond calculation; therefore, to provide for them before such needs arise, the path of self-sufficiency was opened.

As for why Kauṇḍinya is now called the foremost, it is because he was of a noble Śākya clan; when the King selected him to serve as an attendant, he underwent great hardship, and his merit and reward were ranked as being foremost.
Furthermore, he was the first to be converted and receive the Dharma, with no one preceding him; thus he is also foremost.
He was exceptionally skilled at exhorting and nurturing the assembly of noble ones, being the first to receive the address of "Welcome" (*svāgata*); thus he is again foremost.

Among those to whom people look for refuge, Cakravartin is supreme; among lights, the sun is supreme; among the constellations, the moon is supreme; among the myriad rivers, the ocean is supreme; among the Four Heavenly Kings, Dhṛtarāṣṭra is supreme; among the Thirty-three Heavens, Śakra Devendra is supreme; among the six heavens of the desire realm, Pāpīyān is supreme; among the eighteen heavens of the form realm, the Śuddhāvāsa [Heavens] are supreme; among the ninety-six schools of monks, the Buddhist Sangha is supreme; among the ninety-six kinds of paths, the Buddha-path is the highest and most supreme; and among the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, [the Buddha] is supreme.
Speaking from this perspective, Kauṇḍinya was the foremost.
As for the bhikṣu Udāyin, he was the most eminent in exhortation.

Among all the bhikṣus who exhorted others, he was called the foremost because when the Buddha was about to return to convert his native land, he first dispatched him to manifest supernatural transformations.
He engaged in dialogue with the king, explaining each point one by one; the number of people he delivered was beyond calculation, and thus he was called the foremost in exhortation.

As for the bhikṣu Mahātan, his faculties were sharp and swift; while the other bhikṣus had all exhausted their outflows and attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), this bhikṣu attained supernatural powers even though his outflows were not yet exhausted, and thus he was called the foremost.

All who travel through space do so by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*); yet this bhikṣu can traverse the void as if walking upon solid ground. This is the capability of the bhikṣu Śubhūti, and for this reason he is called the foremost.

Maudgalyāyana traveled silently to other lands through his supernormal powers, while the bhikṣu Pāva soared through the air with his supernormal powers, his voice resounding far and wide; because he was able to subdue the non-Buddhists, he was called the foremost.
As for the bhikṣu Ox-Foot, he may not remain in the world for two reasons. What are they?
This bhikṣu’s feet resemble the hooves of an ox, and when his meal is finished, he chews the cud; because of these two things, he may not remain in the world.
If non-Buddhist brahmins were to see him chewing his cud, they would say that the śramaṇa has no moderation in his eating and would give rise to a mind of slander.
For this reason, the Buddha sent him up to heaven to sit in meditative concentration and settle his mind in the Sudharma Hall.
The bhikṣu Sujāta was frequently sent as a messenger for the Saṃgha to the heavens.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa struck the *gandī* and assembled the great multitude of monks, commanding Aniruddha to survey the world and see who had not yet arrived.
Aniruddha then surveyed the entire world and saw that there was only the bhikṣu Kapphiṇa remaining in the heavens.
He immediately dispatched Sujāta to summon him to come.

Sujāta went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and saw [the Buddha] in the Sudharmā Hall, having entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). He snapped his fingers to awaken him, saying:
"It has been fourteen days since the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa."
Kāśyapa has assembled the community and sent word to summon me, saying, 'You should descend to the world and go to the place where the assembly is gathered.
Pūrṇa replied, 'The world is already empty; what would I do by going there?'
Unable to return to the world, he desired to enter parinirvāṇa.
He immediately entrusted his robes and bowl to Sujāta to return to the community of monks, and then entered parinirvāṇa.
By these causes and conditions, he was reborn in a good place in the heavens; therefore, he is called the foremost.
The Bhikṣu Śubhavijaya was originally the son of a noble family.
At the moment of his birth, he was born with natural golden sandals upon his feet.
His parents cherished him and constructed for him palaces for the three seasons, with dancing girls providing entertainment who never left his side.

At that time, the wife was asleep; beholding her white teeth, he saw that although her physical form was exquisite, it was nothing but bone. As he fully contemplated these foul impurities, his hair stood on end in horror. Looking back at the palace and its dwellings, they appeared like a cemetery, and he fled in alarm out through the door.
The two deities came forward to welcome him and asked them,
"Now that we are beset by calamity, who among you can provide salvation?
The two deities replied:
"Only the World-Honored One is truly able to save us from distress.
He asked, "Where is he now?"
He replied, “He is currently nearby at the Jeta Grove; you may go and request his instruction.
Following the light, he went to the Buddha and prostrated himself, touching his head to the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha, responding to his original aspiration, expounded the wondrous Dharma for him; immediately, his mind was opened, his outflows were exhausted, and his fetters were untied.
By this cause and condition, the bhikṣu Śubhavimati became foremost in the contemplation of impurity.

As for why Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is called the foremost, it is because since past lives, these three brothers have always had one thousand disciples following them. Now, having encountered the era of Śākyamuni Buddha, the Buddha converted Kāśyapa’s thousand followers through eighteen miraculous transformations. Thus the Buddha’s assembly was completed, and the fourfold offerings arose from this very source.
Speaking from this perspective, among those who can protect the assembly of noble ones, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is foremost in his offerings.

As for why Nadī-Kāśyapa is called the foremost, it was because when the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he listened with single-minded devotion; his refined understanding penetrated his spirit, and all his fetters were extinguished. His virtue truly filled his inner being, reaching even to his very marrow; thus, the fat and marrow flowed outward, appearing like the breaking out of sweat.
Speaking from this perspective, because his mind was tranquil and he was able to subdue all fetters, he was called the foremost.
As for the bhikṣu Aśvajit, only seven days had passed since he began training under the Buddha, yet he was already fully equipped with dignified deportment.
As he was about to enter Vaiśālī to beg for alms, he encountered Upatiṣya outside the city gate.
Seeing from afar that the horse trainer’s deportment was composed and his dharma-robes were neatly arranged, the Master felt joy in his heart and asked:
"What kind of person are you?"
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa. He asked again:
"Do you know this for yourself, or do you have a teacher and lineage?
He replied, "I have a teacher."
“Who is the name of your teacher?
How does he teach the Dharma? He replied:
"My teacher is named Śākyamuni; he is the God among Gods, the most honored in the three realms.
His teachings take emptiness and non-substantiality as their core, seeking to still the mind and reach the fundamental source; therefore, he is called a śramaṇa."
Upon hearing these sublime words, Upatiṣya immediately attained the stage of the Stream-enterer (srotāpatti).
Upatiṣya’s fellow students had previously made a solemn vow that whoever should first attain the Deathless (amṛta) must inform the others.
He immediately took leave of his horse trainer and went to where Kūṭadanta was.
Seeing him approach with an extraordinary countenance, Kūṭadanta suspected he had attained the Ambrosia (amṛta) and asked:
"Have you obtained the Ambrosia?"
He said, "I have attained it. [The Buddha asked,] "What is this 'ambrosia'?"
“‘Ambrosia’ refers to the realization that all phenomena are empty and non-existent.
As Kūṭadanta reflected on this, he again attained the fruit of the path.

As for why Aśvajit was foremost in dignified deportment, it was because for five hundred past lives he had been a monkey; even now, having become a human, his nature remained restless and agitated, yet within seven days of leaving the household life, he changed from his former ways.

Although his studies were still at an elementary stage, he was adept at proclaiming the Honored One’s teachings, causing those who beheld him first to rejoice in countenance and comprehend the doctrine.
Because he moved others to realization through his dignified deportment, he was ranked as the foremost.
As for why Śāriputra is called "Foremost in Wisdom," the World-Honored One further said:

"If one wishes to know the extent of Śāriputra’s wisdom, were Mount Sumeru used as an inkstone, the waters of the four great oceans as the ink, the bamboo and wood of the four continents as pens, and all the people therein as scribes, they would still be unable to fully transcribe Śāriputra’s wisdom; how much less could ordinary beings with the five supernatural powers possibly measure it?"
Therefore, wisdom is called the foremost.
As for why Maudgalyāyana is called the foremost in spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), the World-Honored One has also spoken of his realization.
In the past, when the three calamities raged, the people suffered from a great famine.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Because this ground has subsided, there is the earth-fat from former days beneath it.
Now that the people are suffering greatly from famine, I intend to turn back this ground and take the earth-fat from below to sustain the lives of the people."
Having reflected thus, he addressed the Buddha:
"I now wish to use the four bases of psychic power to overturn the earth and take the essence of the lower realms to sustain the lives of the people.
I wonder if this may be permitted?"
The Buddha said,
"Stop, stop, Maudgalyāyana!

"Although you possess such supernormal power that it would be no difficulty for you to reverse this, how could the sentient beings therein grasp the insects with one hand while turning the earth over with the other?
The Buddha said,
"It is impossible."
The reason for this is that monks of future generations will mostly lack supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Should there later be a time of famine, the king, ministers, and common people might command the śramaṇas to turn the earth upside down.
"If one cannot do so, they are not called a śramaṇa.
Because he was certified by such supernormal powers (ṛddhi), Maudgalyāyana was designated as the foremost.

As for why the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was called the foremost in ascetic practice (dhutaguṇa): formerly, in the kingdom of Campā, there was a great elder who had a son born to him who was handsome and exquisite; beneath his feet grew hair four inches long that never touched the ground.

As for the reason why hair grew on your feet: in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you were a great elder with boundless wealth and treasures. Having completed the construction of a vihāra and lecture hall for the Saṃgha, you spread white cotton cloth upon the ground so that the monks might walk upon it.
For these reasons, he attained the mark of hair growing upward from the soles of his feet.
As for why he was named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, at the time of his birth, there were naturally produced within his ears precious gems worth twenty koṭis; thus, that became his name.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having heard of his extraordinary qualities and wishing to meet him, sent for him to come.
Calculating the distance, he traveled for fifteen days by carriage; as he was about to alight from the vehicle, he would spread fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) upon the ground before stepping onto it.
Having arrived at the king’s residence, the king ordered him to sit.
After inquiries of courtesy were concluded, the king, hearing that he was skilled at playing the lute, immediately commanded him to play.
Once they had finished their mutual entertainment, they went together to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, as the Buddha was extensively expounding the sublime Dharma to the great assembly, [the youth] saw the Buddha and, filled with joy, prostrated himself at his feet.
The Buddha bade him sit; having heard the Dharma and being delighted, he immediately requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha approved of his resolve to leave the household life, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

With courageous and diligent effort, he practiced walking meditation without ceasing; his flesh became thin and soft, and his feet were wounded and torn, such that where he walked, blood flowed and formed a mire.

Having accumulated these practices for a long time, his outflows (āsrava) were still not eliminated; weariness and indolence arose in his mind, and he wished to return to the white robes [of a layman], thinking:
"The wealth in my home is at my disposal; by extensively performing meritorious deeds, I may avoid the three evil realms."
The Buddha, knowing his thought, suddenly leaped forth from the ground before him and asked the bhikṣu:
"When you first played the lute, if the strings were too tight or too loose, could you produce a wondrous melody?"
He replied, “It would not be formed.
[The questioner asked,] “If all the strings were completely slack, could it then be formed?”
He replied, "It would not be accomplished. [The questioner asked:
"If it were neither too loose nor too tight, and the strings and frets were in harmony, could a wondrous sound be produced?"
He replied, "It can be accomplished.
The Buddha said:
"Practice is also like this: neither too hurried nor too slow, but remaining in the middle with appropriateness; when one is harmonious and attains the proper state, one can then achieve the Way.
Contemplating these words of the Buddha, his mind opened wide in understanding, and he immediately became an Arhat.
For these reasons, he is called the foremost in ascetic practices.
As for why Aniruddha is called the foremost in the divine eye: once, while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma to a great assembly, Aniruddha fell asleep on his seat.
The Buddha saw him sleeping and said to him, "Now that the Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma, why do you sleep?
As for one who sleeps, the mind and consciousness are blocked; how does this differ from death?"
Aniruddha felt ashamed and reproached himself, vowing:
"From this day forward, I shall not dare to sleep again.
Because he did not sleep for such a long time, his eyesight was lost.
The reason for this is that there are six kinds of nutriment in total. The eye has two nutriments:
first, the perception of forms; second, sleep.
Each of the other five sense organs likewise has its own two nutriments.
Only when one obtains food are the six sense faculties complete.
Because his eyes had not eaten for many days, he had lost his visual faculty.
The Buddha commanded Jīvaka to treat him, saying:
"Its sleeplessness cannot be cured.

Having lost his physical eyes, he could no longer see anything; his five hundred disciples each abandoned him and scattered, while he hired someone to thread needles for him as he felt his way to mend his robes.
The thread was exhausted and he had no one to ask for help.
Those around him cried out,
"Whoever seeks merit, let them thread this needle for me!"
The World-Honored One suddenly came before him and took it,
saying, "I shall string it for you. He asked:
"Who is it? He replied, "I am the Buddha."
“The Buddha is already fully endowed with merit; does he still wish to seek further merit?
He replied, “Is merit something to be weary of?”
Aniruddha reflected:
"If even the Buddha seeks merit, how much more so should an ordinary person?
His heart was moved with deep emotion; he rushed toward the Buddha to gaze upon him, and by virtue of his single-minded devotion, he suddenly attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Having attained the divine eye, he further reflected deeply and thereby attained arhatship.
Generally, all arhats possess three eyes:
the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye.
Anuruddha possesses only two eyes:
the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).

To look with three eyes would be chaotic; as the fleshly eye and the divine eye compete for mastery, their observations become a confused mixture of the refined and the coarse. Therefore, it is said to be "chaotic."

Aniruddha employs his divine eye exclusively to observe the great trichiliocosm; he perceives everything, both subtle and coarse, and distinguishes within all forms and substances whether they possess consciousness or lack it, knowing them all with complete clarity.

What gods and humans perceive as pure or impure varies; those with the most refined vision see all forms within the world, whether sentient or insentient, as being in constant motion, leading them to doubt whether they are insects or not.
Regarding the contemplation of impurity, one sees grains of rice moving and takes them all to be worms.
Such distinctions between superior and inferior have long existed.
By this it is said that the divine eye is the foremost.
As for why the bhikṣu Revata is called the foremost among those who sit in meditation and enter samādhi: formerly, King Prasenajit invited him to practice meditation beneath a tree.
At that time, the king invited him to enter the palace for a meal.
Having remained there for six years without wandering elsewhere, he was now about to move to another tree,
but the tree deity would not permit it.
What serves as proof of this?
As he was about to depart, the tree deity scattered flowers as an offering.
Taking this as proof, he knew that his request would not be granted.
How did he know that the deity’s mind harbored no other intention?
At that time, Kauṣṭhila came to where Revata was and said,
"Why do you not sit beneath a fine tree, but instead sit under this withered tree? He replied:
“You, O Virtuous One, are foremost in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), capable of discerning the meaning of the Dharma as well as the appropriate terminology.
I wonder, however, within which of the analytical knowledges does the discernment of this withered tree fall?”
"Since I sat here, six years have already passed, yet no distinction has arisen between the living and the withered.
Why is it that you, O Benevolent One, only now arrive and immediately make such a distinction?
The King invited him into the palace to provide daily offerings, assigning each of his consorts to take turns attending upon him.
When the six years were complete and he was being sent away with gifts, at the time of the *dakṣiṇā*, he did not know the name of his host.
The King said:
"Having accepted your invitation for six years, you do not even know the person's name; how can your ignorance be so extreme?"
He replied, "When I sit beneath a tree, I do not even know whether it is withering or growing; how much less could I recognize human characters?
His merit from practicing dhyāna was so profoundly pure that, according to the king's wishes, he could lead him to nirvāṇa; he was a most excellent field of merit.
Therefore, he was praised as foremost in the joy of dhyāna.

When the bhikṣu Tīrāva-ma exhorted others to organize the establishment of almsgiving and lectures, the Buddha entrusted the monastic affairs to him, assigning each category to its appropriate place: the Sūtras were gathered in one place, the Vinaya in another, the Mahādharmas in another, those for sitting in meditation in another, the high seats in another, the alms-seekers in another, and those engaged in teaching and transforming others in another; thus, according to their respective functions, they were divided into groups so that each followed its own kind.
If there were donors who came to invite [the monks], they were dispatched in order of seniority regardless of their rank.
If there was a private invitation, it was not permitted to follow this same rule.
When the invitations from the donors had ended, the group of six bhikṣus fell in turn upon a poor household; harboring resentment, they returned and spoke these words of complaint to the Buddha:
“Māra has been deceived;
he himself enjoys a place of excellence, yet he sends me away from a poor household—is this not unjust?
The Buddha then addressed Māra:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "No."
At that time, there was no food and the sun was about to pass its zenith; he therefore mixed cow dung with water and drank it as his fast-food.
Upon hearing the words of the group of six, he had no way to clear his name, so he immediately spat out this dung-water before the Buddha.

Of the six groups of monks who felt shame, two attained the exhaustion of outflows through spiritual realization, two returned to the life of laymen, and two died with boiling blood erupting from their faces, falling into the Avīci Hell.

Regarding the "Fasting Lecturer" (zhāijǎng): because they assemble the community for fasting, synthesize and practice what is appropriate, and are skillfully able to encourage and bring others to completion, they are called the foremost.

As for the "Minor Dhārma-bhāṇaka" (xiǎotuóluóbō): they primarily establish monastic quarters and support the *caitya* monks, accomplishing their work collectively; thus, they are no longer designated separately.
The reason the bhikṣu Rāṣṭrapāla is called noble and eminent is that he is of royal lineage; he is intelligent and widely learned, having pursued his studies with devotion since youth.
Hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world to enlighten the ignorant and deluded, he immediately went to the Jetavana Monastery to listen to and gather the words of the Dharma.
Upon hearing the teachings, they entered his spirit; he then contemplated leaving the household life.
He returned and informed his parents, but they would not listen.
He thought to himself:
"All sentient beings are my parents; how could it be only these two?"
Having thought thus, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling and requested to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha asked:
“Have your parents given their permission?”
He replied, "I do not permit it.
His elder brother was the king of the country; he again petitioned the king to become a seeker of the Way, but the king likewise would not permit it.
He thought to himself:
"I must employ skillful means to leave the household life and pursue the Way.
His parents had but this one son, and they did not wish for him to be separated from their sight for even a moment.
He requested a single small couch and sat before his parents; for six days, he neither drank nor ate.
His parents were filled with terror and feared they would lose their son, saying:
"If you kill this child, what use will you have for this dead child?"
"Listen; you shall be released to practice the Way.
He made a pact with the boy, saying:
"Now that I have released you to practice the Way, you must return at regular intervals."
Having received permission from her parents, she went to the place where the Buddha was and asked,
"Have you granted me leave?"
He replied, "I have heard.
The Buddha then commanded him, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣus.

As he stroked their heads with his hand, their hair and beards fell away naturally, as if they had been shaved seven days prior; the saṃghāṭī robes clung to their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas.
He was taught the Four Noble Truths and immediately became an Arhat.
Because of his original vow, he returned home at once; putting on his robes and taking up his bowl, he stood at the gate.
At that time, a maidservant was washing rice and was about to discard the rinsing water; she extended her bowl and asked for some to drink.
The maidservant raised her head, recognized that it was the master of the house, and went inside to announce:
"The young master is outside.
His parents were filled with joy.
"If this child is truly so, I shall release you and make you a free man.
He then went out to welcome him in and prepared a meal for him, saying:
"The time has already passed; according to the Dharma, one should not eat.
His parents said, "Since it is already so today, come early tomorrow."
He immediately returned to his dwelling.
After he had departed, his parents instructed their wives:
"The son will come tomorrow."

"You all should well adorn yourselves with fine attire and ornaments, each exhausting your finest skills; if you can cause my son to return to the state of a layman, it will be a great benefit for you."

He further commanded the treasury official to bring out various precious treasures—gold, silver, and the seven kinds of jewels—each gathered separately, hoping that the boy’s mind would be moved and he would return to worldly life.
The next day at mealtime, [the boy] returned with his alms-bowl and, having taken his seat, sat down.
The various wives and court ladies each assumed graceful postures; some scattered flowers and incense, while others brushed their robes or plucked blades of grass.
Pāra said, "Sisters, why trouble yourselves so?"
The women thought to themselves,
"He who treats us as sisters will likely have no intention of returning [us].
They said to their parents:
"What is the use of these precious objects?
They merely delude people and lead to calamities.
Why not cast them away in the mountains or marshes?"
His parents admonished him, saying,
"If the Way and its virtue reside within your heart, why must you leave the household life?
The elder Citta also attained the Way while remaining at home."
He said: "I have never heard of anyone who, while remaining a householder, attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya).
As for what Citra has attained, it is merely because one more birth remains; how can this be considered anything worthy of praise?"
Although he cast aside noble treasures and exquisite jade as if they were mere refuse, he was thus called the foremost among those who have left the household life.
As for why Kātyāyana was praised as one who excels at discerning the meaning of the Dharma, it was because when he wished to compile the teachings, he reflected in his mind:
"The human world is tumultuous; there, refined contemplation cannot be focused."
Therefore, he remained hidden within the earth for seven days; having completed the compilation of the Great Dharma, he presented it to the Buddha, who exclaimed: "Excellent!"
"Endorsed by the Noble Ones, it is established as one Piṭaka.
This meaning is subtle and profound, subduing the non-Buddhists; therefore, it is called 'foremost.
Furthermore, regarding its being called 'foremost': when the World-Honored One arrived at the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he sat beneath a tree holding a staff."
The Śākyas all came to see the Buddha, saying:
"In the past you abandoned our daughter; her physical marks were even more excellent than before.
What is your intention now?"
He replied: "The mind does not cling to the world, nor is it defiled by the mundane.
The brahmin said:
"Excellent," he replied,
accepted the explanation, and departed.
Later, the bhikṣus did not understand these words and asked Kātyāyana:
“The Buddha has declared that you, O worthy one, are foremost in eloquence, analytical discernment, and understanding the meaning.
Regarding the Blessed One’s response to the brahmin concerning being unstained and unattached—what is the meaning of this?”
Then Kātyāyana explained for him:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that conditioned by the eye and forms, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, perception arises; conditioned by perception, contact arises; and conditioned by contact, consciousness arises. From this, a mind of defiled attachment is produced."
"In this regard, one has forever abandoned all attachment.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, their minds remained dissatisfied. Kātyāyana, observing that the bhikṣus did not yet understand his meaning, drew an analogy, saying:
"Suppose there were someone who, seeking something solid here, instead discarded the root and took the branches and leaves."
"Is it firmly established? He replied, "It is not."
“You all are just like this. The Buddha dwells near you, yet you instead come to question him; is this not to abandon the root and grasp the branches?
The bhikṣus then went to question the Buddha, reporting that Kātyāyana’s explanation was as follows:
"I wonder if what he said was correct?
The Buddha replied, "It is exactly as Kātyāyana has stated; there is no difference whatsoever."
For this reason, he is further called the foremost.

As for why Koṇḍañña is called the foremost in counting the voting sticks (*śalākā*), generally speaking, a voting stick is used to record the number of people and to know whether they are acting with sincerity or not.
The answer is: if one receives the tally with sincerity, one will obtain its merit; however, for one who receives it through falsehood, the accumulated sin becomes ever greater.
In the Han language, this is called a "tally" (chou); in India, it is known as a *śalākā*.
*Śāla* is also called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*), meaning that merit is exhausted by demerit, and demerit is exhausted by merit.
How do we know this is so? Formerly, Ānanda’s maternal aunt married into the country of the Nirgranthas; she asked the Buddha:
"Is this acceptable?
The Buddha said,
"You should know that now is the time."
"Your visit will surely be beneficial.
Once the woman arrived, she invited the World-Honored One from afar.
The Buddha, knowing her intention, silently accepted the invitation.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda, saying:
"Tomorrow we shall accept the invitation of Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son, Śramaṇa-māna.
Ring the *gandī* to assemble the community and perform a supernatural feat."

At the time of the *śalākā* (voting sticks), the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna had not yet attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Upon hearing that voting sticks were being distributed for a formal invitation, he felt self-contempt at his lack of such powers; he looked upon his own form as he sat at the head of the assembly, like an old wild fox atop Mount Purple Gold.
Reflecting deeply on whether to proceed or retreat, he wished to accept the tally, yet it was not according to established custom;
he wished to decline it, yet as the presiding elder, even an eight-year-old śrāmaṇera could attain supernatural powers, while he, despite years of effort, had gained nothing.
Reflecting thus, he thought, "Of what use is it to remain alive?
As he felt this profound resolve and received the tally, in the very moment he returned it, his outflows were suddenly exhausted.
Had he received the tally based on false views, there are nine million pores on a human body; even by that count, one could not have received such a multitude of human lives.
If one receives [the teaching] with sincerity and devotion, one may immediately attain the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya); this Elder can serve as clear proof of this.
As for why he is called an Elder (sthavira), it is because he is well able to preach the Dharma in a manner that suits the assembly, and thus he was elected as an Elder by the multitude.
For these reasons, he is called the foremost among the elders in receiving the tally (*śalākā*).

As for why Piṇḍola is said to be able to subdue the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): in the city of Vaiśālī there was a householder named Citta, who constantly resented the six teachers for their arrogance and pride as they said, "The śramaṇa Gautama claims to be supreme;
we shall compete with him in feats of skill. If he displays one, we shall display two; thus we shall double it up to thirty-two."
Then the elder, having invited all the monks both inside and outside for a meal offering, erected a great banner forty-nine feet high and placed a sandalwood bowl upon it, proclaiming:
"Whoever can reach out their hand and take this bowl shall be the foremost."
At that time, Piṇḍola thought to himself:
"I shall now manifest my supernormal powers to cause the six teachers to be silenced and subdued.
He further thought:
"The World-Honored One has constantly admonished all his disciples that they must not manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
If I do not manifest them now, I fear they will incur sin forever;
yet if I do manifest them, I fear I am violating the Venerable One’s instruction."
After looking up and down repeatedly, he manifested his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and reached out his hand to take this sandalwood bowl.
Ascending into the air, he circled the city seven times and returned to his seat, saying to the brahmins:
"You all must now manifest a second one as well."
The six masters remained silent.
Then a great ghost general named Paṃśu said to the six masters, "Quickly manifest your two [miracles].
At that time, the followers of the six masters did not know where to go.
Speaking from this perspective, it is known that Piṇḍola’s subduing of the non-Buddhists was the foremost.

As for why the Bhikṣu Kṣema is called the foremost in tending to the sick: at that time, there was a bhikṣu in the Jetavana Monastery who was gravely ill; he had been bedridden for a long time, and worms emerged from beneath his back as he groaned all day long.
The Buddha, together with the bhikṣus, was inspecting the dwellings when he saw this bhikṣu so severely ill;
he asked, "Is anyone attending to you?"
He replied, "There is none. He asked again:
"Have you ever previously attended to the illnesses of others? He replied, "No."
The Buddha said,
"Since you do not attend to the illnesses of others, how can you expect others to attend to yours?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata folded his saṃghāṭī robe, rubbed it with his own hands, and washed it for him.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, also came to assist the World-Honored One in attending to the sick monk.
Thereupon, through the grace of the World-Honored One, the sick monk was immediately healed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if there is anyone who is ill, you should look after one another.
Then the World-Honored One turned and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Who is able to constantly attend to the sick?
Only the bhikṣu Caṇḍa. The bhikṣu Caṇḍa constantly attends to the sick by means of five matters."

What are these five? They are: discerning excellent medicines; not being indolent, rising first and retiring last; always delighting in conversation and sleeping little; making offerings according to the Dharma rather than craving food and drink; and being capable of preaching the Dharma to the sick.
This is called the monk Keṇiya attending to a patient with these five dharmas; there has never been one who did not recover. Why is this?

Because in former lives, for five hundred births, this monk was a physician; he was skilled in prescriptions and medicines, able to discern the source of a disease by listening to sounds and observing complexions, and he further attended to and nourished the sick with the four requisites.
For these reasons, he was called the Bhikṣu Śāṇakavāsin, foremost among those who tend to the sick.

As for why the Bhikṣu Puṇyavasu was called one capable of composing verses and hymns: in a previous life, when he was the son of an elder, he possessed natural genius and such brilliant intelligence that he would spontaneously compose eulogies upon encountering any object.

At that time, while out on an excursion, he encountered a courtesan whose appearance was so exceptionally beautiful as to be rare in the world; beholding her, his heart rejoiced and he desired to take her as his wife.
Upon returning home, he informed his parents of what he had seen, saying:
"I pray my parents will arrange a marriage for me."
His parents were displeased and said, "You are of noble lineage; how can you change your course and ruin the traditions of your ancestors?
His son was resolute and replied again with renewed earnestness:
"If you do not take me as your wife, I shall not be able to remain in this world.
Seeing that his son's words were so earnest, his parents could not bear to rebuke or restrain him, and they said,
"It shall be as you wish."
