"This is not something I know," he said, and immediately dispatched a messenger to communicate with the girl's family.
The girl's family were of an artisan lineage, for whom craft was their primary concern; they replied to the messenger, saying:
"I do not covet your wealth;
however, should you be able to master all various arts, I shall then take you as my companion.
Upon hearing this, Pengqi immediately went to a skilled craftsman to study the various arts, and before several weeks had passed, he had mastered them all.
He sent a messenger again with the message:
"Your studies are now complete; you may bestow [the teachings] upon me. The host replied:
"If one is fully proficient in the arts, they should come to the king for a trial.
At that time, during a festival, the king assembled those skilled in various arts to test their talents; to whoever was the most excellent, he would grant a thousand taels of gold.
The king also heard that this woman was exquisite and desired to take her into his palace.
He tested her in various arts and techniques, finding her preeminent in the art of the *yaṣṭi* (pole-climbing).
A pole forty-nine feet high was erected, with swords and blades placed at its base, all with their edges pointing upward, leaving only narrow gaps through which one could pass.
At that time, Paṅkadhvaja spun seven times through the air above and then cast himself down onto the open ground.
Fearing he might lose his daughter, the king feigned not looking at him.
Everyone said, "Excellent!"
The king said,
“I did not see it.
If you have truly mastered this, perform it once more.”
Pengkī thought to himself:
"If I do not comply with the king's command, I will surely lose this woman; I must strive for the sake of this single fruit of my desire.
With death at his heels, Pengkī climbed up once more; having reached the top of the banner, he looked upon the woman’s face and thought to himself:
"Why has this man been brought to such distress?
Her heart was filled with dread and her body trembled, fearing she would not survive:
"A woman's deceptions—what use are they for this?"
The Buddha knew that this person could certainly be saved, for had he not been rescued, he would have fallen into the three miserable realms.
He addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"By means of your supernormal powers, rescue him from his perilous distress."

Maudgalyāyana, having received these instructions, immediately went there to manifest his supernatural transformations; he sat cross-legged in mid-air and further manifested a staircase of the seven treasures beneath the banner, which others did not see, but Puṇya alone beheld.
He descended seven turns down the ladder at a leisurely pace; through his supernormal power, he was supported from within while appearing precarious from without.
The king and the multitude were greatly amazed by this marvel. The king personally led the woman by the hand and entrusted her to Paṅgu.
Peng Qi said:

"Do not use these deceptive and false things to delude and mislead the people of the world and lead the upright astray; there is nothing that causes the ruin of nations and the destruction of families that does not stem from them."
He immediately followed Maudgalyāyana to visit the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said to him, “Welcome, bhikṣu.”
He immediately became a śramaṇa.
For him, the Four Noble Truths were expounded, and he attained arhatship. With joy arising from within and manifesting in his speech, he composed a verse in praise of the World-Honored One:
"On this pure fifteenth day, Five hundred bhikṣus have assembled."
Having severed all fetters and latent tendencies, the seer no longer undergoes conditioned existence.
Like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded on all sides by his ministers,
he governs the four seas and the earth without leaving any trace behind.
Subduing people in this manner, the unsurpassed Teacher protects all his śrāvakas,
whose nature has destroyed the fetters through the three types of supernormal knowledge.
All these sons of the World-Honored One are free from the defilement of dust and impurity.
"Having already torn asunder the net of craving and desire, you now pay homage to the moon among the stars.
For this reason, Paṅkadhā was proclaimed foremost among those capable of composing verses to praise the virtues of the Tathāgata.

The reason Koṣṭhila is called foremost among those possessing the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) is that, generally speaking, the four analytical knowledges of a śrāvaka are not necessarily complete; some may possess the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) but lack the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), some may possess the analytical knowledge of meaning but lack the analytical knowledge of phenomena, some may possess the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) but lack the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and some may possess the analytical knowledge of expression but lack the analytical knowledge of eloquence. Koṣṭhila, however, possesses all four of these analytical knowledges in their entirety.

Śāriputra and Kātyāyana also possessed the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), yet they were not designated as the foremost because Śāriputra considered wisdom to be his primary attribute, while Kātyāyana considered compilation and redaction to be his primary attribute; thus, each was not called foremost for those specific qualities. Furthermore, even with their four analytical knowledges, they could not equal Kauṣṭhila.
Kauṣṭhila could not exhaust the meaning of a single phrase even in seven days; how much less, then, can the four analytical knowledges (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) be measured?
For this reason, he is foremost among those possessing the four analytical knowledges.

The reason Nandika Bhikṣu is called foremost among those who beg for alms is that although other bhikṣus also beg for alms, they may not be fully observant of the precepts, or they may harbor covetous thoughts, or their minds may lack single-mindedness as they glance left and right, or they may seek to avoid the cold and heat.
However, when this bhikṣu went on his almsround, none of these things occurred; since his begging was so pure, the merit of the donors was great.
I now cite this analogy to illustrate the difference between the small and the great.
Someone asked about the art of archery:
"If one person shoots at a dark hair from a hundred paces away, and another person shoots so that dust from the ground rises,
which is more difficult?"
He replied: "The dark hair is difficult; though one shoots at it, it does not hit the ground.
This is not worth mentioning.
Whether one gives to a mendicant or to the Sangha, which is greater?
Giving to a true *āraṇyaka* is superior.
The parable of the blind man shooting at the sky illustrates that giving to one who is not a true practitioner is like shooting into empty space.
Although this matter is difficult, there is both gain and loss.

The arrow hitting the ground is a metaphor for making offerings to the Sangha; though shooting at the hair is refined, there are many instances of failure, whereas shooting at the ground is easy and never misses the ground.
Because the field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) is deep and vast, there is neither increase nor decrease; because the forest hermitage (āraṇya) is either refined or coarse, there is both gain and loss.
Nandika attained mastery over the vital essence (ojas), and was therefore called the foremost.
As for why Śīla is called "One-Sitting-One-Meal," this refers to one of the dhūta practices.
Now, as for the *āraṇyaka* dharma, it consists of either begging for food, sitting beneath trees, or dwelling in seclusion alone.
As for "sitting once and eating once" (*ekāsanika*), from morning until midday, regardless of whether a donor offers food in small or large quantities, one simply sits and eats at a single location.
If one has not yet finished eating and has not yet moved from one's seat, one may eat again; however, once one has risen, one must not eat further.
Because he always eats in one place and never leaves it, Śrāmaṇa is called the foremost.
As for why he is called the Bhikṣu Kumbhīra, he always goes to seven houses to beg for alms and never exceeds seven.
The reason for this is that he established a vow to limit himself to seven.

When begging for alms, one desires to bring blessings and deliver sentient beings; with single-minded devotion, one contemplates the Way without thoughts of greed. Whether obtaining good or bad food, one neither increases nor decreases [one's resolve], begging in due order without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy.
If one receives food from one or two families and there is another donor, one stops if it is sufficient; if it is not sufficient, one accepts more.

If one goes to seven families and receives no food, one returns to one’s dwelling to contemplate and practice the Way, without thinking about whether one will go to such-and-such a house or not go to such-and-such a house tomorrow. Since there is no thought of discrimination at all, they are called "Seven-House Śramaṇas."
Upon returning, he would sit in meditation, withdrawing his mind to dwell in the Way; thus, Kumbhīra was ranked first among the seven families for begging for alms.

The Bhikṣu Dṛḍha took it as his practice to constantly reside in secluded and tranquil places such as mountains and marshes; the Bhikṣu Nandika took it as his practice to always beg for alms and endure insults; the Bhikṣu Kumbhīra took it as his practice to beg from seven families; and the Bhikṣu Śaila took it as his practice to eat at a single location—each of these twelve dhūtas abided in their own respective practice.
As for the bhikṣu Fumi, he maintained the three robes, never parting from them even while eating or resting.
Some say that he made the three robes because of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma;
others say it was for the sake of the three periods of time.
Some say that three robes were established for the sake of the three seasons: one wears heavy ones in winter, light ones in summer, and medium ones in spring and autumn.
For these three seasons, one should possess the three robes: the heavy one with five strips, the medium one with seven strips, and the light one with fifteen strips.
When it is very cold, one may wear the heavy robe as an outer layer to provide protection.
Some say that the three robes were established for the sake of mosquitoes, gadflies, and dragonflies;
because of these reasons, he constantly maintained them without forgetting, and thus they are called "the foremost.

As for why he is called Bhikṣu Pañcasika, when he was originally a householder, he constantly regarded his home as a source of affliction, and after leaving the household life to seek the Way, he frequently sat in the open air.

If one enters a chamber, the breath is constantly stifled and obstructed, as if the mouth were being covered; for this reason, one should always seek to sit in the open air to contemplate and practice the Path, whereby the body will become harmonious, the breath will flow freely, and one may practice the Path without hindrance.
For these reasons, he is called the foremost among those who dwell under the open sky.

As for why he is called Vakkula, the one who dwells constantly beneath trees and is free from doubt: while still on the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), desiring to seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he dwelt beneath trees relying upon mental deliberation to eliminate his fetters and bonds.
Other bhikṣus also sat in meditation under trees, yet they were not so designated because they were unable to achieve single-minded concentration through hearing the teaching just once.
This bhikṣu, however, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching once, was immediately able to practice it with focused intent without abandoning it, and within six years he exhausted all fetters.

As for the former, Pūrṇa, he delighted in roaming through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); his conduct was consistent whether moving or staying still, yet his delight lay in practicing various distinct matters, and thus each was called "foremost" in their respective fields.

As for why the bhikṣu Dharmadāsa is said to delight in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), this bhikṣu understood internal emptiness upon entering a house and understood external emptiness upon leaving it. Internal emptiness is a metaphor for consciousness (*vijñāna*), while external emptiness is a metaphor for the body; entering the house signifies penetrating the emptiness of consciousness, and leaving the house signifies understanding the emptiness of the body.
Having already realized internal and external emptiness, he understood that all phenomena are likewise so.
Upon hearing this teaching on emptiness, the bhikṣu took it to heart; entering a house and seeing its emptiness, he immediately attained realization regarding body-consciousness.
As for the other bhikṣus, they attained emptiness only after their fetters were exhausted; such an empty mind is difficult to obtain.
Because he was valued for his prior attainment, he was called "foremost.

As for why the bhikṣu Nīpa’s five rag-robes are considered supreme: this bhikṣu contemplated that his body was impure and leaking with thirty-six substances, having nothing worthy of greed or esteem. Because he felt weary of and loathed this body, he used these lowly objects to clothe himself.
Some say: "Regarding robes, there are those that may be approached and those that may not be approached.
Which ones may be approached?"
One who wears coarse clothing, causing others to feel shame and self-reproach, is one whom it is appropriate to associate with;
one who wears fine clothing, causing others to become arrogant and conceited, is one whom it is not appropriate to associate with.
Worn-out rags assist one's practice; therefore, he wears the five-patch robe (*pañcakaṣāya*).
This bhikṣu was well able to compare his inner state with external circumstances, and thus he was called the foremost.
As for why the bhikṣu Uttara is called "One Who Constantly Delights in Cemeteries," this bhikṣu was a disciple of Ānanda.
When my late teacher attained the Way, he thought to himself:
"This body wanders through transmigration, undergoing change in every place; when I was in the heavens, I enjoyed natural provisions, yet now they have been cast aside;
if I were among humans as a Wheel-Turning King, followed by the seven treasures, that too has passed away."
Or if one is constantly eating grass and thorns as an animal, this too is past;
or if one is among the hungry ghosts with molten copper for food, or in the hells with swords and blades as adversaries—all such forms of retribution for offenses are likewise past.

Now that we have obtained a human body, once this portion of our allotted time is completed, everything esteemed throughout antiquity and the present will be nothing but discarded objects—illusory and precarious forms, not one of which is worth coveting; all should be cast aside.
He then stayed among the burial mounds and thought to himself:
"I desire to dwell among trees, mountains, and marshes; these are all places coveted by the common people, whereas only the vicinity of burial mounds is unpleasant to them."
Therefore, he dwelt there.
"In these charnel grounds, the only beings who find delight are ghosts, along with foxes, wolves, crows, and owls; now I shall enter the Samādhi of Compassion to deliver those kinds of beings."
For this reason, he again dwelt among the tombs.
By these causes and conditions, he constantly delighted in being among the tombs rather than dwelling among people; therefore, he was called the foremost.
As for why the bhikṣu Rohiṇī is called the foremost of those who always sit upon grass mats, it is because this bhikṣu constantly sits upon grass mats to eliminate all affectionate attachment.
How does one eliminate craving?
Although there may be golden couches and jade desks, one remains entirely free from attachment to them.
Or, as it is further said:
If there is someone who offers an exquisite seat, it is no different from offering a seat of grass.
Once the heart of attachment has been exhausted, all fetters are likewise exhausted; thus, he takes the grass in his hand and pays homage to the grass.
Someone asked, "Why do you prostrate toward the grass? He replied:
"I have exhausted my mind's adornment because of these grasses.
Since it was through them that I attained the Way, they are my teachers; therefore, I prostrate before them.
The five hundred monkeys were reborn in the heavens, and they too scattered celestial mandārava flowers over the former corpse.
Because one is born into heaven from a corpse, they have come here to scatter flowers.
Now, that which is noble must take the humble as its foundation; for this reason, sitting upon a mat of grass is called the foremost.

The reason the Bhikṣu Ujjñāna is called the foremost among those who do not speak with others and walk while looking at the ground is that this bhikṣu was constantly plagued by faults of speech. Desiring to reform them, he reflected to himself:

"It is precisely because of these words that I have been born among gods and humans, yet also suffered the wailing and shrieking of the three miserable realms and the hells; thus, throughout the five paths of existence, I have undergone immeasurable suffering."
"I shall now, like Prince Mupai, bind myself by oath not to speak; how then could the four transgressions and three calamities arise?
Having thus remained silent, he walked with his gaze fixed straight ahead.
The Buddha marveled at his ability to do so and frequently praised his virtue before the bhikṣus.
He said to Ānanda,
"A bhikṣu such as this should be recorded and remembered, so as to serve as a model for future generations."
For these reasons, he is called the foremost.

As for why this bhikṣu is called the foremost in one-pointedness of mind and samādhi: in the past, this bhikṣu had practiced meditative concentration, refining the coarse until reaching the subtle. Now that the power of his concentration is established, his mental activity is like drifting dust; sitting, he forgets all thoughts, and this state of forgetting thoughts is sufficient in principle.
What is this analogy?
It is like a person who has eaten food of a hundred flavors and, being fully satiated, no longer has any desire for more food.
Although they still walk, stop, advance, or retreat, these actions occur only in response to a stimulus and only after being prompted. They move only when there is a reason.
Because he established his characters based on meditative concentration, it is said that he was foremost among those who sat, rose, walked, and entered into samādhi.
As for why Dharmaruci is called foremost among those who delight in traveling afar, there is a reason for this.
When the Buddha was in the world, there was an elder named Dharmaruci who came to the Buddha’s dwelling, paid his respects, and inquired after his well-being.
The Buddha said, “Dharmaruci, it has been a very long time since we last met; it is good that you have come to see me.”
Someone asked the Buddha,
"I wonder why you say it has been a very long time since we last met?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Do you wish to know? He replied, "I wish to know."
The Buddha said:
"In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in the world named Dīpaṃkara.
At that time, I was a brahmin named Vimalacitra."
At that time, as Dipankara Buddha was about to enter the city, I encountered him midway.
Seeing the Buddha’s radiant marks spreading forth their brilliance, I immediately exclaimed:
"The World-Honored One’s radiant marks are more luminous than the sun and moon;..."
"The Virtue of the World-Honored One exalts the two polarities of heaven and earth;
the Mind of the World-Honored One is more benevolent than a compassionate mother.
Looking back upon my own form and shadow, I find nothing with which to offer him.
"Now is precisely the right time; this field of merit is fertile and excellent, fit for planting roots.

Seeing that there was a small amount of mud on the ground, he feared it might soil the Buddha’s feet; he immediately untied his hair and spread it upon the mud, so that the Buddha might tread upon it and pass by.
The Buddha then gave this prediction:
"Your courage is indeed such as this.
After incalculable kalpas (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa), you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
At that time, there was also a brahmin at the edge of the group who, giving rise to a mind of resentment, said:
"This man is no different from a beast; he has even stepped upon another's hair as he passes by."
From that time forward, for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he constantly fell among the animals.
Furthermore, in the great ocean, he became a makara fish, his body seven thousand *yojana* in length.

At that time, there were five hundred merchants who, having boarded a ship to enter the sea to gather treasures, encountered this great fish that swallowed their vessel, on the verge of drawing them into its mouth.
The five hundred men were struck with terror and each invoked the deity they served.
Then the merchant leader spoke to the crowd, saying:
"In this world there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni; there is none superior to him in rescuing people from peril and distress.
Let us invoke his name, hoping to obtain deliverance."
They immediately called out in unison.
Hearing the Buddha’s name, the fish’s fundamental consciousness remained intact, and it thought to itself:
"Śākyamuni Buddha has already appeared in the world."
"Why is my body here among these fish?
Having said this, he immediately sank back into the water.
The five hundred merchants returned in safety.

At that time, the fish emerged halfway out onto the sand altar; for two weeks and seven days, it neither drank nor ate, and upon its death, it was reborn as the son of a householder, named Dharmaruci.
"It is only now that you have come to meet me;
for this reason, I spoke of it as being from long ago.

Upon hearing the full account of these events, Kumārajīva immediately went to the seashore to search for the old corpse. There he saw a large fish by the shore, its bones, skin, and flesh already completely consumed.
He then walked upon the ribs of the skeleton and reflected, saying:
"This was my own corpse. He immediately scattered flowers over the remains of his former body.
Reflecting upon the past, he suddenly attained the Way.
For these reasons, he is called the foremost among those who travel afar.

As for why the bhikṣu Kātyāyana is called the foremost in assembling the multitude and preaching the Dharma, it is because this bhikṣu’s speech was clear and eloquent, and his voice resounded far and wide.
Upon hearing the sound, an immeasurable multitude gathered, and he immediately expounded for them the profound and sublime teaching of the Dharma:
"All you people, you should know that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter, and the nectar of the Four Noble Truths is likewise difficult to hear."
"Whenever you all gather, you should contemplate the True Dharma, eliminate the bonds of the twelve links of dependent origination, and you shall attain Nirvana.

This bhikṣu constantly assisted the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of beings] and perpetually ensured that this teaching did not fall to the ground. For these reasons, he was renowned as the foremost in the sound of his voice when preaching the Dharma to the assembled multitude.

The reason Vakkula is called one whose lifespan is extremely long is that in the past he once made offerings to sixty thousand Buddhas; in the presence of those Buddhas he constantly practiced a mind of loving-kindness, extending compassion and pity at all times to all living beings, even the smallest insects and crawling creatures, never harboring even a hair’s breadth of intent to harm them.
"By virtue of this merit from loving-kindness, I have now obtained its retribution.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As my physical body today is pure and stainless beyond compare—just as a lotus flower is unsullied by mud and water—I am now exactly eighty years of age."

It is not as with Bakula, whose lifespan was one hundred and sixty years; the Tathāgata, conforming to the world’s desires and adapting to sentient beings, does not manifest such extraordinary longevity, and thus his lifespan is eighty years.
"Pakula received the merit of his compassionate heart from a previous life; therefore, he obtained the reward of a lifespan that was doubled.
Someone asked:
"Is it the case that one obtains such a long life simply by means of a compassionate heart?"
"Is there yet another?
He replied,
"There is."
In the past, when the Tathāgata Vipaśyin appeared in the world, there were one hundred and sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus traveling about to teach and transform others.
At that time, there was an elder named Mingzhengxiu who lived among them; he was naturally kind and humble, and did not take pleasure in drinking alcohol.

At that time, during a seasonal festival, he was exhorted by his peers to drink sparingly; yet, under the influence of alcohol, he went to the World-Honored One. Having paid homage and inquired after his well-being, he then invited the Buddha and his disciples, saying:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation for ninety days."
“May all the bhikṣus who are ill come to my house to receive medicine; whatever they require, let them come and take it.
Having finished speaking, he returned home and instructed his household, saying:
“I have invited the Buddha and his disciples to provide them with the four requisites of offerings; you must prepare everything accordingly.”
Having finished his instructions, he fell asleep.
After a long time, he woke up, and his wife said to him, "You previously instructed me to prepare the offerings with great care; yet now you remain silent—this is why it has come to this."
The elder was startled and asked, "What did I say just now?
His wife replied:
"Did you not say anything while you were awake?
He replied, "I do not recall saying anything."
The wife said, "My lord, you previously stated:
'I have already invited the Buddha and his disciples to provide for their needs and deficiencies for ninety days.'"
“Did he not speak these words?
The elder reflected and said,
“The delusion wrought by alcohol has reached such an extreme.”
Having thus felt shame and remorse, he immediately extended an invitation.
At dawn the following day, he burned incense in his house and invited the World-Honored One from afar.
A certain bhikṣu came to request medicine, and the elder asked him:
"What is your ailment? He replied,
"I suffer from a headache."
The elder said, "This must be water above the diaphragm attacking the head from below; that is why there is a headache.
He then offered a harītakī fruit.
"Simply taking this medicine will suffice to eliminate this ailment.
The bhikṣu took the medicine, and his illness was immediately cured.
By virtue of this meritorious retribution, he remained free from illness for ninety-one kalpas.

Born into a householder’s family, he reached the age of eighty before leaving home to study the Way; he practiced for eighty years, making a total of one hundred and sixty years from his birth to the end of his life as a monk and layman combined.
During his time as a layman, he once engaged in a bull-fight, after which he suffered a headache that was immediately cured.
From that time forth, he was always free from illness.
For this reason, Bakula is foremost among those of long life.

That he lived sixty years beyond the standard hundred-year lifespan is most extraordinary amidst the lifespans of this age of five corruptions; it is like a lotus flower growing from within filth and stench.
Ānanda asked Bakkula:
"Why do you not preach the Dharma for others?
Is it because you lack the four analytical knowledges, or is it because you are deficient in wisdom that you do not preach the Dharma?"

He replied: "It is not that I lack the swift wisdom of the four analytical knowledges; it is simply that I delight in tranquility and do not enjoy clamor, and for this reason I do not preach the Dharma."
An objection was raised:
"Why did the long-lived Pāṭikāra not take birth in the other three directions?
The answer was:
The reason the Buddhas were not born [there] was because the people of that land were difficult to transform.

The sentient beings of this land possess sharp and swift faculties; they are extremely fierce and courageous, making it not difficult for them to attain the Way. For this reason, all the Buddhas of antiquity were born within this realm.
Vakkula should have attained enlightenment here; therefore, he was not reborn in the other three directions.
As for why he is called "Pūrṇa, the Son of Fullness," and foremost in preaching the Dharma, there are three matters by which one is designated as foremost:
although other bhikṣus also preach the Dharma, they lack these three qualities that can be recorded, and thus they are not called foremost.

When Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra preached the Dharma, he first employed his eloquence to issue forth sublime sounds, causing those in the assembly to rejoice and look up to him with unified devotion. Next, he used words of bitter reproof to chastise their hearts, causing them to feel inwardly corroded and solemnly awestruck, thereby giving rise to the realization that such an encounter is difficult to find. Finally, he concluded with the teachings of luminous wisdom and emptiness; upon hearing these, the knots of their afflictions were untied, allowing tranquility and insight to nourish one another.

The World-Honored One expounds the Dharma that is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; so too is Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. These three matters are all excellent, and none can surpass them except for the Tathāgata himself.
Śāriputra made a vow:
"From dawn until noon, I shall certainly deliver one person and cause them to reach the stage of the Path."
The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana also vowed to deliver sentient beings; among the four stages of realization, he would only eat after advancing one stage.
The other bhikṣus all likewise delivered sentient beings, yet they were not even a hundredth part as effective as Pūrṇa.

From the time he attained enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra saved ninety-nine thousand people; among all the śrāvakas, he saved the greatest number of persons, and is therefore called the foremost in preaching the Dharma.

The reason Upāli is called foremost in upholding the Vinaya is that, in the past, when the Buddha returned to his native country to accept the invitation of his father, the king, the bhikṣus who accompanied him, though pure in mind, lacked a dignified outward appearance.

At that time, the King, wishing to encourage the sons of noble Śākya clansmen to leave the household life and become bhikṣus to serve as attendants to the World-Honored One, issued a proclamation to all the Śākyas:
"Among those who have two brothers, one of them shall each leave the household life to practice the Way."
"If you do not comply with this command, you shall be severely punished.
At that time, there was a son of the Śākyas named Śimśapāvan, the eldest among the Śākyas, who was next in order to have his hair shorn first.
Then the Buddha commanded Upāli to shave their heads, and he further instructed him, saying:
"These Śākya clansmen have bodies accustomed to luxury and are delicate; you must shave them carefully, slowly, and with a light hand."
Upāli then applied it with a light hand;
however, it was too light and did not adhere. Upāli then turned the blade over and used its back.
The Buddha said:
"No," he replied. Again, he used the belly of the blade,
saying once more, "No."
He then used a razor to shave from the crown of his head, removing it until it was completely gone.
All five hundred Śākya youths did likewise.
The Buddha then addressed Upāli, saying:
“Welcome, Bhikṣu! he said, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha then conferred the precepts upon him, and he attained arhatship.
Next, he conferred the precepts upon five hundred sons of the Śākya clan,
with Upāli serving as the presiding elder (upādhyāya).
Having rubbed the heads of the five hundred men with his hand and completed the ordination of his disciples, they were then required to pay homage to Upāli.
The Śākyas had long been haughty and arrogant, unable to humble themselves, and moreover, since he was their own kinsman, they each said, "This is a servant of our household;
for what reason should we pay him homage?"
The Buddha said, "It is not so.
In the Dharma there is neither noble nor base; those who arrive first are the elder brothers, and those who arrive later are the younger brothers."
He bowed his head repeatedly, restraining his will to perform the ritual.
Immediately, heaven and earth shook greatly, and the devas from above praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Today the Śākyas have subdued their arrogance; because this intention is difficult to overcome, the earth has trembled.
When the five hundred Śākyas entered the Way, ninety-nine thousand others also left the household life to enter the Way.
Since Upāli first received the precepts from the Buddha, he has never committed even a hair’s breadth of transgression; for this reason, he is called the foremost.
Is it only because of this that he is so designated? Or is there yet another reason?
To the north of the Jeta Grove Monastery lived a bhikṣu who had been ill for six years without recovery.
At that time, Upāli went to inquire of the bhikṣu:
"What is your ailment and suffering?"
"If you have something you require, speak of it. He replied,
"That which I require cannot be spoken of."
He asked again, "What do you require? If it is not here,
I shall seek it from the four directions."
"If it does not exist in the world, I shall seek it in the heavens above.
He replied, "That which I require exists within the city of Śrāvastī; however, because it would contravene the Buddha's teachings, I cannot speak of it."
He said: "Simply speak, and there will be no suffering. He replied:
"I was thinking only of wine.
If I could obtain five *śīrṣa* of wine, my illness would be cured. Upāli said:
"Wait a moment; I shall ask the Buddha for you.
Having returned, he immediately asked the Buddha:
"A bhikṣu is ill and requires wine as medicine.
I wonder if it may be drunk?
The World-Honored One said:
"I have prescribed a rule that excludes those who are ill.
Upāli immediately went back to seek out wine and gave it to him; his illness was instantly cured.
Upāli then preached the Dharma to him again, and he attained the path of an Arhat.
The Buddha praised Upāli:
"It is well that you have asked the Tathāgata about this matter, so that the sick bhikṣu may receive healing and further attain the Way.
Had this bhikṣu not attained deliverance, he would later have fallen into the three miserable realms as a sentient being with no prospect of escape."
"You shall expound the prohibitive precepts for future bhikṣus, so that they may discern the gravity of offenses and be delivered from peril.
You are truly capable of upholding the Vinaya; I entrust the Vinaya Piṭaka to you, lest it be lost."
"This treasury is the most innermost among all treasuries; it must not be shown to śrāmaṇeras or laypeople.
For this reason, it is further called the foremost.

The reason the bhikṣu Vakkali is called one who has attained liberation through faith is that this bhikṣu had been bedridden with chronic illness for six years, during which all those who attended to him eventually abandoned him.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:

"I have been afflicted by this illness for a long time; the burden of nursing me has become exhausting and deeply wearying. Furthermore, the Tathāgata has not shown me his compassionate grace. I shall therefore take my own life to end this suffering."
He immediately sought out a knife and addressed it, saying:
"Will you sever my fetters as soon as you kill me? Having finished speaking, he cut his own throat;
by the time the blade reached halfway down his throat, he attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), and upon the severing of his head, he entered *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the great earth shook, which moved Pāpīyas.
Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"What auspicious omen is this, that the earth trembles so violently?"
He then used his divine eye to observe the bhikṣu who had committed suicide.
"Where has his physical form and spirit gone?
He searched throughout all the heavens but did not see his spirit; he further searched among human beings but saw it not; he further searched within the three evil realms, yet still saw it not.
At that time, the Buddha, leading the bhikṣus, intended to perform the cremation; he saw the fire rising from the corpse.
This Pāpīyas had set the fire to seek the spirits of the bhikṣus, but he did not know where they were at all.
The reason they sought it was that they wished to know its progression and to destroy it so that it would not be established.
The bhikṣus then cremated it. The Buddha praised these bhikṣus for attaining liberation through faith (*śraddhā-vimukti*).
Someone asked:
"If one who possesses ultimate sincerity entrusts their life to nature (*ziran*), they would not even grasp a staff; how then could they provide for themselves, let alone harm themselves?
He replied:
The reason one grasps the knife is that the knife is taken as the sword of wisdom, intended to sever all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The body is the very root of these fetters; when the root is cleared away, the branches follow, and when the body is severed, the fetters are eliminated. Therefore, grasping the knife does not constitute an obstruction, for one grasps the knife of faith to cut down the tree of doubt.
The subsequent phrase states: "The mind is free from hesitation.
From the stage of liberation through faith (*śraddhā-vimukta*) to the stage of liberation through non-doubt (*akopya-dharman*), one transforms dullness into sharpness.
For this reason, liberation through faith is designated as the foremost.
*Pinfen Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), Scroll Four; *Pinfen Gongde Lun*, Scroll Five.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Later Han Records.
The reason the Bhikṣu Nanda is called foremost in physical beauty is that while each of the other bhikṣus possesses their own set of marks—
Śāriputra has seven, Maudgalyāyana has five, and Ānanda has twenty— Nanda alone possesses thirty marks.
Nanda was the color of gold and Ānanda was the color of silver.

Their robes shone with brilliance, they wore sandals inlaid with gold, and carrying lapis lazuli bowls, they entered the city to beg for food; among those who saw them, there were none who were not filled with joy.
Apart from the Tathāgata himself, no other disciple could equal him; therefore, he was praised as the foremost in physical comeliness.
He is also called "one whose faculties are tranquil. Once, the Buddha led his disciples to the Āmrapālī Vihāra in Vaiśālī.

At that time, Nanda was walking in meditation outside. Hearing that the Buddha had arrived, the daughter of the Jambu tree felt joy in her heart; wishing to provide a modest offering, she went immediately to invite the Buddha.
Seeing Nanda walking in meditation outside, her feelings of affection and longing were deep; she prostrated at his feet in salutation and stroked them with her hands.
Though one beholds a beautiful form, there is no thought of passion; yet when forms interact, impurity is immediately lost.
Sweet flavors moisten the body, and when the body is full, it overflows; how could this overflow of impurity arise from the mind?
The daughter of the Jambu tree did not understand and suspected that he harbored lustful thoughts.
The Buddha, knowing her intention, said to her:
"Do not give rise to doubt."
"Nanda shall attain Arhatship seven days hence.
From this it may be known that the mind is immutable. As for why Bhikṣu Vātsīputra is said to resolve people's doubts and obstructions:

although all Buddhas of the three periods of time share the eighty-four thousand dharmas as their methods of practice, sentient beings who attain the Way do not necessarily perform every one of these practices; rather, they take as their primary principle that which accords with their own awakening.

Why is this? Because the fetters and afflictions of sentient beings differ; illnesses vary in number and defilements vary in degree. For this reason, the Tathāgata establishes various teachings: there may be a single medicine that cures many illnesses, or there may be many medicines that cure a single illness.
It is like the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) which mutually support one another, yet one practice serves as the primary guide while all other practices follow it.
This "one practice" does not have a fixed name; rather, it accords with the arising of a particular affliction, applying the appropriate remedy in response.
If the mind arises through the calculation of permanence, counter it with impermanence;
if the mind arises through the calculation of having a self, counter it with the emptiness of self.
When impermanence guides one's practice, all myriad practices are impermanent.
It is like performing eighty thousand acts of giving, where all eighty thousand are considered acts of giving; this is what is meant by "briefly explained.

Just as among the Tathāgata’s eightfold voice, one sound encompasses eight resonances, one resonance encompasses a hundred teachings, and one teaching encompasses a hundred meanings—each leading one another up to thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions; one sound responds to ten trillion variations, and its transformations are thus.
The analogy for this concise exposition of practice is likewise so.
Because this bhikṣu takes such concise exposition as his primary focus, he is called the foremost.

As for why the bhikṣu Sthavira is said to be able to expound the Dharma extensively: for thirty years while on the level of an ordinary person, this bhikṣu extensively expounded the Dharma for others, analyzing and distinguishing its meanings and principles.
How is this explained in detail?
Sometimes a single practice gives rise to many practices, branching out and proliferating until they become innumerable.
It is like how illnesses arise from mutual causes; therefore, the medicines prescribed correspond to one another to effect a cure.

This bhikṣu made analytical discernment his primary focus rather than prioritizing the severance of outflows; consequently, it was only after thirty years that he attained the realization of the Way, whereupon he became silent and ceased speaking, leaving behind his former traces.
His original achievements were recorded, and thus he is called the foremost in "Extensive Exposition.
As for why Deva-Subhūti is called the foremost in "Wearing Fine Robes," there were two Subhūtis among the five hundred disciples:
one of royal lineage and one of merchant lineage; Deva-Subhūti was of the royal lineage.

As for why they are called "heavenly beings," throughout five hundred lifetimes, they are constantly reborn above in the Heaven of Response to Sounds (Nirmāṇarati) and below in the families of kings; their enjoyment of blessings is spontaneous and never lacking.

When the Buddha returned to his native land, King Śuddhodana exhorted five hundred Śākya youths to leave the household life, study the Way, and serve as attendants to the World-Honored One; this bhikṣu was among those who left the household life according to that precedent.
At that time, the Buddha exhorted the bhikṣus:

"Those who practice the Way must all restrain their bodies and maintain their integrity; they should wear coarse clothing, eat poor food, use straw mats as beds, and take excrement and urine as medicine."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s urgent instruction, this bhikṣu reflected within himself:

“I was born into a noble and wealthy family where food and clothing were provided naturally; my palaces and dwellings were adorned with intricate carvings and engravings, featuring couches and beds of gold and silver, and dining vessels made of the seven precious gems. My body was clothed in garments woven from golden thread, and my feet were shod in exquisite sandals of thin gold leaf. Yet even so, my desires were not yet satisfied—how much less could I endure wearing these five-fold patched robes?”
"I shall now return home to fulfill my original intention.
Having thought this, he wished to depart.

At that time, the Buddha was at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, having accepted an invitation from King Prasenajit; [the man] immediately went to the Buddha’s location, took his leave, and returned.
Then Ānanda said to him,
"Please stay for one night. Subhūti replied:
"How can a practitioner of the Way find lodging in houses, beds, or seats?
For now, let us go to the home of a layperson to stay for one night;
tomorrow we shall return. Ānanda said:
"Stay for now; we shall prepare the offerings.

He then went to the king's presence and provided various seats, banners, canopies, flowers, and incense, as well as four lamps with oil, all meticulously adorned and fully prepared. The bhikṣu then stayed overnight there.

As he returned to his original state of mind, his thoughts immediately attained concentration; contemplating the Four Noble Truths until the last watch of the night, he attained Arhatship and then soared into the air.
Ānanda thought to himself:
"If this bhikṣu should leave the house, I fear someone will take away the royal items he borrowed."
He went to look for him, but he was not to be seen inside the house; looking up into the air, he saw him flying above.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “The heavenly Subhūti has already attained arhatship; he is now flying in the void.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There are two kinds of robes:
those that may be approached and those that may not be approached."
What may be approached? That which, when one wears fine clothing, increases the mind for the Path—this may be approached;
that which, when one wears fine clothing, diminishes the mind for the Path—this must not be approached.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Whether one attains the Way through fine robes or attains the Way through the five-fold rag-robe of a mendicant, awakening resides in the mind; it is not constrained by physical form or clothing.
Speaking from this perspective, among the gods, Subhūti is foremost in wearing fine robes.

As for why the bhikṣu Nandaka is called foremost in instruction: Śāriputra also provides instruction, yet he instructs all four assemblies of disciples such that, from morning until noon, he ensures at least one person attains the fruit of the path.
This bhikṣu is exclusively devoted to instructing bhikṣus so that they may attain arhatship.
He is like a skilled archer who, with a single arrow, strikes an enemy in a vital spot, causing him to fall and never rise again.
This illustrates how a bhikṣu who possesses skillful instruction and essential wisdom enables those who hear him to sever their fetters and proceed directly to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
One who is unskilled at archery, though he may employ many arrows, can truly discharge but a single one effectively.
To use Śāriputra as an analogy: although he extensively expounded wisdom, it ultimately resulted in but a single stage.
The distinction between superior and inferior is thus clearly evident; therefore, it is said that providing instruction to later students is the most supreme of all.
The reason why the bhikṣu Sumana so skillfully instructed the community of bhikṣuṇīs was that this bhikṣu constantly admonished the nuns with words of bitter urgency, saying:

"Women possess many emotional guiles; their seductive charms and elaborate adornments delude the people of the world. Their physical forms are filthy and leaking, with nine orifices of impurity; among the thirty-six constituent parts, not a single one is worth coveting."
As for the reason she is named Sumana, it is simply the name of a flower; because at the time of her birth this flower appeared spontaneously upon her ear, she was given that name after the flower.
At that time, King Bimbisāra came to where the Buddha was; seeing flowers upon the ear of this bhikṣu, he marveled and asked the Buddha:
"Is it lawful for a bhikṣu to wear flowers?"
The Buddha said to the king, "Your Majesty, pluck them yourself.
At that moment, the king pressed them away with his hand; they grew back immediately as before, and as he did not stop doing so, they eventually formed a cluster of flowers.
The King’s astonishment grew even greater, and he asked for the reason behind it.
The Buddha told the King:
"In the past, when Vipaśyin Tathāgata appeared in the world, this bhikṣu was the son of an elder."
At that time, having finished playing the lute and performing songs and dances for the annual festival, they went to where the Buddha was.
Upon seeing the Buddha, the elder was filled with joy and immediately took the flower from his ear and placed it upon the Buddha’s ear.
The Buddha then used his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to transform these flowers; they changed into a four-pillared platform suspended in mid-air, while the ears remained as they were before.
Upon seeing this transformation, the elder immediately made a vow:
"May I, in all future lives, encounter the Buddhas; may I be born with a handsome and upright countenance, and may flowers grow upon my ears."
"By virtue of past merit and vows, I have now obtained this retribution.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s mind was immediately opened and enlightened; he stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, took his leave, and returned to the palace.
The reason for instructing the bhikṣuṇīs well is that bhikṣuṇīs are by nature full of passion.
When people see a bhikṣu who is upright and handsome, with flowers even upon his ears, their hearts still feel love and delight.

Because of these teachings that admonish with affectionate concern, attachment born of suffering is thereby resolved; for this reason, it is said that the skillful admonition and prohibition of the community of bhikṣuṇīs is the foremost.
The reason why the bhikṣu Śivara is called foremost in merit is that when Śivara was first born, he emerged holding a priceless maṇi jewel in his hand; as soon as it fell to the ground, he said:
"Is there anything in this world—gold, silver, or the seven treasures—that can be taken to give in charity?"
"I now wish to practice great giving.
Having spoken these words, his parents and the entire household were struck with great terror and fled, some crying out that he was a rākṣasa demon, while others said it was a celestial deity:
"When a child is born, one must wait until the months and days are complete before speaking thus."
"It is truly strange that he spoke as soon as he hit the ground.
His mother felt this was not so; she went back to look at him and said to her mother, "Do not be afraid."
"I am not a ghost;
I am truly your mother's son.
His father, Candraprabha, said:
"Now we shall take the child to the son of the Nirgranthas to inquire about his fortune.
He then took his wife and the child to the Nirgrantha's dwelling and reported the circumstances to the teacher.
The Master said, "This child lacks merit; later he will bring about calamity.
The elder asked:
"The child has a *maṇi* jewel in his hand; why do you say he has no merit?

The Nirgrantha replied, "When he reaches the age of eight, all the wealth and treasures of your household shall be exhausted and vanish into this child's hands; because of this, everyone shall die of starvation."

The elder was filled with fear and deep anxiety, and being beset by doubt, he heard that there was a great śramaṇa in the world who might perhaps know whether it would be auspicious or inauspicious; he thought, "I shall go to his place and ask whether this is permissible."
He then proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
On the way, he thought again:
"The Great Śramaṇa is of royal lineage; having grown up in the deep seclusion of the palace, he has not pursued learning."
"Brahmins and others, though they have studied extensively since their youth, cannot yet discern auspiciousness or misfortune; how then could a śramaṇa possibly know it?
Thinking thus, he immediately wished to return home.
A deity in the sky addressed the elder, saying:
"You should simply proceed forward.
Why do you turn back?"
"The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, has no knowledge that he does not penetrate; whenever one approaches him, his doubts are surely resolved.
It would not be right to go there hastily.
Having said this, he immediately proceeded to where the Buddha was, and after performing prostrations and inquiries of well-being, he addressed the Buddha:
"Is it not as you have just described—that there is no discerning of good or ill fortune?
The Buddha told the householder:
"It is auspicious; nothing will be unfavorable."
Thus was this son of merit and virtue born.

When this child reaches the age of twenty, he shall go forth to practice the Way; he will always be accompanied by five hundred youths, and he shall attain the state of an Arhat and return to deliver his parents.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had said, the elder was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately returned home.
Having prepared a variety of delicacies, he invited the Buddha to his residence, saying, "I pray that the World-Honored One will bestow a name upon this young child."
The Buddha told the elder:
"If I were to name him 'Heaven,' people would not understand it.
If I were to name him 'Worthy Sage,' ordinary people would not understand it."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, ghosts were called Śīvala; now, their name is correctly Śīvala.
Śīvala means one who interprets the words and sounds of ghosts and spirits.
"For this reason, he was named Śivara.
When Ānanda was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he ordained two disciples:
the first was named Makhādeva, and the second was named Maṅgalyāyana.
Māndhātṛ was a king of the earth; had he not become a seeker of the Way, he would have reigned as king over this Jambudvīpa and the three other continents, and for that reason he was named Māndhātṛ.
Ānanda instructed this disciple:
"Go to the kingdom of Siṃhaladvīpa and cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish there.
The people of that country have relations with rākṣasīs; they require written texts before they will engage in intercourse.
He traded for sixty kinds of books; among these were ghostly scripts known as *ābu* and human scripts known by the sound *āla*.
Moshen received the teachings and traveled there to propagate the Buddha-dharma, and from that time until today, the traces of his teaching have remained extant.
Śivara opens the way for spirits and deities; he is likewise so named because at the time of his birth, mani-jewels spontaneously appeared in both his hands.
He is called Śivara of Great Merit because, at the moment of his birth, mani-jewels naturally emerged from the palms of his two hands.

In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Tathāgata, this bhikṣu was a merchant who went to sea to gather treasures. Having passed through five perils and reached the place of jewels, he obtained a precious gem which he brought back and offered to the Buddha, making a vow that in whatever place he was born, his rewards would be spontaneously attained.
By this cause and condition, his birth was extraordinary, and his value was twenty billion.
At the time of his birth, a natural jewel appeared upon his ear.
His father gathered merchants to inquire about its worth, and the merchants appraised it, saying:
"It is worth twenty billion.
Śivara’s hand-beads were of such immeasurable value that they were said to be "priceless.
The radiance of those jewels extended to seven generations; throughout those seven generations, there was no lack of anything, and thus he was called the foremost in merit and virtue.

At the age of twenty, he left the household life to study the Way. Upon arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, the Buddha commanded him, "Come, well-come," and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
By contemplating the Four Noble Truths, he attained arhatship.
At that time, there were also five hundred youths who had likewise left the household life to follow the Way, constantly attending upon Śivara.
Śivara provided these five hundred people with clothing and food; wherever they went, he made offerings to them without lack, providing for them in every place where they traveled.
Upon reaching the south of the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great, deep mountain. Within the mountains abounded various venomous insects, tigers, wolves, and rākṣasas. He then thought to himself:
"I wish to seek refuge and hide within these mountains for a time."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing his thoughts, immediately constructed five hundred dwellings and a saṃghārāma within the mountains; he provided various offerings for another period of time.
When the summer retreat had concluded, he thought to himself:
"I have been away for a long time; I should now return to pay my respects.
As the weather was extremely hot, he thought of seeking some coolness.
When the Lord of Devas knows this, he immediately sends down clouds and rain;
when there is little thought of drink, he immediately sends down sweet nectar (*amṛta*).
Whatever one desires reaches one according to one's intention; therefore, it is said that his merit and virtue are supreme.
Śivara had an uncle who served as a non-Buddhist brahmin; by nature he was stingy and did not like to practice giving.
At that time, a close friend exhorted him to provide for his future lives, whereupon he immediately invited several thousand brahmins and bestowed upon them one hundred thousand *niṣkas* of gold.
Śivara thought to himself:

"My uncle was stingy and greedy during his life and failed to cultivate merit; even if he were to practice giving and wisdom now, he would not encounter a fertile field of merit. If I do not deliver him, he will remain forever cast aside."
He then went to his house and held out his bowl to beg for food.
His nephew said,
"Why have you come so late?"
"I gave a great almsgiving yesterday.
Those who came yesterday may obtain a saṃghāṭī robe. He said:
"I already have my own *kṣepa* (staff), so I do not need yours.
[The other] asked, "Why have you come? He replied:
"I wish to beg for alms.
At that time, his nephew would not give him anything; he then manifested his body in mid-air and performed the eighteen transformations, with water and fire issuing from his body.
The elder thought to himself:
"This must be out of anger;
perhaps he will burn my house?
He immediately called for the messenger to come down and gave him a seat.
The one seated said,
"I wish to have food. He was immediately given foul, filthy, and repulsive food.
Even if he were to accept it, he would eat it after reciting a prayer of blessing.
As the food entered his bowl, through the power of his merit, it was transformed into nectar.
A deva above sighed in admiration, saying:
“Excellent, householder!
You have indeed performed this great act of giving, an act of merit that none can surpass.
The householder thought to himself:
"Previously, when I gave a hundred thousand measures of gold to the brahmins, none of them praised me; yet now, for giving this small amount of poor food, they praise it as excellent.
Could it be that they are speaking falsely?"
The deva spoke again, saying:
"Although what was given was small, the field of merit is excellent; therefore, it is called a great gift.
The elder thought again:
"The deity must surely be truthful; let him come again to inform me.
He then gave Śivara one hundred thousand pieces of gold. Śivara said:
"I, as a bhikṣu, ought not to accept gold according to the Dharma.
He then went at once to the Buddha to inquire about the reason for this.
The Buddha replied:
"You may take it and distribute it as you wish.
He then accepted this gold and gave it to his fellow students; he preached the Dharma for his uncle, who immediately attained the fruit of the Path (srota-āpanna).
Because he was able to transform foul odors into ambrosia (amṛta), he is called the foremost in merit and virtue.
From birth until nirvana, he has never lacked for anything; at the time of his parinirvana, various kinds of delicious food and drink rain down from his body.
That he is able to do so is because his own body is sufficient, yet he desires to moisten and benefit all sentient beings as well.
For this reason, he is further called the foremost.

As for why the bhikṣu Upasena is called the foremost among those who are fully endowed with all practices: this bhikṣu’s virtuous conduct was sufficient within, and his appearance was dignified without; thus, inner and outer were in harmony, and all whom he encountered were delighted.
Nanda possessed thirty marks and Ānanda twenty; although their manifest marks were numerous, they could not fully embody the dignified deportment of a śramaṇa.

This bhikṣu, though possessing only eleven marks, was complete in his ritual etiquette; he was so perfectly composed that there was nowhere he went where he did not respond appropriately, and among those of old, middle, or young age, there were none who did not rejoice upon seeing him.

What is called "internal sufficiency" refers to the Four Truths and the Eightfold Right Path being truly wondrous; they fill the spiritual treasury so that it is never depleted. Therefore, possessing the dharmas of the various factors of the path is said to be the most supreme.
The reason the bhikṣu Vatsa is said to speak with harmony and joy, never offending others' minds, is that this bhikṣu constantly guards his speech and does not commit the four transgressions.
When a gentleman dwells in the world, an axe is held within his mouth; it is by means of his evil speech that he cuts himself.

This bhikṣu has forever eliminated such coarse and violent words; he always chooses his words and speaks slowly, reflecting before he reveals them. When he utters a word, it must accord with the truth and surely bring joy.
Whether they be elders, those of middle age, or the young, he is able to please them all according to their inclinations.
This is why this bhikṣu is called one who is skilled in speech; for there was a bhikṣu who, though he had already attained arhatship and his outflows were exhausted, still possessed faults of speech.
While crossing the river, as the water gradually became deeper, he uttered these evil words:
"You wretched slave, you breed of lust!
Hearing these foul words, the goddess of the river thought to herself:
"This bhikṣu has uttered such evil words.
Just as they were about to push him into the water, [they thought], "Because of this bhikṣu, we must first consult the Buddha."
He immediately went to question the Buddha:
"There was a bhikṣu who, while crossing the river where the water was somewhat deep, reviled [a woman], saying, 'You wretched slave, you of lecherous stock.
Is it according to the dharma for a bhikṣu to revile others in this way?"
The Buddha immediately dispatched a bhikṣu to summon the bhikṣu who had reviled him.
When the bhikṣu arrived, the Buddha said to him:
"You have become a śramaṇa; why did you revile me?"
The bhikṣu replied, “I did not insult you;
I was merely stating the fact that you are the offspring of a slave woman.
The goddess of the Ganges said:
“Having seen this bhikṣu, have you insulted him again?
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain the beginning and end of this matter:
does an arhat still possess anger?”
"Why did he revile you?
The Buddha said, "An Arhat no longer possesses anger; it was merely because his mouth was accustomed to speaking such words."

This bhikṣu was formerly a brahmin; according to the brahminical tradition, they delight in reviling others, calling them "slaves from the womb. One need not be angry at such insults, for they are merely the result of habitual speech.
"Furthermore, during the five hundred previous lifetimes when I was your husband, I constantly reviled you as a slave girl.
Because this latent consciousness has not been eliminated, I have reviled you once again.
The River Woman said:
"Even though Arhats still possess verbal faults, I do not seek to be an Arhat.
My vow is that in the future, when I seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path, I shall deliver all beings so as to be no different from a Buddha."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "Confess to this woman.
The bhikṣu immediately repented, and the woman also confessed to the bhikṣu; having performed their salutations, they each departed.
If even one whose outflows are exhausted may still utter coarse speech, how much more so must an ordinary person be cautious with their words?
For this reason, it is known that this bhikṣu is foremost in guarding his mouth.

The reason the bhikṣu Mahākātyāyana is called foremost in *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) is that, among his twelve hundred disciples, only this bhikṣu and Rāhula were able to practice *ānāpāna* to the highest degree.
How do we know this?
Formerly, Rāhula was walking with the Buddha, and the Buddha, by means of skillful means (*upāya*), manifested his ankle so that Rāhula could see it.
Having seen it, Rāhula thought to himself:
"This old man, with such an appearance, has abandoned the sovereignty of a Wheel-Turning King to wear the robes of a practitioner and beg for alms;
why is he not ashamed? I can no longer go begging; I shall return home."
"My grandfather, King Jen-ching (Suddhodana), is still alive; how could I possibly undergo such diligent toil?
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in Rāhula’s mind, addressed him, saying:
"Do you know this or not?"
If even heaven and earth are not eternal, how much less can you, a Wheel-Turning Sage King, endure for long?
You should understand that all things are impermanent; that which has form is suffering, and the body is not "mine"—all must perish and cannot remain for long.
Rāhula contemplated the four aspects of impermanence, yet his mind was still not awakened; the Buddha therefore taught him the practice of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
*Ānāpāna* refers to inhalation and exhalation.
He knows when the breath is long and he knows when it is short.
A short breath returns from the heart; a long breath is said to come from the heels.
Furthermore, he knows its coldness and warmth: the inhalation is cold, and the exhalation is warm.

The reason for knowing length, shortness, cold, and warmth is the desire to discern the depth and shallowness of the destination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and by following their entry and exit, to investigate the beginning and end of the breath in order to know the origin of the disease.

If, when the breath enters, one does not know where it comes from, and if, when the breath exits, one does not know where it goes, one understands that there is no coming or going; illness is likewise thus.
Reflecting in this manner, he subsequently attained arhatship.
Mahākātyāyana’s practice of *ānāpāna* was unlike that of Rāhula; he attained mastery over the breaths, such that if he wished, he could cause them to enter or exit through his eyes or ears at will.
Again, he closed his eyes, ears, nose, and mouth, and [the light] then issued forth from nine million pores.
How is it known that it issued from the pores?
This bhikṣu was originally of royal lineage; there were two brothers, and the younger brother was handsome and exquisite.
At that time, the king passed away, and the elder brother was the rightful successor. The younger brother, considering himself superior, secretly hoped for the people to elect him;
however, according to the laws of the country's custom, one may not bypass the order of succession, so they immediately elected the elder brother as king.
The younger brother’s heart was not submissive, and he refused to acknowledge himself as a subject; he requested to leave the country, and the king immediately granted his wish.
He sought out a military force, and the king gave him as many as he desired; he then selected eighty thousand tusker elephants equipped with armor and swords on their trunks.
Having completed the preparations, he thought to himself:
"Which kingdom is the most excellent?
I wish to attack and seize it."
“Vaiśālī is the most excellent among all nations; we should go and attack it to seize it for our own use.
He then led his army toward it.
Just as they reached the halfway point, five hundred merchants returning from gathering treasures encountered them on the road while heading toward Magadha.
He asked a merchant,
"Among the people in the world, are there any whose physical appearance and features surpass mine?
The merchant then laughed.
The king asked,
"Why do you smile? He replied:
"I was merely laughing at myself.
He asked again: "A laugh must surely have a reason."
"Why do you not speak? He replied,
"If Your Majesty does not become angry, I shall then speak."
The king said, "Just speak; I shall never be angry with you.
The merchant said:

"I have heard that there is a prince of the Śākya clan named Siddhārtha, whose body is sixteen feet tall and the color of purple-polished gold, and who possesses the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence."
At that time, when Kātyāyana heard the merchants' words, his heart was filled with fear:
"If Siddhārtha learns that I have come, he will surely raise an army to come and strike me down."
They halted midway and did not dare to proceed further.

At that time, the people of Vaiśālī, hearing that he had raised an army and intended to come and attack them, could find no peace of mind; they immediately went to ask the Buddha, "How may we avert this?"
The Buddha said, "Do not worry.
I shall transform them myself."
That night, the World-Honored One immediately went to manifest his supernatural transformations; sitting cross-legged in mid-air, he shone like a mountain of gold, illuminating the great assembly.
Raising his head, he looked out and said, "Who are these people?"
He replied, "I am the one spoken of by the merchant. He then said:
"The merchant has deceived me!
Previously he did not say he could fly, yet now he is actually flying.
Terrified in his heart and fearing he might be harmed, he joined his palms and asked:
"I do not understand what instructions you have for me here.
The World-Honored One replied, "Do not harbor fear; I shall not harm you."
"I am called a Buddha; I deliver all beings.
Do you wish to hear the wondrous Dharma of ambrosia? He replied:
"I wish to hear it.

The Buddha, observing that his faculties were such that he should attain liberation through *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), immediately taught him the practice of guarding the inhalation and exhalation, so that he might know the length of the breaths as well as their coolness and warmth.
Upon hearing what the Buddha taught, his mind was immediately opened and understood; he attained the stage of Srotāpanna and then left his military followers to seek the life of a renunciant.
The Buddha accepted him, saying: "Welcome, Bhikṣu."
He then became a śramaṇa.

He again contemplated *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) and analyzed the four great elements and the thirty-six impure substances. Soon he attained the sublime state and reached the fruit of *anāsrava* (the outflow-free), and was thus called the foremost among all bhikṣus in *ānāpāna*.

The reason the bhikṣu Udupāna is called foremost among those who reckon the self as impermanent is that this bhikṣu had practiced reverence and diligence in his past lives: when he saw elders, he served them like a father; when he saw those of middle age, he respected them like an elder brother; and toward those younger than himself, he loved them like a younger brother.
Through the ultimate degree of humility and reverence, one receives the retribution of great beauty and majesty.

Having become a bhikṣu and attending upon the Buddha at his side, although one possesses a tall and imposing form, one never relies upon it; one constantly reflects that this body is not the self and has no permanent master. Through the attainment of clear wisdom and the mind’s transcendence of right and wrong, one is able to cast aside the physical form, relinquish arrogance, and take humility as the foremost principle.
How is it known that his physical form was magnificent and grand?
When the Buddha had first attained the Way, he converted the three brothers of Kāśyapa, and there were a thousand bhikṣus.
While traveling through the kingdom of Magadha, he converted King Bimbisāra and was about to return to his native land; he first dispatched Udāyin to inform King Śuddhodana:
"Seven days from now, he shall come to enter this transformation.

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared, leveled and smoothed the roads, swept and sprinkled them, and burned incense to await the Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata was about to pass through Śrāvastī with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, he thought to himself:
"Now my father, the King, will surely come out to welcome me.
It would not be right for one so venerable as he to have to bow his body; I shall instead manifest my supernormal power and travel by ascending into the air."
"It is level with the person's head; he merely wishes for the King to take hold of the Tathāgata’s feet with his own hands.
The reason for this is that although the Buddha is of supreme virtue, he does not wish to cause his parents to bend their bodies."

At that time, the bhikṣu Upavāna was on the right side of the Tathāgata, and the Malla Guhyapada was on the left side of the Tathāgata; the body of the Tathāgata reached exactly to the shoulder of this bhikṣu.
The king asked,
"What kind of people are those on the Buddha's left and right, that they are so tall and large? He replied:
"The one on the right is the bhikṣu Upavāna; the one on the left is the yakṣa spirit Vajrapāṇi.
He further asked, "What kind of people are from this country that they are so exceptionally extraordinary?"
He replied, “He is a man from the kingdom of Magadha. He asked again:
"Is this a body produced by supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), or is it a physical body left behind?
He replied, "This is a physical body left behind by his parents; it is not produced by supernormal power."
The Śākyas thought to themselves:
“The spiritual power of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; he has even caused a rākṣasa, an evil spirit, and a person of great stature to stand at his side.”
For this reason, it should be known that the body of this bhikṣu is elongated.
This bhikṣu attends upon the Buddha at his side, constantly desiring to obstruct and obscure the Tathāgata; thus, the devas, humans, and worldlings regard this as a source of affliction.
The Tathāgata has two kinds of bodies:
first, the Dharma-body; second, the physical body.
This bhikṣu loves only the golden physical body, but does not love the outflow-free Dharma-body.
It is the duty to entrust the Dharma to close disciples, fearing that the Dharma-body might be left deficient for the future.
For these two reasons, the Tathāgata has initiated this discourse, reaching even unto Ānanda.

The reason Kumārajīva Kāśyapa is called "Skilled in Miscellaneous Discourse" is that this bhikṣu constantly expounded the Four Noble Truths for others, interspersing his teachings with hymns of praise and illustrative parables—one verse of praise and one parable for each truth—up to and including all four truths; thus, he is called the foremost in miscellaneous discourse.
*Kumāra* means "child"; *Kāśyapa* is a clan name.
Thus, Kumāra-Kāśyapī refers to a young girl.
How do we know this is so?
Formerly, there was an elder named Śubhadatta who possessed immeasurable wealth.
He had an unmarried daughter who, while staying at home warming herself by a fire, conceived a fetus as the warmth entered her body.
The parents were startled and amazed, questioning her about the circumstances.
The girl answered truthfully:
"I do not know why it is so."
The parents questioned him repeatedly and subjected him to further flogging with canes and whips, yet his words remained unchanged; they finally reported the matter to the king.
The king interrogated him again, but his response was no different, so the king granted him the death penalty.
The woman then voiced her grievance, saying:
"How could there truly be an unrighteous king in this world who would falsely execute the innocent?
If I am not virtuous, you may test me yourself."
"I see that it is indeed as she has said!
The king immediately conducted an investigation according to what the girl had stated, and found no discrepancy or addition.
The king then spoke to her parents:
"I wish to take it. His parents replied,
"Take it as you please."
"What use is this dead woman?
The king then brought her into the palace and cared for her according to the seasons.
When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son who was handsome and exquisite.
As he grew up, he left the household life to study the Way.
Intelligent and widely learned, he attained the path of an Arhat through diligent practice in no long time, and returned to deliver his parents.

At that time, there was a king named Prasenajit who believed in heterodox and inverted views. He did not understand that performing good deeds in this life and future lives brings blessings, while committing evil brings calamity. He claimed that upon death the spirit perishes and is no longer reborn; he did not believe in the Buddha nor recognize Nirvana. He bound his belly with iron plates for fear that wisdom might overflow, and he boasted of his solitary prowess, considering himself peerless.
At that time, the youth Kāśyapa went to his gate; seeing that Kāśyapa’s attire was extraordinary and his gait was composed and dignified, the king immediately engaged him in debate.
The king asked the practitioner:
"The practitioner says:
'Performing good brings merit; committing evil brings calamity.'"
The King said: "Now there was one person in my own family whose goodness was most pure.
When he was on the verge of death, I and several others went together to his side and spoke to that person, saying:"
"According to your conduct, you ought to have been reborn in heaven; if you have indeed ascended there, come back and tell me.
A long time has passed since your death, yet you have not returned to inform me. For this reason, I know that performing good deeds brings no merit.
The practitioner replied to the king:
"Generally, the wise understand through parables.
For example, suppose there were a man who fell into a latrine containing a hundred *śata* of grain."
Someone pulls him out, bathes him, dresses him in fine clothes, perfumes his body with incense, and seats him upon a high couch.
Someone then says to this person:
"Go back and enter the latrine."
"Would this person be willing to enter?
The king replied, "He would not."
The practitioner said:
