"The analogy for those born in the heavens is like this: their bliss in the heavens is such that they indulge in the five desires at will; they take ambrosia as food, which digests of itself without the affliction of excrement or urine; their bodies are fragrant and pure, and their breath is sweetly scented."
Looking down upon the world, it is like a pig dwelling in a latrine; even if they were to come here, they would turn back immediately upon smelling the stench.
Speaking from this perspective, by what means could they possibly communicate with one another?
Through such analogies and dozens of similar instances, the king’s mind was opened and he placed his faith in the Three Jewels.
For this reason, among the Kāśyapa brothers, Aññā-Koṇḍañña is foremost in his ability to engage in diverse forms of debate.
Therefore, can one who calls the Bhikṣu Māndhātṛ shameless for wearing tattered and foul robes be said to practice the eleven dhūtas? Some say: No.
Why is this called the foremost?
A bhikṣu wears a single type of robe and does not change it for the rest of his life.
How do we know this is so?
This bhikṣu was originally a son of the Śākyas; at the time of his birth, there were extraordinary divine portents.
When his mother first became pregnant, she requested a brahmin to perform a divination of his marks.
The Brahmin said,
"This child has the mark of a celestial crown upon his head.
Upon hearing this, his mother was filled with joy, yet she feigned displeasure and thought to herself:
"Furthermore, the celestial crown is the mark of a sovereign; within a single state, there cannot be two kings.
Fearing that the King might harm him, he was therefore unhappy.
As for why she was inwardly joyful: if he were truly a king, he would naturally have protection; why then should she worry about not being saved?
When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son whose head bore the reflection of a celestial crown.
He further requested that a brahmin give him a name, and the brahmin said:
"There is the mark of a king upon his head; as this mark cannot be removed, he shall be named 'King of the Face' (Mukharāja)."
He was thus named Māṇava.
When King Brahmadatta heard this, his heart was filled with sorrow and anxiety, thinking:
"This child possesses the marks of a sovereign; he will surely seize my throne in the future."
"What should I do? He wished to kill him immediately, yet the crime did not merit death;
he wished to leave him alone, yet he feared that the man would surely seize his power.
Looking up and down in anxiety and dejection, he could not find peace within himself.
When the Buddha returned to his home country, the King issued a proclamation to the Śākyas, saying:
"If there are brothers, send one of them to leave the household life to practice the Way and serve as an attendant to the World-Honored One."
"This child is but one individual; he cannot be permitted to leave the household life as part of the company of five hundred men. Because of this, [the King] grew even more sorrowful and distressed.
At that time, Māṇava was ten years old, and he thought to himself:
"Even a Wheel-Turning Sage King is subject to impermanence, yet he still does not equal those Śākyas who have left the household life."
"A human body is difficult to obtain, and an encounter with a Buddha’s era is rare; now that I have encountered a Buddha’s era, it is fitting that I should leave the household life.
He then said to his mother, "I wish to leave the household life and study the Way."
The mother said, "I have only you, my one child; if you abandon me, I shall surely die.
King Māndhātṛ then addressed Bimbisāra:
"I wish to leave the household life;
would Your Majesty please grant me permission? Śuddhodana replied with joy:
"It is indeed possible," said Māṇava. The King replied,
"It is only because I have no one else to whom I may entrust my daughter that I harbor this regret."
The king said, "If you are able to renounce the world, I shall take your mother as my own sister and grant you half the kingdom as a portion.
The prince was filled with joy; he immediately returned home and informed his mother of the situation, and she gave her consent.
At the time of his renunciation, he was clad in a single white cotton cloth and went to where the World-Honored One was, seeking to enter the Path.
The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu."
He immediately became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha had prescribed that bhikṣus possess three robes; this King-of-the-Region bhikṣu simply dyed these white cotton cloths to make his kāṣāya, and did not use any other garments at all.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, your disciple, wish to wear this single robe for the rest of my life.
I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission."
The Buddha then silently consented.
From that time forth, he constantly wore this single robe.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"Among my disciples, there is none who wears more tattered and coarse clothing than the bhikṣu Māṇava.
This, among the eight thoughts of a great man, is that having few desires and being content is foremost.
Regarding why Rāhula is called one who maintains the precepts without violation, some say:
"Rāhula delighted in false speech; how can he be said to maintain the precepts? Others say:
Rāhula did not speak falsely; he was simply angry with the Buddha.
Why was he angry with the Buddha?
Because the Buddha did not become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin).

If he were to become a holy king, he would have eighty-four thousand ministers and eighty-four thousand noble women; for every category—elephants, horses, and carriages—there would be eighty-four thousand.
Having abandoned such a position to become a śramaṇa and wander from east to west begging for alms—is this not shameful?
It is merely out of a desire to calculate the benefit of a sage-king and a resentment toward the Tathāgata that you have uttered these false words.
When people asked Rāhula where the Tathāgata was, although the Tathāgata was actually at the Jeta Grove Monastery, he replied that he was at the Divyāvasa Garden;
and although he was actually at the Divyāvasa Garden, he falsely claimed to be at the Jeta Grove.
He repeatedly spoke falsehoods to deceive those who came to him.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“Rāhula has spoken falsely.”
The Buddha called Rāhula and said,
"Is it true that you have spoken falsely? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
"Rāhula! Why have you spoken a falsehood?"
The reason I have renounced the position of a noble wheel-turning monarch is that such a position cannot be relied upon; all things ultimately revert to impermanence and nothing endures.
Even the status of Śakra or Brahmā cannot be guaranteed, let alone the position of a noble wheel-turning monarch—how could it ever be depended upon?
"Rāhula! I have previously and subsequently renounced things beyond measure and calculation, yet you still harbor resentment.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Rāhula.
"Bring me some water," [the Buddha said].
Rāhula immediately filled his bowl with water and presented it to the Tathāgata.
Taking the bowl of water, the Tathāgata said to Rāhula:
"Do you see this water? He replied, "I have seen it."
The Buddha said:
"This water filling the bowl without any deficiency or decrease is a metaphor for upholding the precepts in their entirety, without any breach or loss.
He then poured out half of it and discarded it, saying to Rāhula:
"Do you see this water? He replied, "I see it."
The Buddha said, "This water has lost half of it; this is a metaphor for the incompleteness of one's precepts.
He then poured out the remaining water until it was gone and showed it to Rāhula, saying:
“Do you see this empty bowl?
He replied, “I have seen it.”
The Buddha said,
"When violations of the precepts are completely exhausted, it is like an empty bowl.
He then turned the bowl over onto the ground and showed it to them, saying:
"Do you see it? He replied, "I see it."
The Buddha said:
"Those who have violated the precepts will all fall into hell;
it is like a bowl turned with its opening facing the ground."
Since Rāhula was personally admonished and instructed, he has never again committed even a hair’s breadth of transgression; therefore, he is called the foremost in observing the precepts. Some say:
"There is yet another matter."
Śāriputra was leading Rāhula into the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
At that time, a brahmin saw Rāhula walking behind him and, giving rise to an evil intent, struck Rāhula on the head; blood flowed, staining his face.
Rāhula immediately conceived an evil thought:
"I must employ skillful means to take revenge upon this enemy.
As for those who call themselves Brahmins, I shall utterly destroy them all and never let them remain."
Śāriputra, already knowing what Rāhula was thinking in his heart, wiped away the blood for him and said to Rāhula:
"You should remember how when your father was formerly King Mandhātṛ, someone came to beg for his eyes; he immediately gouged out his eyes and gave them, feeling no regret."
While sitting in meditation within the garden, even when the king cut off his hands and feet, he felt no regret or lamentation.
When he was an elephant, he gave his tusks to others without ever growing weary or resentful.
"How is it that you have now given rise to such an evil thought?
Upon hearing his teacher's words, Rāhula immediately reproached himself:
"How could I have directed an evil mind toward him?"
He immediately endured it as the earth does, not giving rise to a thought of malice even as much as a hair’s breadth.
At that time, the one who struck Rāhula on the head fell into the Avīci Hell.
By this cause and condition, it is known that Rāhula was foremost in upholding the precepts.
As for why the bhikṣu Pañcaśikha is said to be able to conceal his form and remain invisible: "Pañca" means the Way (mārga).
There were twin infants who were abandoned on the road; someone picked them up, raised them, and brought them to adulthood.
Each of them left the household life to pursue the Way; as no one had given them names, they were immediately named Dao-sheng (Born of the Way), which in the Hu language is *Bāntuó*.
At that time, in the kingdom of Magadha, thunder and violent rain fell frequently, and the five grains failed to ripen.
The king was named Bimbisāra, the grandfather of King Ajātaśatru. He issued a proclamation throughout the four quarters, saying:
"To whoever can ward off a torrential rain, I shall grant great wealth and treasures."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Brahmā who was skilled in incantations; he came forward to offer his services, saying, "I can ward off the rain.
The king immediately granted permission, ordering him to manifest his arts to stop the rain.
At that time, the yin and yang were harmonized and the five grains ripened in great abundance. A brahmin requested from the king a reward for his service in stopping the rain.
Although the king verbally promised it, he ultimately did not repay the favor.
When the ministers and the people saw that the king would not grant it, they each in turn promised him.
The brahmin’s household was impoverished; he requested it from them repeatedly, but as they all refused, he could not obtain it anywhere.
The brahmin became greatly enraged and vowed to become a venomous dragon to destroy people's crops, saying:
"If anyone plants the five grains and their sprouts and stalks grow well, I shall strike them with great thunder and hail to kill them, so that not even roots or stems remain, let alone leaves."
Having made this vow, his life came to an end, and he was immediately reborn among the nāgas, where he was named Leafless (Anapatra).
At that time, when the crops of the people of the kingdom of Magadha had just begun to sprout, the nāga struck them down with hail.
Thus, after several years had passed, the people were so famished and distressed that many died.
The Buddha took pity on them and, wishing to convert this dragon, took Mijie (Guhyaka), Ānanda, and Bantuo (Panthaka) to the kingdom of Kuci, where they went to the place where the dragon resided.
At that time, when the dragon saw the Buddha approaching, an evil thought arose within him, and he said:
"I shall now release hail to kill this śramaṇa.

He immediately rained down mountain rocks; the Buddha turned his gaze to the right toward Guhyapada. Guhyapada, knowing the Buddha’s intention, immediately brandished his vajra-pestle at them, causing a great rocky mountain to fall and block the dragon's abyss.
The dragon became greatly enraged, and fire issued from its eyes.
The Buddha turned his gaze to the right and looked at the bhikṣu Paṭā; the bhikṣu Paṭā immediately understood that the Buddha intended to cause the dragon to be subdued.
Pañcaśikha immediately concealed his form through supernatural power and extinguished the fire from the dragon’s eyes with water.
The dragon again emitted fire from its ears, nose, and mouth, which he likewise extinguished with water.

The bhikṣu further employed his supernormal powers, repeatedly entering and exiting the dragon’s eyes, ears, nose, and mouth without the dragon seeing him; he remained invisible within while manifesting his hand outside.
Upon seeing this transformation, the dragon immediately submitted in his heart.
The Buddha again walked back and forth in *caṅkrama* with the three men; there were traces of four people upon the stone, yet only those of three appeared.
The dragon then asked the Buddha,
"Where is that one person?
The Buddha replied:
"This is the footprint of your teacher.
He asked again,
"What is the name of your teacher?"
"Why do you not manifest now?
He replied, "His name is Paṭā."
The Buddha wished for him to appear from afar; knowing the Buddha’s intention, he manifested his form at a distance of a hundred paces.
Seeing him from afar, the dragon was filled with joy and paid homage. The Buddha then conferred upon him the Eight Precepts of the Upavāsa fast.
From that time forward, the winds and rains were harmonious and well-ordered, the five grains ripened in abundance, and the people lived in peace.
By these causes and conditions, it was known that Paṭā was foremost in the art of concealing her form.
As for why it is said that Jūlibānta could transform his physical form and perform various metamorphoses: "Jūli" means extreme darkness. This bhikṣu’s faculties were dull and sluggish;
when the Buddha taught him to recite the word "broom," whenever he grasped "broom" he forgot "sweep," and whenever he grasped "sweep" he forgot "broom."
For six years he devoted himself single-mindedly to reciting this; his mind subsequently attained awakening, and he reflected to himself:
"The broom is for sweeping, and sweeping is for clearing away.
The broom is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path, while the filth is the defilement of the three poisons."
"By using the broom of the Eightfold Noble Path, one sweeps away the defilements of the three poisons; is this not precisely what is meant by the meaning of 'sweeping'?
Upon contemplating this principle deeply, his mind was immediately opened and liberated, and he attained the path of Arhatship.
What is called "transforming the physical form" refers to transforming the forms of the five aggregates through the sublime wisdom of the Four Noble Truths.
There is indeed this transformation, but there is yet another.
It is said that there was a Brahmin named Brahmā, also known as the World Scripture.

As for why it is called a "worldly classic" (shidian): because it extensively surveys a multitude of texts and is thoroughly proficient in all matters—whether they be secret charts, prophetic records, celestial phenomena, or terrestrial geography—it is therefore named a worldly classic.
Proud of his own superior virtue, he went forth to challenge his opponents, asking: "Who is able to debate with me?
He heard that among the Śākya bhikṣus, the least esteemed was Cūḍapanthaka, and among the upāsakas, the least esteemed was Ghaṭīkāra.
"I shall debate with these two men.
He then came and debated with Pāṭa, saying to him:
"Can you debate with me? Paṭā said, "I could even debate with your grandfather, Brahmā; how much more so with you, a blind man without eyes?"
The brahmin immediately challenged him, saying:
"What difference is there between being blind and having no eyes?
Paṭācara remained silent and did not answer, reflecting in his mind:
"I shall not respond with words, but shall answer you with my supernormal power (ṛddhi).
He then flew up into the air by means of his supernormal power, four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground, and sat down cross-legged (*paryaṅka*).
The brahmin looked up and beheld this divine manifestation; a feeling of reverence arose within him, and he hoped for a pure response.

At that time, Śāriputra was walking in meditation at Jetavana; with his divine ear, he heard the brahmin’s discourse with Paṭṭa and knew that the brahmin’s words were exhausted, so he manifested a miraculous sign in response.
"If I do not go, the bhikṣus will suffer humiliation and the brahmins will not attain deliverance.
He then employed his supernormal powers to manifest in the form of Pañcaśikha, causing Pañcaśikha’s original form to disappear.
The transformed being asked the brahmin, "Are you a deva or a human? He replied:
"This person. He asked again: "Is this person a man?"
He replied, “It is a man. He asked again:
"What difference is there between a man and others?
He replied, "There is no difference."
He asked again:
"The term 'person' (pudgala) is a general designation;
'man' is used in reference to physical form."
How can they not be different?
What was said previously regarding the "blind" refers to those who do not see the retribution of good and evil in this world and the next;
the "sightless" refers to those who lack the eye of wisdom to sever the fetters and latent tendencies.
The brahmin’s mind was liberated, and he immediately attained the pure Dharma-eye.
By this cause and condition, it is known that Jūlibānta was foremost in transforming his appearance.
Regarding why the Bhikṣu Śreṇika is called a noble king, a wealthy and high-born member of the celestial lineage, and one who is gentle: generally, there are four types of lineages.
They are kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and householders.
As for why they are called "noble," it is because, having become śramaṇas, they share the same Śākya clan; for this reason, they are termed noble.

It is like the waters of the four Ganges rivers—the Ox-mouth, Lion-mouth, Horse-mouth, and Elephant-mouth—each having five hundred branches, which together enter the great ocean and become a single body of water, possessing no variety of tastes.
Therefore, the ocean earns its title as "Great" and attains a status more noble than the hundred rivers.
It is the same with the Śākya clan; thus, they are called the foremost among the noble and illustrious.
King Śuddhodana had three younger brothers. The youngest brother was named Amitodana, who had a young son four years of age.
At that time, King Śuddhodana was seated upon the main throne, assembled with his various ministers.
The king thought to himself:
"If my son had not left the household life, I would surely have become a Wheel-Turning Sage-King."
"My son, having been born, was destined to be a noble wheel-turning monarch; yet he has now gone forth into homelessness. Of what use is this celestial crown to me?
He then removed the celestial crown and placed it on the ground, and whatever needed to be done, he did.
The ministers were despondent, each lacking any sense of joy.

At that time, the young son of the Śākya king was wandering ahead when he saw a celestial crown upon the ground; he immediately picked it up, placed it on his head, sat down, rested his left hand upon his shoulder, and stroked his beard and mustache with his right hand.
The king and his ministers were astonished by the reason for this.
The king said, "It is Heaven that has caused this child to be so; perhaps he will become a holy king."
"The marks of a noble wheel-turning monarch are all present in this child; that is precisely why it is so.
All the ministers agreed, saying, "It may indeed be as the King has said."
The King thought to himself:
"Since Siddhārtha has already left the household life,
and seeing furthermore the signs of a child, I shall now abdicate the royal throne."

After eight years had passed, he heard that Siddhārtha had attained Buddhahood and had converted the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their disciples, totaling one thousand bhikṣus, as well as the disciples of Upatiṣya and Kolita, numbering two hundred and fifty; thus, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus in all. They were returning from the kingdom of Magadha to Śrāvastī, and [Bimbisāra] first dispatched Udāyin to announce the news of their return.

Upon hearing this, King Jinjing was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately donned his celestial crown, leveled the roads, swept and sprinkled them, and burned incense to await the Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata arrived, the king beheld the bhikṣus, whose hearts were indeed refined, yet whose outward appearances were unassuming.
"Five hundred Śākyas of handsome appearance shall be selected to renounce the world and serve as attendants to the World-Honored One.
Among them, the Śākya king Bhikṣu was the very first.
At that time, while the Buddha was among the great assembly in the vihāra, he addressed the bhikṣus, extensively discussing the reasons why certain lineages are noble and eminent.
At that moment, King Śuddhodana arrived among the assembly and paid homage to the bhikṣu Śākyarāja.
The entire assembly marveled at the reason for this.
Knowing their thoughts and wishing to resolve their doubts, the Buddha asked the king:
"Why do you pay homage to this bhikṣu?"
He replied: "The reason for my prostration is that this bhikṣu excels me in two matters.
Now, there are three kinds of heavens: "
On the first day there was the *uddhagga* heaven; on the second day, the *jāta* heaven; on the third day, the *visuddha* heaven.
I indeed had the *uddhagga* heaven, while this bhikkhu had the *jāta* heaven and the *visuddha* heaven.
The reason it is said that he was born in heaven is that when he was four years old, he took my celestial crown and placed it upon his own head.
Spontaneously, the thought arose within him; there was no one who gave it to him. Therefore, it is called "being born in heaven."
As for the Pure Heavens (Śuddhāvāsa-devas), their outflows have now been exhausted and their fetters untied; being free from further defilement, they are called the Pure Heavens.
Because these two matters surpass my own, I pay them homage.
For these reasons, it is known that the bhikṣu Śreṇika was foremost among the noble clans.
